docs.title: Scope of this guide
docs.text: This guide is for CiviCRM users. It covers the functionality available through CiviCRM's web-based interface.

docs.title: User Guide and System Administrator Guide
docs.text:
The System Administrator Guide covers installation, upgrades, and some of the more complicated setup tasks.

The guides overlap on some setup and configuration topics. In general, the User Guide covers actions users can perform within CiviCRM's user interface. The System Administrator Guide covers actions that require work outside that interface, such as file-system or shell access.

docs.title: How to search the entire documentation
docs.text: To use this documentation within the CiviCRM Dashboard, you can use the docbot-extension. See installing an extension for installation instructions. The extension provides a dashboard widget for quickly searching the CiviCRM documentation.

docs.title: Editing this guide
docs.text:
• This guide is made with MkDocs and stored in a GitLab repository.
  • For simple editing instructions, see contributing to this guide.
  • For a more in-depth editing tutorial, see writing documentation in the Developer Guide.

docs.text:

docs.title: Free software?
docs.text:
CiviCRM is Free Software - this means it is developed by a community and licensed in a generous way so you can use it for free for whatever you want.

Free Software (sometimes also referred to as Free and Open Source Software, FLOSS, FOSS, Software Libre, or Open Source is software that anyone can download, share, and -- significantly -- change in any way they want. Practically speaking, you might never want to change the software, or even have a staff person who can read the source code (the instructions written by programmers). But the ability to change the software protects you in many ways:

  • CiviCRM will not go away, unlike non-free software from some companies that gets abandoned if the company goes bankrupt or decides to discontinue a specific product.
  • The software can be used and customised free of charge.
  • Nobody can suddenly take away features or change the terms under which you are allowed to use the software and its features.
  • If an organisation wants a feature that CiviCRM doesn't provide, the organisation can hire someone to create it. Of course, the organisation can also submit a feature request to the CiviCRM team as with any software product.
  • Similarly, anyone can fix a bug (error in the software) if they have the skills to do so. Because the source code is available, clients can also find bugs more easily.
  • Members of the community have much more input into how CiviCRM develops than is traditionally available via closed source/commercial software, because they can understand the product by reading the code and can make changes. Furthermore, many people can try different implementations of features and the community can decide by vote or consensus which one to make official.

That may be enough for you, but for the sake of completeness we'll offer some widely used definitions:

"Free software or software libre is software that can be used, studied, and modified without restriction, and which can be copied and redistributed in modified or unmodified form either without restriction, or with minimal restrictions only to ensure that further recipients can also do these things and that manufacturers of consumer-facing hardware allow user modifications to their hardware. Free software is available gratis (free of charge) in most cases."* (from: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_software)*

"Open source software (OSS) is defined as computer software for which the source code and certain other rights normally reserved for copyright holders are provided under a software license that meets the Open Source Definition or that is in the public domain. This permits users to use, change, and improve the software, and to redistribute it in modified or unmodified forms. It is very often developed in a public, collaborative manner." (from: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_source_software)

Nearly any software that qualifies as free also qualifies as Open Source, and vice versa. The main reason that two different terms exist is that "free software" emphasizes the freedom aspect (that you aren't under the control of the original programmers) whereas "open source software" emphasizes the convenience and potential for innovation provided by having the source code available.

When you install and use CiviCRM, you'll notice there is no annoying click-through software license imposing a thousand things that you can or cannot do with it. That's because free software doesn't limit your right to do with the software whatever you want. Free and open source software have licenses, but they're simpler than and quite different from proprietary software ('closed software') licenses. CiviCRM itself is available under Affero General Public License version 3.0, one of the popular free software licenses used by many other projects.

docs.title: Free software and non-profits
docs.text:
Explaining all of the possible considerations on using FOSS in non-profit and advocacy work might take a really long time, so let's focus on the most important highlights:

  • One of the priorities of FOSS projects, including CiviCRM, is to involve the community of users in the process of designing and building the software. In the long run, this not only assures that the software is doing exactly what it should do to sustain the needs of its users, but it also allows indirect exchange of knowledge and experience between organisations. By using CiviCRM, you are basically taking advantage of other non-profit and advocacy practitioners' experience.
  • Having access to the source code gives you and your organisation a certain level of independence. With proprietary software it is usually impossible to customise the tools to meet your specific needs. With FOSS, you can hire a developer or consultant and work with them on providing specific functionality needed in your work. Additionally, if you contribute your improvements to the project community other organisations will probably start using them. It means you can receive testing and further improvements of your functionality for free.
  • When a company which provided you with closed software goes out of business, the usual procedure for an organisation reliant on that software is to abandon the software and start investing in a new one (which is resource intensive and costly). It's less likely to happen with Free and Open Source Software - there is always a community of users and developers around it and there is no single "point of failure." With FOSS projects, if the main organisation behind a specific piece of software shuts down or changes their focus, the community takes over, a new organisation is formed and the software development and support continues.

Apart from the practical advantages listed above, there is also a more philosophical approach to answering the question of importance of FOSS for non-profits and advocacy organisations. Without getting too deep into philosophical discussions, there is a great overlap between values shared by non-profit organisations and those shared by Free and Open Source Software communities. By working with the community of users, providing your feedback, contributing your changes back into the project, you are actually strengthening the non-profit sector.

docs.title: Accidental Techie
docs.text: Someone who has inherited the role of IT technical support but whose primary role may be something else; often has little or no formal IT training (which is not always a bad thing!).

docs.title: Accordion
docs.text: A javascript-based effect on a web page that allows additional content to be revealed or hidden (often referred to as collapsed or uncollapsed) without the user leaving the web page.

docs.title: ACL (Access Control List)
docs.text: ACLs define permissions for a group of contacts to perform an operation (e.g. edit, view, delete) on a set of data or a type of record. For example, you could set up a group called "Administrators" that allows people to view and edit all contact records, and a group called "Volunteers" that can view contact records but not edit them.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text: An activity in CiviCRM is a record of any scheduled or completed interaction with one or more contacts. Examples include meetings, phone calls, emails, event attendances and contributions. You can define additional types of activities as needed.

docs.title: Admin / Administrator
docs.text: The person or persons that maintain a server or web-based software like CiviCRM. Administration includes maintenance, configuration, backup, security, creating and deleting user accounts and so on.

docs.title: AGM (Annual General Meeting)
docs.text: An AGM is a meeting held every year by an organisation to inform its members of previous and future activities. Certain types of organisations are required by law to hold an AGM.

docs.title: AGPL (Affero General Public License)
docs.text: A license for open source software. CiviCRM uses the AGPL version 3.0 license, which gives you the right to do with the software as you like and guarantees that the source code will always protect your rights in this way.

docs.title: Alpha Version
docs.text: A software version that contains very new source code with new functionality and bug fixes. An alpha version is released for testing purposes, and for people who want to follow its development, but it is not considered to be anywhere near ready for general release or use.

docs.title: Apache
docs.text: The most popular web server software. Apache is free and open source (see also FLOSS).

docs.title: API (Application Programming Interface)
docs.text: An interface employed by a software application to enable interaction between itself and other software.

docs.title: Backup
docs.text: Protecting your data by regularly making copies and storing them independently of the original files so they can be restored if necessary.

docs.title: Bandwidth
docs.text: The speed at which you can transfer information through a network or internet connection. If a connection can transfer a lot of information it is said to be "high bandwidth" or "high speed."

docs.title: Beta Version
docs.text: A software version that is in good condition but still needs testing to make sure it functions as intended before general release. Testing beta versions is a helpful way to participate in the CiviCRM community.

docs.title: Blog
docs.text: Short for web-log. A website which is regularly updated with news and views from one or more individuals.

docs.title: Bug
docs.text: An error that prevents software from behaving as the user would expect.

docs.title: Bug Reporting / Bug Fixing
docs.text: The process of reporting bugs to the software developer(s), and then fixing the bugs so the software operates as intended.

docs.title: Bug Tracker
docs.text: An official repository for recording bugs. The CiviCRM bug trackers can be found here: https://lab.civicrm.org/ with the main core tracker at https://lab.civicrm.org/dev/core/issues

docs.title: Cache
docs.text:
A recent copy of frequently used data that can be quickly and easily accessed. This is especially useful if the data is complicated or takes a large effort to generate. The disadvantage of caching is that data can become out of date, but this normally isn't a problem. Even caching data for 5 minutes might be useful in certain circumstances. If a page is accessed 1,000 times in 5 minutes, having a cached version means the data will only need to be generated once.

A web cache holds copies of recently visited web page files. Sometimes a user may need to clear their web cache in order to see updated information on a web page.

docs.title: Canvassing
docs.text: Is the systematic initiation of direct contact with a target group of individuals commonly used during political campaigns. A campaign team (and during elections a candidate) will knock on doors of private residences within a particular geographic area, engaging in face-to-face personal interaction with voters. Canvassing may also be performed by telephone, where it is referred to as telephone canvassing.

docs.title: Captcha
docs.text: A spam prevention tool. See reCaptcha.

docs.title: CiviCase
docs.text: The case management component of CiviCRM. CiviCase provides service organisations with tools for structuring, scheduling and recording case activities.

docs.title: CiviContribute
docs.text: CiviContribute is an online fundraising and donor management component which enables you to track and manage contributions to your organisation.

docs.title: CiviCRM
docs.text: What this whole manual is about! CiviCRM is web-based, open source software that allows you to record and manage information about your various constituents including volunteers, activists, donors, employees, clients, vendors, etc.

docs.title: CiviDog
docs.text: See Scout.

docs.title: CiviEngage
docs.text: CiviEngage was a Drupal module that enhances CiviCRM's core functions for non-profits focused on community organizing groups and civic engagement work. CiviEngage is now deprecated.

docs.title: CiviEvent
docs.text: CiviEvent provides integrated online event registration and management for paid and free events.

docs.title: CiviMail
docs.text: CiviMail is a mass-mailing component which allows you to engage constituents with personalised email blasts and newsletters.

docs.title: CiviPledge
docs.text: CiviPledge is a component that allows the flexibility to create various types of fundraisers. Allows to individuals to donate daily, weekly, monthly or yearly.

docs.title: Client
docs.text:
A term used sometimes instead of constituent or contact, more often in a context involving a financial transaction.

Client is also a term for a system (computer) or application that accesses a remote computer such as a web server to receive information; examples include a personal computer that is connected to the internet, or an email application that downloads email from a server.

docs.title: Closed Software
docs.text: Software that does not allow users to access its source code, as opposed to open source software. See also proprietary software.

docs.title: CMS (Content Management System)
docs.text: An application used to create, edit, manage, search and publish various kinds of digital content (text and other media such as images and videos). Web-based CMS allow organisations to add and manage content on their website without requiring advanced technical skills. Every instance of CiviCRM must be integrated with a CMS (currently WordPress, Drupal, Backdrop or Joomla!) which helps to facilitate client interaction.

docs.title: Component
docs.text: Components are a particular type of Extension in CiviCRM which provide major chunks of core functionality. Examples include CiviEvent or CiviCase. See also Extension.

docs.title: Community Advisory Group
docs.text: A representative group of people from the CiviCRM community who work with the CiviCRM team on project development.

docs.title: Cookie
docs.text: A file stored on your computer and used by a website to identify you on return visits. Some websites cannot be accessed unless you allow your computer to accept and store cookies.

docs.title: Constituent
docs.text: A constituency is usually defined as a group of people bound by shared identity, goals, or loyalty. In CiviCRM, "constituents" is used to a describe all supporters, current or potential, of a given organisation. See also contact and client.

docs.title: Contact
docs.text: In CiviCRM a contact is either an individual, an organisation or a household about whom information is stored in the database. See also constituent and client.

docs.title: Contact Summary Screen
docs.text: A page that displays at a glance all the data about an individual, organisation or household that is stored in the CiviCRM database.

docs.title: Core Code
docs.text: The source code that constitutes the official code of CiviCRM. Also called core.

docs.title: Core Data Field
docs.text: A field that is included in a record structure "out-of-the-box". For example, the CiviCRM contact record includes First Name as a core field.

docs.title: Core Team
docs.text: The people most closely involved with CiviCRM development.

docs.title: CRM
docs.text: Acronym for Contact (or Constituent, Customer or Client) Relationship Management. CRM (or eCRM) software was originally developed from a sales perspective, to help companies track and organise their interactions with current and potential customers. CiviCRM is oriented specifically toward the needs of non-profits, advocacy and non-governmental organisations, so the term "customer" is replaced with "constituent". Outside the USA it is often referred to as Contact Relationship Management.

docs.title: Cron
docs.text: Cron is the time-based job scheduler in Unix-like computer operating systems. Cron enables users to schedule jobs (commands or shell scripts) to run periodically at certain times or dates. It is commonly used to automate system maintenance or administration. Cron is used to in CiviCRM to trigger specific tasks, such as sending membership renewal reminders or processing ongoing payments, or to run all jobs enabled under the Scheduled Jobs page at their configured frequency.

docs.title: CRUD
docs.text: Create, Read, Update and Delete: the basic functions performed on databases.

docs.title: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets)
docs.text: A way to control the style of a website by defining design and layout elements in a single file which is linked to all files in a website and applies the style across the site. An element, such as the formatting of a heading or a background colour, can be changed once in the CSS file to effect a change on all pages of the site.

docs.title: CSV (Comma Separated Values)
docs.text: A simple format for a spreadsheet. CSV files are text files where each cell is separated by a comma, and each row is separated with a return. This very simple format is understandable by many different programmes.

docs.title: Custom Data Field
docs.text: A field that is added to the data structure of a CiviCRM record by your organisation. Custom data fields extend the information that can be stored in that type of record. For example, your organisation might need a custom field to record each contacts' professional qualifications, or the food preferences of event participants.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text: A user's homepage, which displays when the user logs in to CiviCRM and which can be personalised with dashlets.

docs.title: Dashlet
docs.text: A report on some data in the CiviCRM database, configured to appear on a user's dashboard. For example, monthly figures in graph and/or numerical form, appointments for the day, or a list of new memberships.

docs.title: Data Centralisation
docs.text: Storing all your data in one place.

docs.title: Database
docs.text: Is a collection of information that is organized so that it can easily be accessed, managed, and updated. In one view, databases can be classified according to types of content: bibliographic, full-text, numeric, and images.

docs.title: Demo Site
docs.text: A website that allows you to test and explore the functionality of a piece of software. CiviCRM maintains three demos sites: one integrated with Drupal, one integrated with Joomla! and one integrated with WordPress.

docs.title: Dedupe
docs.text: Refers to the task of finding and merging multiple entries for one contact.

docs.title: Developer
docs.text: Someone who develops software.

docs.title: Domain
docs.text: See DNS.

docs.title: Donor
docs.text: Someone who makes a donation, i.e. voluntarily gives money to an organisation.

docs.title: DNS (Domain Name System)
docs.text: The Domain Name System (DNS) converts domain names, which are made up of easy-to-remember combinations of letters (example.com), to IP addresses (123.456.123.234) which are hard-to-remember strings of numbers. Every computer on the internet has an unique address (a little bit like an area code + telephone number).

docs.title: Drupal
docs.text: An open source CMS that integrates with CiviCRM to provide a user-interface and additional website functionality (http://drupal.org).

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text: A way of disguising data when it is being transferred from one computer to another so that it is unreadable by any other computer that it may pass through on the way.

docs.title: Environment
docs.text: The specific hardware and operating system on which you are running your software.

docs.title: Event Listing Feed
docs.text: A RSS feed containing the list of events defined in CiviEvent.

docs.title: Extension
docs.text: A package of functionality for CiviCRM that can be installed, enabled, disabled or uninstalled on a particular site to provide for particular use cases.

docs.title: Firefox
docs.text: A popular free and open source web browser, developed by the Mozilla Foundation (http://www.mozilla.org)

docs.title: FLOSS (Free/Libre Open Source Software)
docs.text: Software that is licensed so as to guarantee the essential freedoms of users to its source code and reuse. A combination of "free software" and "open source software", with "libre" added in to emphasise that software freedom is essentially a matter of rights, not price.

docs.title: FOSS
docs.text: Free and Open Source Software - see FLOSS.

docs.title: Forum
docs.text: A web-based online discussion tool (see http://forum.civicrm.org/).

docs.title: Free Software
docs.text: Software that is licensed so that you can use and distribute it without restriction. CiviCRM is free software. See also FLOSS.

docs.title: FTP (File Transfer Protocol)
docs.text: The FTP protocol is used for file transfers from one computer to another over the internet. Many people use it for downloads, and it can also be used to upload files to web servers. A popular free and open source FTP client for Windows is FileZilla. There are also web-based FTP clients that you can use with a normal web browser like Firefox.

docs.title: Functionality
docs.text: The set of tasks that a piece of software can perform.

docs.title: Geocoding
docs.text: The process of finding associated geographic coordinates (often expressed as latitude and longitude) from other geographic data, such as street addresses, or zip codes (postal codes).

docs.title: GUI (Graphical User Interface)
docs.text: User interface offering windows, icons, mouse control, multiple fonts, and so on - the normal way for non-programmers to communicate with their computers. The alternative to a GUI is a command line interface with text only.

docs.title: Hook
docs.text: Hooks are a common way to extend systems and a powerful way to extend CiviCRM's functionality, incorporate additional business logic, and even integrate CiviCRM with external systems.

docs.title: Household
docs.text: Is a family or group of people who share a physical location.

docs.title: Hosting Service
docs.text: A service (usually commercial) that provides server space for your website. Hosting services also can provide physical space to put your own server in so that it is connected to the internet.

docs.title: ICT
docs.text: Acronym for Information and Communication Technology.

docs.title: Internationalisation: i18n
docs.text: The process of making software ready for adoption in different countries and different cultures, without the need to modify it technically. This is done by the developer (software engineer) when writing the software. See also Localisation.

docs.title: Internet Service Provider (ISP)
docs.text: A business that provides services such as internet access, email and website hosting.

docs.title: Intranet
docs.text: A network of computers that are connected within a home or office but not accessible from outside the local network.

docs.title: IT
docs.text: Acronym for Information Technology.

docs.title: JavaSacript
docs.text: A scripting language primarily used in web pages to display dynamic content.

docs.title: Joomla!
docs.text: A CMS that can integrate with CiviCRM to provide a user interface and additional website functionality (http://www.joomla.org).

docs.title: LAMP
docs.text: Is an acronym for a solution stack of free, open source software, originally coined from the first letters of Linux (operating system), Apache HTTP Server, MySQL (database software) andPerl/PHP/Python, principal components to build a viable general purpose web server.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text: A type of operating system (other common operating systems are Windows and Mac OS). Linux has been popular as a web server for a long time and is now gaining popularity on personal laptops and desktop computers. Linux is free software and open source.

docs.title: Local Computer
docs.text: A computer that runs CiviCRM but is not publicly available via the internet. This could be your personal or home computer, or it can be in your office. It can also be called a client computer in the context of receiving information from a server

docs.title: Localisation: L10n
docs.text: The process of translating a product into different languages or adapting a language for a specific country or region. This is done by translators with no need for technical wizardry.

docs.title: Mail Server
docs.text: A computer that transfers email from one computer to another.

docs.title: Mapping Provider
docs.text: A service provider that allows displaying contact locations on maps - Google Maps or Yahoo Maps in CiviCRM.

docs.title: Module
docs.text: Sometimes used in place of extension.

docs.title: MySQL
docs.text: A popular database engine. CiviCRM uses MySQL to hold its data. MySQL is free software. (http://mysql.com)

docs.title: NGO (Non-Governmental Organisation)
docs.text: A legally constituted non-business organisation with no participation or representation from government. In the United States, this type of organisation is more often referred to as a Non-profit. They may be also called civil society organisations or not-for-profits.

docs.title: Non-Profit
docs.text: See NGO

docs.title: Online Contribution Page
docs.text: A function of CiviCRM which allows the creation of a page on the website where visitors can make online donations using credit cards.

docs.title: Open ID
docs.text: A convenient free system to use a single digital identity across the internet.

docs.title: Open Source Software
docs.text: Software with source code that is publicly available, as opposed to proprietary software; see also FLOSS. Open source software is based on the philosophy that sharing and collaborating on code leads to better software and greater benefit for everyone.

docs.title: Payment Instrument
docs.text: Medium or method that is used for online payments.

docs.title: Payment Processor
docs.text: A company (usually a third party) appointed by a merchant to handle credit card transactions for merchant banks. A payment processor is required to handle online transactions through a system such as CiviCRM.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: Allow you to limit access for different users to different parts of the system.

docs.title: Personal Campaign Pages
docs.text: A feature of CiviCRM that can be enable to allow constituents to create their own fundraising pages.

docs.title: PHP
docs.text: The programming language in which the majority of CiviCRM is written.

docs.title: Ping
docs.text: Sending and receiving small amounts of data to and from a server; often used to measure the response time across the network.

docs.title: Point Person
docs.text: Someone given the responsibility to keep their eye on a certain issue.

docs.title: PhoneBank List
docs.text: A list created using CiviReport to make it easy for volunteers to call constituents en masse. This is often done to invite them to vote, request that they volunteer, take action, or donate.

docs.title: Premium
docs.text: A gift that can be offered to contributor in exchange for donation. CiviCRM allows offering premiums as a part of the donation gathering process.

docs.title: Price Sets
docs.text: A way of storing and re-using complicated price structures for events. For example, you can charge for different elements of an event.

docs.title: Primary Location
docs.text: The information that a constitutent wants to be used as their main point of contact for mailings etc.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text: A set of fields used for collecting, modifying, and sharing data. See Profles for more information.

docs.title: Proprietary software
docs.text: Also called closed software or closed source software. Software licensed so that you cannot access the source code and modify it without first coming to an agreement with the authors. See also open source software.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text: An agreed-upon method of doing something. HTTP and SMTP are two examples, one being an agreement on how to transfer website data across the web, the other an agreement on how email will be transferred across the web.

docs.title: Radio Button
docs.text: An element of a web-based application user interface that allows the user to choose only one of a predefined set of options. Usually indicated by a white circle that can be filled with a click.

docs.title: reCAPTCHA
docs.text: A common tool for testing whether a user is a human or a computer, used to prevent spam.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: The things that you require a particular software application to do.

docs.title: Rich Text Editor
docs.text: A text editor that allows you to add formatting, such as bold, italic and underline, to text (as opposed to just plain text).

docs.title: Root Domain
docs.text: The 'raw' URL of a website without 'www' or any other subdomain. For example, http://civicrm.org/ is the root domain while http://www.civicrm.org/ is not.

docs.title: RSS (Really Simple Syndication) Feed
docs.text: RSS feeds are a way to publish frequently updated information, either for inclusion on a website or to be read by an RSS reader.

docs.title: RSVP
docs.text: "Répondez s'il vous plaît", a French phrase that translates to "please respond". Commonly used to request confirmation (or declining) of attendance at an event.

docs.title: Script
docs.text: A script is a short programme that does one specific task. Many web pages include scripts to manage user interaction, so that the server does not have to send a new page for each change.

docs.title: Scout
docs.text: The CiviCRM Book Sprint official dog. Scout likes dog biscuits, rolling on the ground, eating snow and proof-reading.

docs.title: Sendmail
docs.text: Sendmail is one of the most popular mail transfer agents (MTA) used for handling email on a server. Sendmail is free and open source software.

docs.title: Server
docs.text:
1. Software that "serves" content to a client. See Apache, or Mail Server for two examples.
  2. A computer that is used primarily to serve content. Any computer can be set up this way, but the term traditionally refers to those that deliver web content. See also client computer.

docs.title: Shared Hosting
docs.text: A website hosting service, where multiple websites reside on single server.

docs.title: Smart Group
docs.text: A group in CiviCRM to which contacts are automatically assigned. Smart groups are created by running and then saving a search. They are useful for groups that might change frequently, for example "donations over $1000 in the last month".

docs.title: SMTP
docs.text: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol. A standard or protocol used by email software to transfer (send) email.

docs.title: Soft Credit
docs.text: Allows you to credit a contact for a donation made by someone, for example the person who inspired the actual donor to make a donation. See Personal Campaign Pages.

docs.title: Software
docs.text: Applications (also called programs or programmes) that enable specific functionality on your computer. There are many broad categories of software such as web browsers, word processors and email clients. Within each category there are many available softwares that perform the functions you require. For example, Firefox and Internet Explorer are two commonly-used web browsers.

docs.title: Software License
docs.text: The terms you must accept before using a piece of software.

docs.title: Source Code
docs.text: Software is created by writing instructions that a computer understands. These lines of instructions are known as code or source code.

docs.title: SSL (Secure Sockets Layer)
docs.text: One way of making internet communication secure. You can easily see if you are using SSL by looking at the URL in your browser: if it starts with https instead of http, your connection is using SSL.

docs.title: SSL Certificate
docs.text: Provided by the server to prove its identity, in the same way that a person carries a passport or driving license. See also SSL (Secure Sockets Layer).

docs.title: Stable Version
docs.text: A version of software that has been tested and is considered to be ready for general use.

docs.title: Token
docs.text: Tokens are used in CiviCRM to insert elements such as a contact's name or a standard greeting into emails being sent from the system. In an email sent to a group of people, the token {first.name} will be replaced with actual name of each message recipient, in the email that each individual receives.

docs.title: Upgrade
docs.text: The process of replacing software with a newer version of the same software. An upgrade may fix bugs, improve security, enable the software to continue to work with upgraded operating systems, or provide new features and other enhancements.

docs.title: URL
docs.text: Acronym for Unique Resource Locator, sometimes referred to as a Universal Resource Indicator, or URI. The technical convention that identifies the location of a resource on a network. The resource might be a web page, in which case the URL refers to the location of that web page on the internet, for example www.civicrm.org is the URL for CiviCRM.

docs.title: Use Case
docs.text: Use case is a central concept in software development. A use case is a story or scenario that documents the experience of performing a specific task with the application. Generally, a use case should avoid technical or database-specific language, such as 'fields' or 'record', and concentrate on real world objects and scenarios in order to communicate the idea clearly to people who may not be familiar with technical terms.

docs.title: Version
docs.text: Updates to software are released periodically, and these releases are referred to as a version of the software. There are different types of version, for example the most recent release of a software which has been tested and is intended for general use is referred to as the stable version, while a very new untested version is the alpha version.

docs.title: VPN (Virtual Private Network)
docs.text: A method of sharing information between members of an organisation over encrypted connections.

docs.title: Walk List
docs.text: Is a list created using CiviReport to make it easy for volunteers to go door-to-door. This is often done for voter engagement.

docs.title: Web Application
docs.text: A software application that provides a website with additional functionality. CiviCRM is a web application.

docs.title: Webmail
docs.text: Webmail is email service through a website. The service sends and receives email messages for users in the usual way, but provides a web interface for reading and managing messages, as an alternative to running a mail client like Outlook Express or Thunderbird on the user's computer. For example a popular and free webmail service is https://mail.google.com/

docs.title: Web-Server
docs.text: A Web server is a computer that is set up with software and networking capabilities to deliver Web pages on the Internet or an Intranet. Web servers use programs such asApache or IIS to deliver Web pages over the http protocol.

docs.title: Wiki
docs.text: A web-based software that enables anyone to edit content via a web browser. Wikipedia is the best known example of a wiki.

docs.title: Wildcard
docs.text: A character that can match an any number and collection of characters, normally represented by *. For example, when used in searches, ab* finds ab, abba and abracadabra but not fabulous; *ab* finds fabulous.

docs.title: WordPress
docs.text: The most popular CMS in use on the internet today, WordPress integrates as of CiviCRM version 4.1 and WordPress version 3.3.1. Prior to these versions, CiviCRM didn't work directly with WordPress, although a Drupal/CiviCRM installation could be installed in parallel on the same server as WordPress.

docs.title: Work Station
docs.text: A computer used for working; often in a situation such as an office where there are other computers that may include servers.

docs.title: WYSIWYG (What You See Is What You Get)
docs.text: An application that provides a visual tool for editing web content, so that the user can see how the page will look in the browser as they are editing, instead of working in the HTML code. See also rich text editor.

docs.title: History of this book
docs.text: This book is the result of the collaborative effort of many people. A lot of the content was written during two book sprints held in 2009 and 2010 in Tahoe, USA. Many contributions have also been made by individuals in the times between and following these sprints.

docs.title: Fifth edition
docs.text: The fifth edition was written at the Woolman Sierra Friends Centre (woolman.org) in April 2012. Woolman use and contribute to CiviCRM. We are grateful for their hospitality.

docs.title: Fourth edition
docs.text: The forth edition was written in Bourne, Lincolnshire, UK in September 2011. We were too busy writing this edition to say much about how it was put together.

docs.title: Third edition
docs.text: This edition includes minor updates to reflect changes in CiviCRM 3.3 which was released in December 2010. It is being published on the eve of the second annual CiviCon conference. Thanks to the generous contributions of our CiviCon Sponsors (listed in the front of the book) - a copy has been provided to each conference participant.

docs.title: Second edition
docs.text:
The second edition of the CiviCRM manual was published after a four-day Book Sprint organised by CiviCRM and led by Adam Hyde (FLOSS Manuals). The sprint was sponsored by the Information Program initiative of the Open Society Institute (http://www.soros.org/initiatives/information). We are especially grateful to Janet Haven for pushing this forward.

The second edition includes new sections on CiviReports, CiviCase, CiviEngage and Extending CiviCRM. This edition also included an extensive rewrite of nearly every section of the text, including a reorganization of all sections to break up information into Introduction, Planning, Configuration and Everyday Tasks sections, the latter to serve as an easy-to-follow user manual for individuals working with CiviCRM on a daily basis.

We also added an entire new section to assist developers in getting into the code. Finally, we updated the book to match CiviCRM 3.2 (which was a few weeks away from release at the time of writing).

We think that the reorganisation adds a lot to the book and increases it's readability because it helps people who work with CiviCRM in a specific capacity get directly to the chapter relevant to them.

The following photo shows the people who worked on this second edition of the book.

In the back row, starting from the left, you are looking at Dave Greenberg (San Francisco, USA), Kyle Jaster (NY, USA), Xavier Dutoit (Geneva, Switzerland and Brussels, Belgium), Kurund Jalmi (Mumbai, India), Michael McAndrew (London, UK), Wes Morgan (Washington DC, USA), Josue Guillen (DC, USA). The front row from the left is Jack Aponte (NY, USA), Mari Tilos (San Francisco, USA), Sarah Gladstone (Chicago, USA), and Alice Aguilar (NY, USA).

docs.title: First edition
docs.text:
The first edition of this manual was written during a five-day book sprint organised by CiviCRM and led by FLOSS Manuals. The sprint was sponsored by the Information Program initiative of the Open Society Institute****(http://www.soros.org/initiatives/information.)), and again, we are especially grateful to Janet Haven for pushing this forward.

Having secured sponsorship, the CiviCRM Core team invited a group of people from around the globe to gather for a week at Lake Tahoe in California. The modest goal was to transform our diverse experience of CiviCRM into a manual that we hope will help people to use this great piece of software. This turned out to be an interesting, and at times difficult, challenge.

The following photo shows the people who wrote this book.

In the back row you are looking at Michael McAndrew (London, UK), Tony Guzman (Salt Lake City, USA), Brian Shaughnessy (Albany, NY, USA), Dave Greenberg (San Francisco, USA), Yashodha Chaku (Mumbai, India) and Adam Hyde (Berlin, Germany). In the front row are Mari Tilos (San Francisco, USA), Cynthia Tarascio (Philadelphia, USA), Michal Mach (Warsaw, Poland) and Peter Davis (Wellington, New Zealand). In the very front is Eileen McNaughton (Wellington, New Zealand).

We came from different backgrounds, used CiviCRM in different ways, and worked with very different organisations. It was often a challenge to meld these perspectives into a cohesive whole, but we hammered away at it and we think this made for a better book. We had some lively discussions about important issues, such as whether there is a "z" or an "s" in organis/zation or a "q" in check/que, and finally agreed to use both spellings in the spirit of internationalism. We also struggled with the word "constituent", which is core to the non-profit sector in America but was unfamiliar to those of us from outside America.

It was a pretty intense five days. Adam (our friendly Floss manuals taskmaster) kept us realistic, on track, and hard at work - even hauling us back to work after dinner each evening. Overall it was both fun and productive and we really appreciate the way Adam helped us actually produce a book within a week. Thank you.

For most of us, however, the highlight of the week has been the breathtaking cuisine cooked by Jill Klein (http://www.partiesthatcook.com/about-us/). We love you, Jill, and wish we could take you home with us. We are also grateful to Dave Greenberg, Bob Concannon and Mari Tilos for their hospitality, and to Scout (aka "CiviDog") just for being there.

We had help from around the world during the preparation process, and over the course of the Sprint. Andy Oram helped us both in the planning process and then with editing and feedback during the Sprint. We also had a number of people log in to write and edit the manual during the Sprint. They include Robert Santiago, Xavier Dutoit, Joe Murray, Sarmeesha Reddy, Jay Maechtlen, Dream Gomez, Leila Johnson, Duncan Hutty, and Kurund Jalmi.

Our office for the week was Dave and Bob's house.

We mitigated the hardship of late-night work with some tasty beverages.

And occasionally they let us out for a bit....

docs.title: Manage campaigns and campaign activities
docs.text: This page describes everyday tasks related to managing campaigns with CiviCampaign.

docs.title: Manage campaigns from the dashboard
docs.text:
The Campaign Dashboard allows you to create, configure, manage, and view campaigns. You can also manage surveys and petitions from the dashboard. For details, see Surveys and Petitions.

To view the Campaign Dashboard, go to Campaigns > Dashboard > Campaigns.

From the Campaign Dashboard, you can edit, disable, and delete existing campaigns or create new ones. If you have many campaigns, open the campaign search accordion and set filters to display only the campaigns you want to see.

docs.title: Create a new campaign
docs.text:
1. Go to Campaign > New Campaign.

  1. Enter information about your campaign:

  2. Title (required): Enter a unique name that describes your campaign. A naming convention can help campaigns alphabetize in drop-down lists and make them easier to find when associating an activity with a campaign.

  3. Campaign Type (required): Select the type of campaign, e.g. Constituent Engagement. To add options to the Campaign Type drop-down list, see setting up CiviCampaign.
  4. Description: Enter text that describes your campaign.
  5. Include group(s): If appropriate, select the group containing the individuals you are targeting. To learn more about creating groups, see Tags and Groups.
  6. Start Date & Time (required): Enter the start date and time of the campaign.
  7. End Date & Time: Enter the end date and time of the campaign. If these fields are empty, the campaign will be considered ongoing.
  8. Campaign Status: Select the status of the campaign, e.g. In Progress or Planned. To add options to the Campaign Status drop-down list, see setting up CiviCampaign.
  9. Campaign Goals: Describe the goals and/or objectives of your campaign. You may also want to describe the activities you plan to conduct to meet those goals.
  10. Revenue Goals: If applicable, enter the amount you plan to raise during your campaign.
  11. External ID: If you want to track the campaign ID from another database, enter the ID number of your legacy campaign.

  12. Is Active?: Check the box if the campaign is active. If the campaign is inactive, uncheck the box.

  13. Click Save to save the campaign.

docs.title: Target constituents: create a group
docs.text: You may want to target a specific group of individuals for all campaign activities. Create a group to target those individuals. See Tags and Groups for more information about creating a group.

docs.title: Send a mass mailing
docs.text:
A mass mailing to your target audience can generate interest and participation or call for donations.

  1. Create the email using CiviMail. See Email to learn more about configuring and using CiviMail.
  2. Select the appropriate campaign from the drop-down list when setting up the mailing.

docs.title: Associate an event with a campaign
docs.text:
Events created using CiviEvent can be associated with a campaign.

  1. Create and configure the event.
  2. Select the appropriate campaign from the drop-down list when setting up a mailing for the event.
  3. Send a mass email using CiviMail to your target audience using a group or groups, and ask people to register for the event.
  4. Again, select the name of the campaign on the mailing set-up.
  5. Search for individuals who have indicated they want to register for the event.

docs.title: Record campaign contributions
docs.text:
As contributions come in, either online or offline, associate them with a campaign by selecting the appropriate campaign from the drop-down menu when recording the contribution.

To learn more about configuring and using CiviContribute, see Contributions.

docs.title: Record event participation
docs.text:
During and after an event, organizers can record who participated by collecting sign-in sheets and entering participants manually, or by recording participation directly online.

Have participants write their contact information on sign-in sheets when they arrive. If you have an internet connection at the event venue, you may be able to enter participants directly into the database.

To learn more about recording participant information for an event, see Events.

docs.title: Reports and analysis
docs.text: You can use searches and reports to analyse your campaigns.

docs.title: Campaign searches
docs.text: Searches for components that can be part of a campaign, such as events and contributions, have a campaign filter. The component tabs in advanced search also have a campaign filter, so you can search for contacts based on their participation in campaigns.

docs.title: Campaign reports
docs.text:
Because campaigns can include many components, there is no specific campaign report. Once CiviCampaign has been enabled, you can add a column showing the associated campaign to contribution, pledge, event, mailing and membership reports. You can also "filter by campaign" to restrict the records displayed in these reports.

The activity report can be configured to display both the campaign and the engagement index. It can also be filtered on either or both criteria.

docs.title: Set up CiviCampaign
docs.text: Set up CiviCampaign to track related activities, such as contributions, surveys, and mailings, that are part of a campaign or project.

docs.title: Enable CiviCampaign
docs.text:
1. Go to Administer > System Settings > Components.
  2. Select CiviCampaign and click Enable then Save.

Once enabled, CiviCampaign appears as a new Campaigns menu item along the top of your CiviCRM screen.

docs.title: Add a new campaign type
docs.text:
CiviCampaign provides three default campaign types:

  • Direct Mail
  • Referral Program
  • Constituent Engagement

You can add campaign types appropriate for your work and disable those that aren't.

  1. Go to Administer > CiviCampaign > Campaign Types. This displays the existing campaign types:

  1. Click Add Campaign Type and give the new type a label and, optionally, a description.
  2. Optionally, change the default weight. This affects the order in which this new event type appears in drop-down menus; smallest numbers appear highest.
  3. Click Save.

The campaign type will be available to assign the next time you add a campaign.

docs.title: Campaign status
docs.text:
Assign a status to a campaign to track internally which stage it is in. The default statuses are Planned, In Progress, Completed, and Cancelled.

  1. Go to Administer > CiviCampaign > Campaign Status.
  2. Click Add Campaign Status and give it a name and, optionally, a description.
  3. Changing the weight is not necessary, but it affects the order in which the new status appears in drop-down menus.
  4. Click Save. The new status will be available to assign to campaigns.

docs.title: Engagement index
docs.text:
CiviCampaign lets you track an individual's level of interest or engagement in a particular activity. The Engagement Index can be recorded for general activities or actions, such as Send an Email, Meeting, Phone Call, and Interview, as well as additional custom activities or actions you create. To find out more about recording an activity for an individual, see Contacts in the Organising Your Data section.

To configure the Engagement Index:

  1. Go to Administer > CiviCampaign > Engagement Index.
  2. Configure the engagement index as a number, e.g. 1 is a high level of engagement, and 5 is low level of engagement.

This information can supplement your outreach employees' or organizers' assessment of member engagement or interest in your organization.

docs.title: What is CiviCampaign?
docs.text:
CiviCampaign lets you link events, mailings, activities, and contributions under one campaign so you can track progress toward a programmatic goal. This helps organizations measure and analyze the effectiveness of their outreach and mobilization efforts.

CiviCampaign allows you to:

  • Create surveys and petitions.
  • Record responses to surveys and petitions.
  • Link activities such as donations, mailings and events to a particular campaign.
  • Track who has voted using Get Out The Vote (GOTV).
  • Record individual members' levels of interest and engagement in a particular activity.

CiviCampaign is integrated with other CiviCRM components so you can select which activities are part of the overall campaign or goal.

docs.title: Scenario: Year-long mobilization campaign
docs.text:
To kick off a year-long campaign to mobilize community members, the Townsville Organisation For Tenants (TOFT) held a protest at the Capitol. The organizers used CiviCampaign to connect related activities over the course of the campaign.

The lead organizer created a campaign called "Mobilize the Masses 2011" to link communications about the mobilizing event, participation, and financial contributions for transport and food during the action.

Using CiviCampaign, the organizers:

  • Created a Campaign as the umbrella for all related activities, including the duration of the campaign and the revenue goal.
  • Created a group consisting of the individuals they wanted to target for the activities in the campaign.
  • Called their most active members to help organize other constituents in their neighborhoods to participate. They recorded the activity phone call in the individual's record, indicating the specific campaign and the member's response.
  • Sent a mass fundraising mailing and indicated the campaign, which was then recorded in the contribution information of individuals' records.
  • Created an event to track who would be attending the mobilization and indicated the campaign in the event setup.

Periodically throughout the campaign, the program lead searched for activities related to the campaign, individuals with activities related to the campaign, or both. This helped them monitor the effectiveness of their outreach and fundraising efforts and adjust strategies if necessary.

Organizers can relate subsequent events, mailings, and other activities to the same campaign as it proceeds over the year. At the end of the campaign, they can review this information in the context of the whole campaign.

docs.title: Popular extensions
docs.text:
These are widely used extensions in the relevant category of the official CiviCRM Extensions Directory. Usage is a popularity signal, not a compatibility or suitability guarantee.

  • Campaign Manager — reported usage: 102
  • Campaign Tools — reported usage: 15
  • CiviRepresent — reported usage: 11
  • Petition Email — reported usage: 10

All extensions for this component

Check development status, current CiviCRM compatibility, CMS requirements, and release notes before installation.

Usage snapshot reviewed: 2026-10-13.

docs.title: Planning a campaign with CiviCampaign
docs.text: Before you create a campaign, review how CiviCampaign can support your organisation’s work and consider what your campaign needs.

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text: Your organisation will likely have its own campaign strategies and processes. You can use CiviCampaign alongside your existing methods to streamline and automate certain processes.

docs.title: Campaign goals and revenue
docs.text: Define and document the campaign’s concrete goals and the funds you hope to raise, if applicable. Record this information in the campaign so you can use reports to analyze its effectiveness at its conclusion.

docs.title: Planning your campaign activities
docs.text: As you plan your strategy and identify your target audience, determine which activities and information you can record within CiviCRM. Connect everything you record to the campaign so you can track campaign efforts and individuals’ activities. This allows you to evaluate the effectiveness of your activities, strategies and outreach efforts both periodically and overall.

docs.title: Key questions
docs.text:
Answer these questions for your organisation or a specific campaign:

  • Who is your target audience, and how will you reach them? The audience for your campaign activities may differ from the audience you are trying to reach with the campaign itself. Understanding your target audience will help you choose strategies and communication activities to achieve your campaign goals.
  • What activities and strategies, such as events and mailings, will be associated with this campaign?
  • How will you gather data during the campaign (e.g. surveys, petitions, event registrations), and who will be responsible for entering the data into CiviCRM?
  • What reports will be useful for monitoring progress and evaluating the campaign at its conclusion?

docs.title: Everyday tasks
docs.text: This page describes everyday tasks you can perform using CiviCase.

docs.title: Viewing the Case Dashboard
docs.text:
The Case Dashboard helps you keep track of case-related tasks. It provides:

  • A summary of cases in the system (Summary of Case Involvement).
  • A list of your cases with upcoming activities scheduled in the next 14 days.
  • A list of your cases with activities completed in the last 14 days.

If you have permission to view cases other than those you are working on, you can also see lists of all cases with upcoming activities and all cases with recently performed activities. Click the link at the top right of the content area to switch between Your Cases and All Cases.

Click the Edit icon next to the Next Sched. activity name to work on that task. In the following screenshot, the Next Sched. activity is Medical evalution. Click its title to view it in a pop-up window, or click the edit pencil to the right of the title if you are ready to work on it.

Click the triangular expand icon (►) to the left of a client’s name to see all activities for that case. You can view or edit any activity in the list. Click Manage Case to work on several tasks within a case, change its status, print a case report, or view case roles.

To add a case from the Case Dashboard, click Add Case at the top left of the content area.

docs.title: Finding cases
docs.text:
If you know the Case ID, you can use full-text search from Search > Custom Search > Fulltext Search, or from the fulltext search block if you have enabled it.

To search for cases, go to Search > Find Cases or use Cases in the menu bar at the top of the CiviCRM screen. You can use the search options individually or combine them:

  • Client name or email address: Type characters from the name or email address into the Client name or email input field.
  • Case types: Check the types you want to search for.
  • Case status: Select a status from the dropdown menu.
  • All cases or your cases: If unselected, the default is to filter by your cases.
  • Deleted cases: Click the Deleted cases checkbox.

Selections across different sets of criteria are combined: results must meet at least one requirement in each set. For example, if you enter a client name and select a case type, results must match the client name AND case type. Multiple selections within one set are treated differently: if you check two case types, results can match at least one of them.

docs.title: Opening a new case
docs.text: You can open a case for an existing contact or create a contact while opening the case.

docs.title: Open a case for an existing contact
docs.text:
Creating a case from an existing contact’s summary screen or actions menu automatically links the case to that contact.

  1. Go to the contact’s summary screen.
  2. Select Add Case from the Actions dropdown menu, or click the Cases tab.
  3. Fill in the required fields in the Add Case form.
  4. Click Save.

docs.title: Open a case for a new contact
docs.text:
When you open a case for a new contact, CiviCRM creates the contact record at the same time.

  1. Go to Cases > New Case or select the Create New > Case dropdown button. This button is provided as a block in Drupal or on the left hand side in Joomla!.
  2. If you have not navigated from an existing contact, you may want to check whether the contact is already in the database. Type the contact’s name or email in the Select Contact field to see potential matches.

  1. If you do not find the contact, select the contact type from the create new contact list. A pop-up window lets you enter the contact’s name and other information while opening the case. Its fields are controlled by the Add Individual profile, so you can add or modify the fields provided. You can read more about profiles in the Profiles chapter.

Complete the case fields as appropriate:

  • Medium and Location record where and how the case came to your attention. For example, you might select In Person for Medium and At the Annual Gala for Location. To manage Encounter Mediums, select the edit icon.

  • Details holds information about the overall case, rather than a specific activity. For example: “Jane is concerned about some illegal land use that she has witnessed in her neighbourhood, and would like us to see what can be done about it. I told her that the best person to look into this was Tom, and she asked whether her husband could be included on any correspondence.”

  • Subject appears next to the case client’s name in search results and other case listings. A brief, unique description is more helpful than using the client’s name as the subject.
  • Case Type lets you choose the type of case. Many case types have specific activities and timelines, so choose the appropriate type at this point. You can change it later by clicking Manage Case next to the case in the CiviCase Dashboard, or from the contact’s record Case tab, then selecting Change Case Type from the New Activity dropdown menu. Changing an ongoing case may require you to update or re-enter some data.
  • Case Status indicates the current status. Generally you will use a status such as Ongoing or Urgent. If you are adding a case that has already been completed for tracking purposes, select Resolved.
  • Case Start Date defaults to the current day. Adjust it if you are entering a completed case or an upcoming case that has not yet started.

  • Duration records, in minutes, the time spent collecting the data needed to fill out the create case form—not the time spent filling out the form. For example, you might record the minutes spent on the phone with a constituent as they described the case.

  • After completing the fields in the pop-up window, choose an action:

  • Save saves the case and opens the Manage Case page, where you can modify activities, add attachments, and assign case roles.
  • Save and New saves the case and resets the form so you can add more cases without interruption. This is particularly useful for data entry.
  • Cancel discards the case data you entered and returns you to the CiviCRM dashboard.

docs.title: Manage Case Page
docs.text:
The manage case page lets you manage these aspects of a case on one screen:

  • View summary case information.
  • Change case status or reassign.
  • Create/manage activities.
  • Create/manage timelines.
  • Create/assign case roles.
  • Identify/manage client relationships.
  • Run case audits (reports).

docs.title: Assigning case roles
docs.text:
You can assign case roles to contacts who work on a case or need to stay informed about its activities. Users with access to CiviCase who are assigned a case role will see the case in their My Cases view. The case displays each role holder’s phone number and email address.

To assign a contact to a case role:

  1. Click the Case Roles area to open it.
  2. Find a role showing (not assigned) in the Name column, then click its edit icon.
  3. In the Assign Case Role pop-up window, begin typing the contact’s last name until their name appears in the dropdown list.
  4. Select the contact and click OK.

To assign more than one contact to a given case role, click Add New Role. In the pop-up window, select a role defined in your case configuration and a contact from your database. The new role relationship appears in the Roles pane of the case management screen.

Generally, anyone who might be assigned to a case should already be in the database. If you cannot find the person, add them as a contact first using Contacts > New Individual.

Each assigned case role has mail, edit, and delete icons under the Email and Actions columns. You can email contacts with roles in the case or modify their relationships to it. Click the edit icon to change a case role or the delete icon to delete one. Emails sent from here are automatically added to the case activities in sequence, providing an audit trail of case-related communications.

docs.title: Bulk add contacts to a case with a specific role
docs.text:
An action on contact search results lets you add several contacts to a case with a specific role:

  1. Perform a search on Contacts.
  2. Select the contacts to add from the search results.
  3. Choose the Add to case as role action.
  4. Use the form to choose the case and the role the contacts will have in it.
  5. Click Submit to add the contacts, or Cancel to return to the search results.

docs.title: Finding activities within a case
docs.text:
To find an activity for reference or modification, scroll to Case Activities and click it to open it. By default, scheduled activities appear first, sorted by date, followed by completed activities. Click a column header to sort by that column—for example, by activity type.

If a case has many activities, click Search Filters to narrow the list. For example, you can find all Follow up activities performed for the case. The filters are:

  • Reporter/Role
  • Activity Status
  • Activity Dates: Fill in both date fields for a range, or only the first field for a specific date.
  • Activity Type: For example, select Follow up to find follow-up activities.
  • Deleted Activities: Available to people with permission to view deleted activities.

After selecting your criteria, click Search on the right. The table filters out activities that do not match.

docs.title: Adding and managing activities
docs.text: After working on an activity, click Save to save it and return to the case page, or Cancel to discard your work.

docs.title: To add a single new activity to a case
docs.text:
1. Navigate to the case using Find Cases or the Cases Dashboard.
  2. Choose an activity type from New Activity in the Case Summary.
  3. Click Go.
  4. Fill out the activity form. The Client field is pre-populated with the case’s client data.

Note

The drop-down list of activities is configurable. Refer to the set-up chapter for more information.

docs.title: Adding a set of activities
docs.text:
The Standard Timeline is added when the case is created. You can add an additional set of activities when appropriate.

  1. Navigate to the case using Find Cases or the Cases Dashboard.
  2. Choose a Timeline or Sequence from New Timeline in the Case Summary.
  3. In the dialog box, confirm that you want to add the activities by clicking "OK".

The set of activities is added to the case.

docs.title: To send a copy of the activity to anyone with a case role for the case
docs.text:
1. Open Send a Copy.
  2. Check the contacts or case roles you want to alert about the activity.

docs.title: To schedule a follow up activity
docs.text:
1. Open Schedule Follow-up.
  2. Select the follow-up activity type, the number of days until the follow-up should occur, and its subject—for example, “confirm that Jane’s problem is fixed”.
  3. Click Go.
  4. Complete the form and click Save.

docs.title: To add an attachment to the activity
docs.text:
1. Open Attachments.
  2. Click a Choose file button.
  3. Select an attachment from your file browser. You can attach up to five files to an activity.
  4. Click Choose. The attachment’s name appears to the right of the Choose file button.

The attachment is not saved into CiviCRM until you save the activity.

docs.title: Editing an activity in a case
docs.text:
1. Navigate to the case from the Case Dashboard, the Find Cases search form, or the contact’s Cases tab.
  2. Click Edit at the far right of the activities table at the bottom of the case form.
  3. Edit the activity form as you would when creating an activity for a case. Many fields will already be filled in.

To assign a scheduled task to a staff member while adding or editing a case:

  1. Start typing the staff member’s name in Assigned to. A list of possible contacts appears.
  2. Select from the suggestions and check that the staff member’s full name appears in Assigned to.

You can assign multiple contacts to an activity. If you select the wrong contact, click the X by their name to remove them.

docs.title: Updating the status of case activities
docs.text:
You can update an activity’s status from the Activities table without opening its edit form:

  1. Navigate to the case from the Case Dashboard, the Find Cases search form, or the contact’s Cases tab.
  2. Click the status text, such as “Scheduled”, in the activity’s table row.
  3. In the pop-up form, select a new status and click Ok to save the update.

docs.title: Changing the status of a case
docs.text:
The case status helps you determine how a case is progressing. Sample values include Ongoing, Resolved, Not Assigned, and Urgent.

  1. Navigate to the case from the Case Dashboard, the Find Cases search form, or the contact’s Cases tab.
  2. Click Manage Case.
  3. Click the Edit icon next to the current status column in the Case Summary table.
  4. The Change Case Status form opens. This is an activity with an additional Case Status field.
  5. Set the case status to the new status.
  6. If the case has linked cases, they appear in a table within the form. To update their statuses too, check Update Linked Cases Status.
  7. Modify the other fields as you would when editing an activity in a case. Set the Status field: it is required but not set by default.
  8. Click Save to return to the case page. A message states that the Change Case Status Activity has been created.

An activity is recorded when a case status changes because something happened. Recording who and why is usually as important as recording what. This behaviour is consistent throughout CiviCase. An activity is also recorded for a linked case if Update Linked Cases Status was checked and that case’s status differed from the parent case’s new status.

docs.title: Reports and analysis
docs.text:
You can review casework in several ways. Within a case, you can run an audit of its activities. The case dashboard gives a quick overview of current cases, with a row for each case type and columns showing totals for each status. Clicking a number takes you to a list of cases of that type and status; 0 is not linked.

For more detailed or customised views for case workers and administrators, use CiviCRM's search features and CiviReport.

docs.title: QA audit / redact
docs.text:
Run this report from the contact's case management screen. It is similar to the Print Report link on that screen, but includes only activities defined in a selected timeline. You can include activities with any status or exclude those with 'Completed' status.

If you select Redact (hide) Client and Service Provider Data, the report uses randomly assigned numbers instead of names. The same contact has the same number throughout the report.

docs.title: CiviCase reports
docs.text:
There are four report templates specifically for cases:

  • Case Summary Report
  • Case Time Spent Report
  • Contact Demographics Report
  • Case Detail Report

Because cases are made up of activities, the Activity report template is also useful for providing a dashlet for each user involved in casework to track activities assigned to them. These case activities appear alongside non-case activities, so you may want a protocol for activity names that includes a case reference.

docs.title: Printing case reports
docs.text:
To print a report listing all case and case activity data:

  1. Navigate to the case from the Case Dashboard, the Find Cases search form, or the contact's Cases tab.
  2. Click Print Case Report in the Case Summary section.

Your installation may define additional reports for audit or quality assurance purposes. If so, they appear in the "Run QA Audit/Redact" dropdown menu.

docs.title: Searching based on cases
docs.text:
Find Cases lets you search by Case Type, Status, client name, or email. It can help you identify cases needing specific input when the case dashboard is large or cluttered.

Advanced search combines these options with other normal search criteria, so you can find case types filtered by location or custom fields applied to the contact.

Activity Search, under Search > Custom Searches > Activity Search, is based on activities rather than contacts, unlike Advanced search.

docs.title: Print/merge document
docs.text:
You can create a letter or document using case tokens on the case management screen, or on multiple cases through a Find Cases search. On the case management screen, beside "Print Report," the "Export Document" option exports a PDF, DOCx, ODT, or HTML page. Alternatively, select multiple cases through a search and use "Print/merge Document" to create a document for each case, compiled in a single PDF.

When working with DOCx, turn off spelling and grammar check for best results.

docs.title: Further analysis
docs.text:
If the Case Dashboard, CiviReport, and contact and activity searches do not provide what you need, consider commissioning a new report or custom search.

Read the section on reporting and the page on searching for more information.

docs.title: Custom fields for cases and activities
docs.text:
You may want to collect structured data in a case. Custom fields can be connected to a specific activity type or to the case type. For example, an Employment Counselling case might include a Skills Assessment activity in which an employment counsellor records client job skills, perhaps using a set of checkboxes. Alternatively, a generalized application case might need a custom field indicating the type of application being tracked.

Custom fields attached to a case are visible inside the case management screen. Fields attached to an activity are visible only when the user views details of that activity.

If you are transitioning from a paper-based system, refer to existing forms to determine which information is relevant to include. Please review the section on configuring custom data fields prior to beginning these steps.

  1. Go to Administer > Customize Data and Screens > Custom Fields.
  2. Click Add a Set of Custom Fields.
  3. Under Used For, select Activities or Cases.
  4. Select one or more specific activity type(s) or case type(s) for which this set of fields will be used.
  5. Enter any help information you want displayed to your users.
  6. Click Save.
  7. Enter one or more custom fields for this set.
  8. Repeat these steps for each activity type or case type that requires custom data.

If you need many fields for one activity type, consider dividing them into logically related sets that make sense to users and avoid an endless tunnel of fields.

docs.title: Filing emails on cases
docs.text:
Some organizations find it useful to record case-related emails in CiviCase. For example, the coordinator of a work disability case might send an inquiry to a state agency representative and want both the sent email and the reply to become part of the case story.

You can send outbound emails directly from the Manage Case screen. You can also set up CiviCRM to integrate with your usual email client, so you can send and receive emails as usual and have them filed in CiviCRM.

The CiviMail chapter describes the Email Processor as a way to get inbound and outbound emails into CiviCRM as non-case activities. When you enable CiviCase, a new action becomes available to file any non-case activity onto a case. If the Email Processor has been set up, replies to email activities sent from the Manage Case screen will automatically be filed directly onto the case.

You can also record an email or an activity on a case by adding the string "case" to the subject field, followed by a space and the case's #id in square braces. For example, an activity or email with the subject "[case #123] Any subject" would be recorded under case id = 123.

docs.title: CiviCase permissions
docs.text:
Create a contact record for each staff member or service provider who will use CiviCase to enter or view case information. These individuals also need a Drupal, Joomla! or WordPress user account.

For Joomla! and WordPress installations, staff members must have back-end (administrator) access. All CiviCase functions are done within the Joomla! and WordPress Administrator interfaces.

Also add contact records for service providers who will be assigned case roles but will not access CiviCase. This lets staff email them pertinent case and client information via CiviCase and record case-related interactions they report.

To let users add and manage cases, configure CiviCase-related permissions in your CMS. You may want case management-specific user roles for staff based on their responsibilities. Permissions control access to the CiviCase component and the case data users can see.

The CiviCase-related permissions are:

  • Access my cases and activities: Allows a user to create new cases, add activities to cases they've created, and edit those activities. Users with this permission can NOT see cases or activities created by others.

To restrict users to ONLY seeing case data—that is, to hide all other contact information from them—assign "access my cases and activities" permission WITHOUT "edit and view contacts" permission. This permissioning model is useful for users external to your organisation who should not see contact details.

  • Access all cases and activities: Allows a user to create new cases, and view and add activities to any case, regardless of who created it.

  • Delete in CiviCase: Allows a user to mark cases or case activities as deleted. They are never physically deleted from the database, but are hidden when marked as deleted.

Users with this permission can also find and undelete them by checking the Deleted Cases option in Find Cases and the Deleted Activities option in the Case Activities Search Filter.

  • Administer CiviCase: Gives access to Administer > CiviCase options, including:
  • create and edit case types and case statuses
  • set rules for redacting case data. These rules disguise data that could identify the case client in case reports shared with external reviewers.

docs.title: Set-up
docs.text: Now that you've gone through the planning process and determined the types of cases, activities and case roles that you need, you're ready to configure your CiviCase installation.

docs.title: Enable the CiviCase component
docs.text:
The CiviCase component is included in CiviCRM downloads, but it is NOT enabled by default. To enable the component:

  1. Go to Administer > System Settings > Components.
  2. Select CiviCase.
  3. Click Save.

You will now see Cases in the navigation menu.

docs.title: Define case types
docs.text:
You can create one or more new case types. To add a case type:

  1. Go to Administer > CiviCase > Case Types.

  2. Click New Case Type. Enter a "Title" and an optional "Description" of the case type.

    The case type has both a "Title" and a "Name". The title will be displayed to users, and the name is used internally by CiviCRM. CiviCRM will autofill the name field. The default name is usually fine, but an advanced user may unlock and change it. Once the case type is created, the name should not be changed.

  3. Optionally choose to restrict Activity Assignment.

    By default, any contact can be selected as the assignee for case activities. You can optionally restrict this by group or by contacts with a user account on your website.

  4. Include Case Roles.

    This section lists the types of people involved in the case. Roles listed here will be automatically included in each case when a new case is opened. Select the roles you want from the "Add role" drop-down shown below the listing of roles.

    To create a new custom role, click the drop-down and type its name into the field. Alongside any matches from the existing roles, a blue bar will show your keyed entry, underlined.
