Click it to define the new role. The role will be created when you save your new case type. You can use this method to create as many new roles as you need.

    Each selected or created role appears in the listing of Roles, where you can set "Assign to Creator" and "Is Manager":

    • A role marked "Assign to Creator" is automatically assigned to the person who creates the case.
    • You may mark one role as the manager. The case manager's name will be displayed prominently in case listings and reports.

    Specific people may be assigned to case-roles after a case has been opened.

    New roles/relationship types created through the Case Type interface are individual-to-individual relationships. If you want roles that are individual-to-organisation relationships, once you have finished creating your case type, you can change the relationship definition at Administer > Customize Data and Screens > Relationship Types. There you can also review and edit other details of the roles/relationships.

  5. Include Activities.

    When working on a case, the user has an Add Activity drop-down menu in the case summary for quickly recording a new activity as part of the case. For example, a case manager could make a phone call to check a point with a colleague, then select Phone Call from the menu and record the call's details. The Phone Call activity automatically gets filed on to the case.

    When defining the Case Type, you can choose which Activity Types are available in this menu. If you include most or all of your custom Activity Types in the Standard Timeline, or another timeline or sequence, you may not want to include them in the 'Add Activity' menu, particularly if you want tight control over the workflow pattern. Alternatively, including some or all of them gives users more control over the pattern and flow of activities.

    First, create a list of the Activity Types you want readily available from within the case. This is the listing under the 'Activity Types' tab. Select the types users will find useful, such as Phone Call, Email, Meeting, Follow Up, and any custom activity types. CiviCRM also includes special activity types such as Open Case, Change Case Status, and Change Case Type; you do not need to add these manually.

    The Activity Types listing needs only activities a user might choose to add to the case. Activities included in a Timeline or Sequence do not need to be in this list.

    Select the types you want from the "Add activity type" drop-down below the listing. To create a custom activity type, click the drop-down and key its name into the search field. Alongside any matches from existing activity types, a blue bar will show your keyed entry, underlined. Click it to define the new type. It will be created when you save your new case type. You can use this method to create as many new activity types as you need.

    Each selected or created type appears in the listing of Activity Types. You can optionally use 'Max Instances' to specify how many times a type can be used in a case.

    Once you have created your case type, you can review and amend any new activity types at Administer > Customize Data and Screens > Activity Types. New types created through the Case Type interface have default settings that should be fine in most situations. You may wish to amend the label, add a more useful description, or make the type available outside CiviCase by changing the 'Component' setting from 'Cases only' to Contacts AND Cases'.

  6. Define the Standard Timeline, any additional Timelines and/or a Sequence you want to use within the case type.

    These are groups of activity types that define a series of interactions, allowing you to pre-define one or more standardised workflows.

    In a Timeline, you control the scheduling of each activity relative to the date the case is opened or to another activity, using the 'Reference' and 'Offset' fields. All activities in a timeline are created when that timeline is added to the case and are visible in the case summary. You can create multiple timelines for a case type.

    The Standard Timeline is the default for each new case type and provides essential elements that make case types work correctly, so each case type must have one. Its activities are added automatically when the case is opened. It starts with one predefined activity, Open Case; additional timelines start empty. Because you control when an additional timeline is added, you choose its first activity, which may also be a key reference activity for that timeline.

    A Sequence defines the order of a set of activities but, unlike a timeline, has no information about time intervals. The next activity in a sequence is created only when the preceding activity is marked as completed. Make sure an activity type included in your timeline(s) is not also included in your sequence, and vice-versa.

    You may add additional timelines or a sequence from the (Add) menu. Currently, you can add only one sequence to a case type.

    To add activities to a timeline, select the tab for the timeline you want to work with:

    1. Select or create an activity using the drop-down list.
    2. Select a status for the activity (the default is Scheduled).
    3. Enter a Reference Activity. The default reference activity is Open Case and this is often appropriate. For the Standard Timeline any activity in the timeline can be selected as the reference for any other activity. For other timelines you can select any activity in the case type as a reference, bearing in mind that at the point in alive case where the additional timeline is activated, the reference activity must already exist in the case.
    4. Enter an Offset (in days). Offset values can be positive, negative or zero.
    5. The 'Select' option is helpful if there are multiple instances of the reference activity type, as it allows you to select whether the oldest or most recent instance of the reference activity should be used.

    You can use the "end date" of a case (i.e the final defined activity) as your reference and use negative offset values to schedule activities, as in this example:

    You can rename additional timelines or a sequence using the fields in the 'Advanced' section below the main Activities section of the page, as shown above.

    To add activity types to a sequence, select or create them using the Add Activity drop-down menu. Once you have all the types needed for your timeline(s) or sequence, you can re-order them using the drag and drop handles to the left of each activity type.

A set of sample case types is installed when you enable the CiviCase component. You can use these to see what a complete case type looks like or as a starting point for your own case types.

docs.title: What is CiviCase?
docs.text:
CiviCase is a tool for tracking and managing sequences of interactions between people in your organisation and contacts in CiviCRM. It's similar to a case management system. In addition to tracking and managing your organisation's interactions with clients or constituents, CiviCase can also help you manage internal organisational interactions.

Cases are used to track complex interactions or communication processes. A case can be used to:

  • Track a specific workflow or set of procedures that must be followed and that involves a number of different organisational staff.
  • Allow staff to manage and track interactions while avoiding duplication.
  • Automate the task of remembering and scheduling follow-up activities.

CiviCase relies heavily on Activities, and a solid understanding of activities will help you understand CiviCase more easily.

Organisations have employed CiviCase in a wide variety of situations. The following scenarios show how different types of organisations use it.

docs.title: Scenario: managing legislator-constituent interactions
docs.text:
A legislator's staff manages hundreds of interactions with constituents and communities daily. Legislative staff can manage and track these interactions while avoiding duplicating work. For example, if a constituent calls in about an issue, the staffer taking the call can look at the activities in the case related to the issue, see that another staffer is already working on it, and relay that information to the caller.

CiviCase also automates the task of remembering and scheduling follow up activities by presenting staffers with a list of upcoming case activities that require their attention.

CiviCase came in handy to track a series of related tasks that legislative staff do as a result of interactions with constituents, including:

  • A legislative staffer received a phone call about illegal dumping near the caller's home. The staffer created a case recording the details and location of the reported issue. She then assigned the task of following up with the Health Department to another member of the legislator's staff. Upon logging-in to CiviCRM, the other staff member saw that the task was assigned to them. He then contacted the Health Department on behalf of the constituent, and contacted the constituent to confirm that the Health Department was informed of the situation.
  • The legislator's office received a phone call from a constituent requesting support from an agency. A staffer logged the call in CiviCase and then set up a follow-up call for the next week to make sure that action was taken on the agency's behalf.
  • The legislator's staff records event invitations on an ongoing basis that a legislator's scheduler must respond to.

docs.title: Scenario: complex application process
docs.text:
An organisation administering a health department grant programme to distribute several million dollars worth of grants used CiviCase to manage the grant applications process. When interested parties submitted their initial applications, a case was automatically created to manage each. The case created contained several activities which were automatically assigned to different staff managing the application process.

In this instance the users were actually from three separate organisations who each had to apply their assessment of the application in turn. First, a basic initial assessment was made to check that certain criteria were met. Then an external organisation made a more technical assessment. The activities were all offset from the start of the case by the number of days in which it was anticipated they should be completed and a coordinator from each organisation assigned the case activities to members of staff according to their capacity as they came in.

At various stages in the process, the status of the case was changed for one reason or another. In this process the main options were:

  • passed basic checks
  • failed basic checks
  • technically feasible
  • technically infeasible
  • suppliers approved
  • suppliers disallowed
  • deferred to next round
  • accepted

Even though there were thousands of applications and tens of thousands of parts of the application review process, the coordinators from the first two organisations assigned activities to staff members so they each saw a case dashboard showing only the work assigned to them, helping them focus their energy on just their segment of the applications.

For the final assessment, the two organisations hired an external organisation to process the remaining applications. For this process, a review committee was able to view the key details of applications with different statuses, and finally, just review the summary details of all applications with an accepted status to make a final determination.

docs.title: CiviCase in use
docs.text:
Here's a simple example of a Housing Support case. The Open Case activity is marked as Completed when the case is opened. Three additional activities are automatically scheduled when the case is opened. A medical evaluation is scheduled for the following day (reference offset is 1); then secure temporary housing (reference offset 2); and finally a follow-up three days later.

In this example there are three case roles. The Homeless Service Coordinator is both the creator and manager of these cases. In addition, a Health Services Coordinator and a Benefits Specialist role are created when the case is opened.

docs.title: Popular extensions
docs.text:
These are widely used extensions in the relevant category of the official CiviCRM Extensions Directory. Usage is a popularity signal, not a compatibility or suitability guarantee.

  • Documents — reported usage: 337
  • CiviCalendar — reported usage: 250
  • New CiviCase UI — reported usage: 206
  • CiviProspect — reported usage: 176
  • CiviCase Tokens — reported usage: 123

All extensions for this component

Check development status, current CiviCRM compatibility, CMS requirements, and release notes before installation.

Usage snapshot reviewed: 2026-10-13.

docs.title: Relationship type status warnings
docs.text:
CiviCase may, in unusual situations, cause some status warnings related to Relationship Types. Some general principles applicable to all of these warnings are:

  • If you haven't created any relationships yet between contacts you can delete the relationship type and recreate it.
  • If you have created relationships between contacts, but not many, you may consider deleting those relationships, then deleting the relationship type, recreating the type, and then recreating the relationships between the contacts.

docs.title: Relationship type internal name duplicates
docs.text:
This situation can come up if you get confused about A/B directions when setting up relationship types, which is quite easy if you're new to it. For example:

  1. Create a type called "Candy maker is" (A to B) / "Candy maker for" (B to A).
  2. Thinking that you need to create another type to have both directions appear properly, create another type called "Candy maker for" (A to B) / "Candy maker is" (B to A).
  3. Realize that you don't need that, so rename the second to something else you were planning to add, such as "Gum maker is"/"Gum maker for".
  4. This will cause problems when assigning roles of type Gum maker.

docs.title: Relationship type display label duplicates
docs.text: Somehow you have two different relationship types with the same display label. The simplest solution is to change the label for one of them or delete the duplicate. If they really are the same relationship it's a bad idea to have two anyway.

docs.title: Relationship type cross-duplication
docs.text:
This situation can come up if you change your mind several times when setting up relationship types and you make those changes in a specific order. For example:

  1. Create a type called "Candy maker".
  2. Create a type called "Gum maker".
  3. Create a type called "Sweets maker".
  4. Later, decide you don't need Gum so delete Gum.
  5. Later still, decide you don't need both Candy and Sweets but you wanted Gum, so you rename Sweets to Gum.
  6. Then you decide you like the word Sweets better than Candy so you rename Candy to Sweets.
  7. At this point the system will get confused about what means what.

docs.title: Relationship type ambiguity
docs.text:
This situation can come up if you do something like create a new Relationship Type that is bidirectional, like "Spouse of", and then change your mind and edit it so that direction matters. The system will still function but you may find some relationships of that type appear backwards.

The reverse is also possible, where you initially created it as unidirectional and then later edited it so that it's bidirectional.

docs.title: Missing roles
docs.text: One way this situation can come up is if you are using external XML files and you have made a typo in the file so that the relationship type doesn't match any existing type. Another way is if you deleted a relationship type referenced in the file but have not updated the file, so it still references it.

docs.title: What you need to know
docs.text: The CiviCase component allows for a high degree of customisation to meet the needs of a wide variety of organisations and workflows. It is important to understand CiviCase's underlying principles and assumptions, as well as the elements that can be customised, before you begin to plan and configure the component based on your requirements.

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
Activities: CiviCRM tracks most interactions with activities. These are particularly useful for single interactions. For example, if a constituent calls to request information and the staff person directs them to a web site, this would be recorded as an activity. Activities have a start date/time, a duration, a status, and a priority. They also have a creator, a subject/target and can be assigned to someone for action.

Cases are used to track more complex interactions or communication processes than can be handled by a single activity. CiviCase provides additional structure around activities:

  • Multiple activities can be grouped together into a case.
  • Activities can be optionally structured using a Timeline or a Sequence.
  • The set of possible activities to track interactions can be optionally restricted.

CiviCase also identifies the people involved and their role(s) in the case:

  • Case Coordinator is a pre-defined role.
  • Additional roles can be added as required.

CiviCase also provides additional options for managing activities:

  • The Case Dashboard allows users to see the cases they are involved in.
  • Cases provide an extra layer of access control.

Using these features, a case can define a workflow with specific steps that must be followed. For example: a client fills out an intake form, then has an initial meeting with a staff person, and finally receives a certificate from the organisation for meeting certain goals.

docs.title: Case types
docs.text:
One or more Case Types are defined that describe a specific group of related tasks, interactions, or processes.

For example, the Physician Health Program provides support for physicians who are experiencing problems related to emotional health issues, the inappropriate use of alcohol and/or drugs or coping with physical illness. Some of the case types they use are:

  • In-patient Treatment
  • Referral to Counsellor

For a community services organisation, examples of case types might include:

  • Housing Assistance
  • Job Training
  • Prenatal Counseling

Think about the multi-step tasks that staff in your organisation do on a regular basis and make a list of potential case types.

docs.title: Case activities
docs.text: Activities track specific interactions and tasks within a case. Activities may be scheduled in advance or created ad-hoc, and they may involve the case client (a.k.a. the constituent), a third party (such as a family member or a professional who is assisting with the case), and other case workers. Each organisation needs to determine the level of detail to be recorded, but many organisations find it helpful to include every phone call, meeting or internal discussion in the case story by recording it as an activity.

docs.title: Activity types
docs.text:
CiviCRM is preconfigured with a number of activity types including Phone Calls, Meetings, Emails Sent, Interviews and Follow-ups. These may be sufficient for your needs. However many organisations will want to track other specific tasks, and activity types can be added for these.

During the life of each case, some activities will be automatically created, such as:

  • Open Case: created at the same time the case is created.
  • Follow up: you can use this type when it isn't necessary to define a more specific one (see Activity Data below).
  • Change Case Type: created every time the type is modified.
  • Change Case Status: created every time the status is updated.

For a community services organisation, additional activity types might include:

  • Client Intake
  • Skills Evaluation
  • Review
  • Consultant Referral

For each of the case types you identified, create a list of the specific activities involved. Creating new activity types instead of relying only on Follow-up will make the list of activities easier to read.

docs.title: Activity data
docs.text:
A standard set of information can be entered whenever an activity is recorded in CiviCase:

  • who recorded the activity and who reported the activity
  • when and where the activity will (or did) occur
  • free-form subject and detailed description
  • time spent on the activity.

This is sufficient for some types of activities; however, it is often useful to collect additional structured data. The Open Case (intake) activity is a common example where you may want to include a set of specific questions about the client and their situation. If need be, you can use Custom Fields to associate additional data with each activity.

docs.title: Timelines and the standard timeline
docs.text:
CiviCase allows you to define one or more expected sets of activities for each type of case and when they should occur. These are called timelines.

For really simple cases, the timeline might include only two items:

  • Open Case
  • Follow up - scheduled for two days after the case is opened

Even in this example, the timeline is useful as it allows you to predefine when the people assigned to the case should follow up with the client or constituent. For more complex processes, the timeline provides a case plan that can help the people involved to stay on track. The timeline lists all the activities which are expected to occur and should be accomplished within a certain time-frame. When a timeline is added to a case the activity dates are pre-computed and do not update automatically. Any changes to dates must be made manually.

Each case type must have a standard timeline. The standard timeline is created automatically when a new case is opened. At its simplest it consists of just one completed Open Case activity. You can leave it at that or add more activities as required. In a standard timeline you define the expected number of days between the beginning of the case and each of the subsequent activities in the timeline.

You can create multiple (non-standard) timelines for a case and add them if/when it is appropriate to do so. For these timelines you can use any activity as the reference for subsequent activities. So, for example, if one of the activities in your standard timeline is a medical evaluation, you could have 2 or more timelines that outline different schedules of medical treatment and add one of these to the case depending on the outcome of the original medical evaluation. For this example the timelines would typically use "medical evaluation" as the reference activity.

You might also want to define a (non-standard) timeline based on the end date for a case. When a case has to be completed by a specific date (e.g. by the start of the school year), each activity can be defined as needing to happen a number of days before this end date, i.e. you would define negative offsets in the timeline. You would open the case, add the final activity with the scheduled end date, then add the timeline. This would create a series of activities with the scheduled date for each being the latest it could be completed if the entire case is to be completed by the end date.

docs.title: Sequences
docs.text:
CiviCase lets you define one sequence instead of, or as well as, timeline(s). A sequence is a set of activities that should follow one after the other, but no time-offsets are defined for the activities. Instead the activities are created one at a time, with the first activity in the sequence created when the case is opened, and the second activity in the sequence being created as soon as the first activity is completed and so on. The scheduled date is always the date the activity is created.

Defining a sequence rather than a timeline may be useful if the completion of activities in your case are outside your control. However, as the activities are created progressively it will not provide the same at-a-glance overview of the case that a timeline does.

Note

If you want to use both a timeline and a sequence in the same case you must make sure that there is no overlap in activity types between the two. For example, you cannot include the activity type of "Meeting" in both a timeline and the sequence within the same case as this will create problems.

docs.title: Case roles and relationships
docs.text:
CiviCase provides three mechanisms for relating people to cases and clients:

  • Case Roles: people directly involved in this case. Examples include Intake Specialist, Case Coordinator, Addiction Counselor, Employment Counselor, etc. You can identify one of these roles as the case manager for a particular case type.
  • Other Relationships: people related to the client, with relationships that exist beyond the context of a particular case. Examples include Spouse, Sibling, Family Doctor, etc. Generally, use relationships when you want someone to appear on ALL cases for the same client, otherwise use a case role.
  • Case Resources: people and organisations that have involvement with many or all cases in your case management setting. Examples include: regulatory agency contact(s), service provider, frequent referral contacts, etc.

CiviCRM provides relationship type definitions for most of the standard relationships you might track (e.g. Spouse, Child). However you will probably need to define additional relationship types for your case roles, such as:

  • Case Coordinator
  • Addiction Specialist
  • Job Counsellor

Make a list of the expected case roles for each type of case you've listed, then determine which role will normally be considered the case manager for that case type.

docs.title: Key questions
docs.text:
Think about these questions with regard to your organisation's use of CiviCase:

  • What case types do you have? The first step in planning your CiviCase configuration is to think about the types of cases your organisation needs to manage. Complex processes which include several activities, span several days or weeks, and involve multiple people are potentially good candidates for case management. Start by listing these processes and defining a case type for each one.
  • What activity types do you need to have in those cases?
  • Who should activities be assigned to? By default everything might be assigned to a case coordinator who will then reassign to whoever has capacity, or certain activities might require the intervention of a particular individual.
  • Do you have a default timeline and what does it look like?
  • Do activities need to be offset from the start, each other or from the end?
  • What roles are involved? Are existing relationships adequate, or do you need to create some case specific ones?

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text:
Although CiviCase is quite flexible, there are a number of case-management assumptions built-in to the component. These assumptions have been arrived at through an extensive trial and error process and although some of them may seem new or foreign at first, we encourage you to approach them with an open mind.

  • Activities are single tasks or interactions between your organisation and a client or constituent, or between people within your organisation.
  • Cases involve a succession of interactions (activities). The record of these activities forms the case story and almost all information about a case should be stored as an activity.
  • Classifying cases by case type allows you to define work-flows and evaluate results.
  • Cases often have a predictable succession of activities (a standard timeline). Creating a schedule with the expected timeline helps people working on the case to manage their work, and is a useful way to measure progress.
  • Cases often involve a predictable set of people involved (staff, professionals, etc.). These are case roles. Knowing who is playing what role in a case is helpful, and provides an easy way to communicate case activities to other people who are also working on that case.
  • Organisations may have additional people and/or outside organisations (case resources) who are frequently contacted or involved with most or all cases.

docs.title: What is deduping?
docs.text:
Duplicate contacts can enter your database in several ways:

  • An administrator or user creates a contact through the admin interface when that contact already exists.
  • A contact signs up online using a different email address or name from the one already on their record.
  • Duplicate contacts are included in an import.

Duplicates can also arise when people fill in forms about themselves without realising they are already in your list of contacts, perhaps with a differently spelled name or another email address.

docs.title: CiviCRM features for deduplicating contacts
docs.text:
CiviCRM has features that attempt to prevent duplicate contacts from being created and features that help you find and merge duplicates already in your database. Some act automatically, or unsupervised; others involve a user, or supervised.

These features include:

  • Scanning your database for duplicates using a selected dedupe rule and merging duplicate contact data as needed.
  • Selecting two contacts from search results and choosing to merge them.
  • Automatically suggesting duplicates when contacts are added or edited via the user interface.
  • Automatically merging a person's details into an existing contact when they sign up online for Events, Membership, Contributions or Profile pages.
  • Automatically merging a person's details when importing contacts.

docs.title: Dedupe rules
docs.text: Dedupe rules specify when CiviCRM should consider contacts to be duplicates. For example, a rule could treat two contacts as duplicates when both their email addresses and first names match.

docs.title: Using the default rules
docs.text:
If you do not want to configure dedupe rules at this stage, you can use the default rules to find duplicates.

To view the rules, go to Contacts > Find and Merge Duplicate Contacts in the navigation menu.

Different rules are configured for each contact type: individuals, organizations and households. A default supervised rule and a default unsupervised rule are set for each type. CiviCRM uses these default rules for automatic checking, as described below.

docs.title: Understanding supervised, unsupervised and general rules
docs.text:
CiviCRM now includes three categories of dedupe rules:

  • Unsupervised: The 'Unsupervised' rule for each contact type is automatically used when new contacts are created through online registrations, including Events, Membership, Contributions and Profile pages. These rules are also selected by default when you Import contacts. They are generally configured with a narrow definition of a duplicate to avoid accidentally merging a false match.
  • Supervised: The 'Supervised' rule for each contact type is automatically used to check for possible duplicates when contacts are added or edited via the user interface. The UI alerts the user if a contact they are creating matches another contact under the rule. The user can decide whether to edit the existing contact or continue creating a new one. Supervised Rules should have a broader definition of a duplicate because the user can decide whether to act on the match.
  • General: You can configure only one 'Unsupervised' and one 'Supervised' rule for each contact type, but you can configure any number of additional 'General' rules to provide other criteria for finding possible duplicates.

docs.title: Configuring rules
docs.text:
To determine whether two contacts are duplicates, CiviCRM checks up to five fields that you can specify. You can set a length value to determine how many characters in a field are compared. For example, a length of 2 on First Name makes “Mike” match “Michael” because their first two characters are the same. At a length of 3, they do not match. If the length is blank, CiviCRM compares the entire field value.

Each field also has a numeric weight representing the relative importance of a match on that field. When a field matches, its weight is added to the rule's total weight. After each field is checked, contacts are flagged as suspected duplicates if the total weight equals or exceeds the rule's numerical threshold.

docs.title: Using rules and merging duplicate contacts manually
docs.text:
Tip

An alternate UI is available in the deduper extension.

  1. Go to Contacts > Find and Merge Duplicate Contacts.
  2. Click the Use Rule link to scan for duplicate contacts using the selected rule.
  3. Choose whether to search all contacts or limit the search to a particular group. If you choose a group, CiviCRM looks for duplicate pairs where at least one contact is in that group.

Contacts of the type assigned to the rule are scanned and compared. If a pair's match meets or exceeds the rule's threshold score, the contacts appear in a list of possible duplicates. The list has show/hide tickboxes for Street Address, Post Code, Conflicts and Threshold.

  1. Click Merge for a pair to view a table of their details. CiviCRM designates the record in the left column as the duplicate. The record in the right column is the original, into which selected data from the duplicate will be merged.
  2. To move information in the opposite direction, choose Flip between original and duplicate contacts at the top of the page.

  1. Review the colour-coded rows on the merge screen:
  2. Green indicates that the information is the same for both contacts. You can hide these rows by clicking Show/Hide rows with the same data on each contact record.
  3. Red indicates that the information differs. For each field, leave the check-box in the middle column unticked to keep the original data shown on the right, or tick it to use the duplicate contact's value. For email addresses or phone numbers, you can keep both values by ticking both the checkbox in the middle column and “add new” in the right column to copy the duplicate data.
  4. Yellow indicates that the check-box is ticked by default, meaning data from the duplicate will be added to the original record. This applies to tags, groups and activity data, including event attendance and contributions. If you untick the check-box, the duplicate's data will be lost.
  5. Click Merge... to complete the merge, or Mark this pair as not a duplicate if the contacts are not the same.
  6. Contacts marked as 'not a duplicate' are excluded from all dedupe results listings. To review them, click the “View the Dedupe Exceptions” button on the main “Find and Merge Duplicate Contacts” screen.

docs.title: Merging multiple contacts simultaneously
docs.text:
You can merge multiple pairs from the possible duplicates screen, which can display up to 100 rows.

Beneath the list, you can choose Batch Merge All Duplicates, which merges all duplicates found, not just those displayed on your screen. Alternatively, choose Batch Merge Selected Duplicates to merge rows selected using the box on the left. Flip Selected Duplicates is in the same area. When duplicates are merged, Contact 1 is kept and contact 2 is merged and then deleted, so you may want to switch their order first.

Batch merging merges all contacts under the given rule, or all selected contacts, provided there are no data conflicts. For example, two contacts named “Michael Blake” might match on their first and last names while neither has an email address. They can be merged if their data is identical or one has information the other lacks, such as a work phone number on one contact and a mobile number on the other. If both have different home telephone numbers, they are skipped rather than merged.

After a batch merge, you return to the original list. If records were skipped because of data conflicts, a message is displayed. Click Refresh Duplicates to see the updated list of contacts that were not merged; the page does not refresh automatically because searching a large database could cause a significant delay. You can then assess and merge the remaining duplicates manually.

To increase the number of pairs that can be resolved in a batch merge, the deduper extension provides a range of resolutions, including options to make conflicts on certain fields non-blocking or to handle diacritic names.

Batch merging can also be done from the command line, for example:

 echo '{"search_limit": 10000, "criteria":{"contact" : {"id" : {">" : 200}}}}'
   | drush --in=json cvapi Job.process_batch_merge

Would find any contacts that match any of “the first 10000 contacts found with an id greater than 200” and attempt to automtically merge them using the defaults of 'safe' mode (skip when there are conflicts) and the default rules for individuals.

Warning

Before you begin to consider using batch dedupe, please take note of the points below.

  • This feature is intended for use with large data sets that have strictly managed field structures. If you have a small database with only a few duplicates, we recommend you merge them manually using your own judgement.
  • Once merged, the links between the duplicate contact and records elsewhere in the system will be transferred to the original contact (e.g. event participant records, groups, tags, contributions, activities, cases and memberships). You will NOT be able to reverse this change.
  • Duplicate records, once merged, will be deleted and are not recoverable, unless you have database logging enabled. We strongly recommend backing up your data before running a batch merge.

docs.title: A multi-stage deduping process
docs.text:
Using only one dedupe rule can leave duplicates in your system. The following process applies multiple rules systematically. If your individual unsupervised rule is strict enough, you may be able to batch de-dupe in the first stage and dedupe manually in the second.

  1. Look for duplicates using the “Individual unsupervised” rule: click the Use Rule link for contact type “Individual” at the usage “unsupervised”.
  2. Select All Contacts or a particular group.
  3. Click Continue.
  4. If duplicates are found, merge or delete the duplicate contacts.
  5. Look for duplicates missed by the stricter rule using a “supervised” or “general” rule: click the Use Rule link for “Individual supervised” (contact type “Individual” at the usage “supervised”).
  6. Select All Contacts or a particular group.
  7. Click Continue.
  8. If duplicates are found, merge or mark them as 'not a duplicate'.

docs.title: Merging contacts from search results
docs.text:
If you notice duplicate contacts in search results, you can merge them there instead of using the separate Find and Merge Duplicate Contacts process.

  1. Select the duplicate contacts by clicking the check box at the left of each record.
  2. Select Merge Contacts from the Actions menu.
  3. Follow the normal steps for merging duplicate contacts.

docs.title: Exporting your contacts
docs.text:
Exporting provides a copy of CiviCRM data in comma separated value (CSV) format for use in external applications. You can view and edit a CSV file in a spreadsheet application, import it into another database application, or merge it with a word processing document.

You can export a predefined set of fields or create a custom export mapping and save it for reuse.

Exporting is available:

  • In any of the search tools.
  • When viewing contacts in a group.
  • In component-based search results, where the records reflect component-specific data rather than only core contact data. For example, from Contributions > Find Contributions, you could export donors and their contact information for a thank-you letter that includes the total amount donated.

docs.title: Export contact information
docs.text:
1. Search for contacts using your desired criteria in Quick search, Find Contacts, Advanced search, Search Builder, or a custom search. For more information, see Searching.
  2. Select all records, or use the check-boxes to the left of each record to select individual contacts.

  3. From the - actions - dropdown menu, choose Export Contacts. This opens the export wizard.

  4. Choose whether to export the primary fields or select your own fields.

    A primary fields export contains 80 fields: core contact fields with primary email, phone, and address data. Selecting your own fields lets you include non-primary email, phone, and address data, custom contact fields, and data from related contacts. You can also use a previously saved export mapping, if you have one.

    • For mailing labels, choose whether to export one record per household or one per address. If you choose one record per address, you can specify the format for Addressee and the postal greeting.
    • You can exclude contacts with "do not mail" privacy, no street address, or who are deceased.
    • You can add contacts from an additional group to the export.

  5. Click Continue. If you chose the primary fields, the export happens immediately; go to step 7. If you chose your own fields or a saved field mapping, continue to step 6.

  6. Select the fields to export.

    • If you chose a saved export mapping, its fields are displayed. You can use the mapping as is or modify it. If you modify it, you can update the existing field mapping or save the changes as a new field mapping.
    • If you are creating a new mapping, choose the fields you want, then decide whether to Save this field mapping for later use.
    • When the fields and other options are correct, click Export.

  7. The file is exported in .CSV format. By default, a comma is used as the field separator for import and export functions. If required, change the separator at Administer > Localization > Languages, Currency, Locations by selecting the appropriate Import/Export Field Separator.

docs.title: Importing related contact data
docs.text:
Import a separate CSV file for each type of related data, such as organisational addresses with employees, parent–child relationships, activities or contributions.

CiviCRM has specific tools for importing related contact data, and specific import tools for contributions, memberships and event participation. See their respective chapters for details. To import relationships, run multiple contact imports.

For example, importing a child and both parents takes three imports: one for the child, one for the father and one for the mother.

  1. Import the child with an external identifier that can be used to match the child to the parents.
  2. Import the father as a related contact, linking him to the child using the child’s external identifier.
  3. Import the mother as a related contact in the same way.

In the example below, one CSV file contains both father and mother information. It is used twice during the import. The images show the fields used.

The father is linked to the original child using the external identifier, and the related father name is imported using the ‘Child of’ relationship type.

After the import, search for the parent and examine the relationship tab. The parent should have a relationship linking them to the child. Repeat the process for the mother and for other relationships as necessary.

docs.title: Import requirements for activities, contributions, memberships, participants and tags
Import activities
docs.text:
To insert new activities, the CSV file must include at least:

  • Activity Date
  • Activity Type ID
  • Target Contact ID (Match to Contact)
  • Subject

To update existing activities, the CSV file must include at least:

  • Activity ID
  • Activity Date
  • Activity Type ID
  • Target Contact ID (Match to Contact)
  • Subject

Target Contact ID attaches the activity to the contact the activity is done on. Import contacts before running the activity import; these are separate import jobs.

docs.title: Import contributions
docs.text:
You can insert new contributions or update existing ones. If you are on a recent version of CiviCRM and enable the Civi-Import extension, you can also create or update the contact and any soft credit contacts in the same import.

To insert new contributions, the CSV file must include at least:

  • Fields to match (or create) the contact.
  • Financial Type
  • Total Amount

The contact fields required depend on whether Civi-Import is enabled. If it is not, you need:

  • Contact ID or External Identifier or all the fields used in your Unsupervised Duplicate Matching rule (to match to an existing contact)

If CiviImport is enabled, the above still applies to matching contacts, but you can specify which Dedupe rule to use.

See also

Importing contributions in the Contributions chapter.

To update existing contributions, the CSV file must include at least:

  • Transaction ID or Invoice ID or Payment ID (to match to an existing contribution)
  • Financial Type
  • Total Amount

You can also use update existing contributions to import new data or change existing data in other core or custom contribution fields. Include an ID to match the existing contribution, plus Financial Type and Total Amount in the CSV file, even if the values for those fields have not changed.

docs.title: Import memberships
docs.text:
You can insert new memberships or update existing memberships.

To insert new memberships, the CSV file must include at least:

  • Contact Id or External Identifier or all the fields used in your Unsupervised Duplicate Matching rule (to match to an existing contact)
  • Membership Type
  • Membership Start Date

To update existing memberships, the CSV file must include at least:

  • Membership Id (to match to an existing membership)
  • Membership Type
  • Membership Start Date

You can also use update existing memberships to import new data or change existing data in other core or custom membership fields. Include Membership ID to match the existing membership, plus Membership Type and Membership Start Date in the CSV file, even if the values for those fields have not changed.

See also

Importing memberships in the Memberships chapter.

docs.title: Import participants
docs.text:
In each import session, you can either insert new registrations or update existing participant records.

To insert new registrations, decide whether to restrict registrations for each event to one per person (set On duplicate entries to Skip) or allow duplicate registrations for the same event from a contact (set On duplicate entries to No Duplicate Checking). In either case, the CSV file must include at least:

  • Contact Id or External Identifier or all the fields used in your Unsupervised Duplicate Matching rule (to match to an existing contact)
  • Event ID
  • Participant Status

To update existing registrations, set On duplicate entries to Update. The CSV file must include at least:

  • Participant ID (to match to an existing registration)
  • Event ID or Event Title
  • Participant Status

You can also use update existing registrations to import new data or change existing data in custom participant fields. Include Participant ID to match the existing registration, plus Event ID or Event Title and Participant Status in the CSV file, even if the values for those fields have not changed.

docs.title: Import tags
docs.text:
There is currently no inbuilt way to import tags or tag sets. You can use this advanced extension.

To assign individual tags during a contact import, either:

  • Split the CSV file by individual tags and import each subset separately as described above.
  • Create temporary custom fields and import tags into them as standard data. After import, use advanced searches to isolate contacts with particular values and mass tag them. You can remove the custom fields when finished.

docs.title: Importing data into CiviCRM
docs.text:
Most organisations have data outside CiviCRM, such as data in previously used database platforms, spreadsheets created for specific events or other purposes, and email address books. Manually entering large amounts of data can be tedious. CiviCRM provides a way to import data en masse if the source can export it into a common format such as a Comma Separated Version (CSV) file.

Imports can also update existing data. The options for updating contacts are covered under Running an import.

docs.title: Considerations before importing
docs.text: For more detail on how to think about your data before importing it into CiviCRM, read “Organizing your data”, especially “Mapping your data into CiviCRM”.

docs.title: Preparing to import data
docs.text:
Importing data requires attention and care. You can import core and custom data for contacts, as well as data for event attendance, activities, memberships, and contributions. This page focuses on the contact import process; the processes for other data are similar.

There are two ways to import data:

  • From CSV files. Most database and spreadsheet applications (e.g. OpenOffice.org Calc, Google Spreadsheets, Microsoft Excel) can create and manipulate CSV files. It is often easier to view and clean data in a CSV file than in an old database. Each column maps to a CiviCRM field, so use a different column for every distinct bit of information.

    Depending on your country or region, fields in CSV files might be separated by semicolons (;) instead of commas. If so, change the Import/Export Field Separator value in the CiviCRM Localization settings by going to Administer > Configure > Global Settings > Localization in the navigation menu.

  • From another SQL or MySQL database stored on the same server, using an SQL query. This option is only for advanced users with a clear understanding of server and database administration.

If you do not understand your existing data and how it maps to CiviCRM fields, you may encounter problems during import. Read about each type of data in the other sections of this CiviCRM Manual.

The following recommendations can help you prepare:

  • Test an import with a small subset of records. After importing the test set, visit the records in CiviCRM and check that the data was imported and functions as expected.
  • Consider creating a test contact with every attribute defined in your existing data set. Import that contact and check that CiviCRM represents all the data correctly.
  • When mapping source columns or fields to CiviCRM fields, you can save the mapping as an import map for future use. This helps when importing multiple files with the same structure. To save one, click the “Save this field mapping” check-box at the bottom of the Match Fields screen of the import wizard, then enter a name and description. To reuse it, select it from the Load Saved Field Mapping dropdown menu on the Choose Data Source screen (step 1).
  • If imports time out or take too long, try smaller batches. If you have the appropriate permissions on your web server, you can also increase the memory_limit and max_execution_time values in php.ini.
  • You can add all contacts in an import to new or existing groups or tags. Every contact in a single import receives the same groups and tags:
    • Assign only groups and tags that apply to every contact in the set. For contact-by-contact assignments, import small, discrete batches whose contacts share the same groups and tags. Alternatively, create searchable custom data fields containing the groups and tags you want to assign. After import, search those fields and use the “Add Contacts to Group” or “Tag Contacts” batch actions on the results.
    • You can use a new group or tag to identify an import batch. This can help you find when contacts were imported and undo an entire import if necessary.
  • Put first and last names in separate CSV columns, because CiviCRM stores them in separate fields. Do the same for city and postal code/zip code. Most spreadsheet programs have tools for splitting text across fields.
  • Express country names as they appear in CiviCRM: for example, ‘United States’ rather than ‘United States of America’, and ‘United Kingdom’ rather than ‘Britain’.
  • If importing multiple locations, the first becomes the primary location address. You may need to move columns so that the desired location becomes the Primary Location, or split the import if different records need different types of Primary Location.
  • If you choose the location type ‘Primary’ for an address field, it updates an existing contact’s primary address, if there is one. For a new contact, or a contact without an existing address, the location type will be your site’s default.
  • When importing into multi-choice custom fields, such as check-boxes or radio buttons, the data source can use either the label visible in CiviCRM or the value stored in the database. For multi-choice core data fields, specify only the value(s), not the label.
  • When updating multiple-choice options, new values replace the entire field. For example, updating a contact’s Colors field from “blue” to “orange” results in orange, not orange and blue.
  • To import multiple values into a multiple-choice field, use the “,” (comma) character as a separator, using either the Label OR the Value of the required options: for example, “1, 2, 3” or “fred, red, yellow”.
  • Use an accepted date format in the data source and select the same format on the Choose Data Source screen of the import wizard.
  • Set up any name prefixes and suffixes you use in the administration interface at Administer > Option Lists in the navigation menu.
  • If you plan later imports of related data, such as contributions, event participation, or memberships, give contact records unique IDs that also appear in the related data. In the initial contact import, map those IDs to CiviCRM’s External ID field. You can then use the original, or legacy, IDs to match contacts in later imports.
  • Master Address Belongs To is a special import field that works only with CiviCRM_Address.id. The information needed to use it is available only directly from the MySQL database tables. It is not shown elsewhere in CiviCRM, including data screens, link urls, profiles, or exports. Information on how to use this special field is available in the Wiki.

docs.title: Required fields for contact imports
docs.text:
Include the required fields in your CSV import file. They are marked red and starred in the interface. If you have less data, selecting one field is enough. The External Identifier field is useful only if you want to update existing contacts. The field marked (Match to Contact) is required for deduplication purposes.

  • Email (Match to Contact)
  • External Identifier
  • First Name
  • Last Name

docs.title: Setting up a CSV file for importing
docs.text:
The following image shows an example spreadsheet in .csv format:

Plan your column headings around the data you are collecting. You may need more than one .csv file and multiple imports.

If you plan to import related data for a contact, such as event participant information or contributions, make sure each contact record has a unique identifier, or has First Name, Last Name and Email, so you can link related data in later imports. If you have a unique ID, map it to CiviCRM’s External Identifier on import.

docs.title: Address standardisation
docs.text:
For many organisations, standardising addresses is an important part of cleaning data. In the US, this means conforming to conventions defined by the United States Postal Service’s Standards for Addresses. Standardised addresses can improve address search results because CiviCRM can parse addresses based on USPS standards if you choose to do so.

For more on how Address Parsing is handled and used in CiviCRM, refer to the Installation chapter of the Configuration section of this manual. When adding or editing contacts, enter and edit elements such as street number, street name, and Apt/Unit/Suite number according to these standards.

docs.title: Running an import
docs.text: The import process has four steps.

docs.title: Step 1: Setup
docs.text:
Specify the basic details of the import, including its data source: a CSV file or an SQL query of a database on your server. A check-box lets you indicate whether the first row of the file contains column headers.

Imports use the default unsupervised Dedupe Rule to decide whether a contact is a duplicate, unless you select another Dedupe Rule during this step. Refer to the Deduping and Merging chapter in this section for information on duplicate matching rules.

Choose what happens when the import encounters a duplicate:

  • Skip: Leave the original record unchanged.
  • Update: Update the original record with database fields from the import data. Fields absent from the import data remain unchanged.
  • Fill: Add imported data to fields that are missing or blank in the original record. Fields with existing values remain unchanged.
  • No Duplicate Checking: Insert all valid records without comparing them with existing contacts.

You can match imported data directly to existing Contact IDs only in Update, Fill or No Duplicate Checking modes.

Import mappings tell CiviCRM how fields in the import file correspond to CiviCRM fields. The first time you import from a particular data source, it is a good idea to check “Save this field mapping” at the bottom of the page before continuing. You can request that the saved mapping be loaded at this step for a later import of similar data.

docs.title: Step 2: Match the fields
docs.text:
If the file has column headings, they appear in the first column on the left-hand side of the Field Map. The next two columns show two rows of data to be imported; the fourth shows the Matching CiviCRM Field. If you loaded an import mapping in Step 1, its choices appear here. You can change them for this import.

Matching CiviCRM fields include standard fields such as First Name and Last Name, as well as custom data fields configured for contacts on your site. Use the dropdown list to match each field. For example, match a source column headed Surname to Last Name.

Select “- do not import -” for columns you do not want to import.

You can modify and save a mapping when a spreadsheet gains new columns. Put new columns to the right of those previously mapped in CiviCRM. This lets you reuse the saved mapping for the original fields and then map the new ones.

If you add new columns before previously mapped columns, you cannot use the saved mapping and must map all import fields again. After mapping, either leave the original saved mapping unchanged or check “Update this field mapping” to include the new mappings.

docs.title: Step 3: Preview
docs.text:
The preview reports the number of rows to be imported and lets you check the field matches.

If rows contain data that does not meet CiviCRM’s requirements for one or more fields, an error message shows the number of invalid rows. Click Download Errors, review the errors in the downloaded file, and fix them before importing.

At the bottom of the form, you can add contacts to an existing group, import to a new group, create a new tag, or tag imported records. Adding imported records to a separate group is strongly recommended so you can find them quickly and, if necessary, delete and reimport them.

docs.title: Step 4: Summary
docs.text:
The final screen reports successful imports, Duplicate Contacts and Errors. If you set the import to add all contacts to a Group or Tag, you can click through to see the imported contact records.

Search for the contacts you imported. Examine their fields and custom data to check that the import worked as expected.

docs.title: Postal mail communications
docs.text: CiviCRM supports postal mail and postal mail campaigns. This page assumes a strong understanding of CiviCRM's search features, custom fields, activities, profiles, and mail merges using word processing software.

docs.title: Planning your mailing
docs.text:
Before sending postal mail, identify your goals and plan the steps. Consider:

  • What types of mailing do you send to your constituents?
  • Do you send mailings to everyone in the database, or do you frequently target a select group of contacts?
  • How do you want to greet recipients (for example, "Dear Jane" or "Dear Jane Doe")?

There are three ways to use CiviCRM for postal mailings:

  1. Generate labels: print standard address labels when you don't need to personalise the content, for instance to send a printed brochure.
  2. Export contacts and do a mail merge in an external tool, such as OpenOffice or Microsoft Word. See Exporting for detailed exporting instructions.
  3. Use CiviCRM's Print/merge document function to do the merge directly in CiviCRM.

Many nonprofit organisations in the USA need to sort mailing recipients by zip code for bulk mailing. If this applies to your organisation, create mailing labels in a word processor where you can control the sort order, rather than in CiviCRM. You can reuse the same spreadsheet for your mail merge.

docs.title: Greetings and salutations
docs.text:
You can set a postal greeting format for each contact, from the friendly "Dear John" to the more formal "Dear Mr. John Doe". You can also enter a customized greeting, such as "Your royal highness".

Edit postal greetings in the Communications Preferences section of the contact edit form. To set or reset postal greetings en mass, see Scheduled Jobs and the wiki documentation.

docs.title: Print/merge document
docs.text:
CiviCRM provides tools to create merge letters directly from the interface. You can insert tokens representing database fields into a letter, optionally save it as a template, and output it in PDF, HTML, Word (.docx), or Open Document (.odt) format.

To create a letter:

  1. Conduct a search (for example Search > Find Contacts > Advanced Search, or a Custom Search. If you want to print letters for members of a Group, go to Contacts > Manage Groups and click "Contacts" next to the Group you want.
  2. Enter your search criteria and click Search (not applicable if using a Group).
  3. Select the contacts who will receive the letter.
  4. From the Actions dropdown menu, choose Print/merge document.
  5. Optionally select a template as the basis for your letter. You may also associate the letter with a Campaign.
  6. Review Page Format and make any desired adjustments to the paper size, margins, and page orientation.
  7. Enter your text and adjust its formatting in the WYSIWYG editor. You can also insert image files, such as your organisation's logo or a signature. Click in the body of the letter where you want the image to appear, then click the Image icon.

  8. Personalise the letter with tokens, which are placeholders replaced with field values for each selected contact. Postal Greeting is a commonly used token. Click in the body of the letter where you want the token, then click the Insert Tokens dropdown above the letter at the top right and select the desired token.

  9. Decide whether to save the letter as a new template for future use. If the letter was based on a template, you can update the existing template. Saving a letter as a template can streamline future workflows.

  10. Select an output format: PDF, HTML, MS Word (.docx), or Open Document (.odt). Depending on the complexity of the letter, some formats may handle its layout and design better than others.
  11. Click Download Document to generate the letter(s). Depending on your browser configuration, a pop-up may ask where to save the file, or you may be prompted to open it immediately. After the download completes, review the file's formatting. The window remains open so you can adjust the letter and generate it again.

You can also use Print/merge document for documents other than letters, such as attendance certificates for a workshop.

Generating many letters can be resource intensive, particularly with PDF output. If this happens, consider implementing the wkhtmltopdf alternate PDF generation tool, which scales to higher volumes better than the default tool. Visit Administer > Misc > Path to wkhtmltopdf executable for details.

The Print/merge document action is also available from the Actions dropdown in a contact record. For contributions, you can use the Thank you letters search result action after using Find Contributions.

docs.title: Generate mailing labels
docs.text:
1. Perform a search to select the contacts you want to target.
  2. Choose Mailing Labels from the Actions dropdown menu and click Go.
  3. Select the mailing label style.
  4. Decide whether to exclude people with "do not mail" checked in their privacy options (checked by default and recommended), and whether to merge records with the same mailing address into one label.

Merging records with the same mailing address helps avoid duplicate mailings to households or organisations. Each name at that address appears on a separate line on the label.

Your system administrator can configure the fields included in mailing labels. See the information on configuring address settings in the Contacts chapter for the available options.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: You can use data in your CiviCRM database to set up mail merged communications both for emails and printed materials such as letters and mailing labels. The mail merging functionality relies on "tokens", which represent fields in your database. For example, use the Postal Greeting token to include a customized greeting for each recipient in your PDF letters. Most contact fields, including custom fields you've created, are available as mail merge tokens.

docs.title: Basic contact data tokens
docs.text:
If you want each email to address the person by first name after "Dear," type a space and then click Insert Tokens at the top right of the HTML Format field.

In the popup, type "First name" in the box and choose the corresponding token. Click Close. Your message now reads "Dear {firstname}." When the email is sent, the appropriate first name will be inserted into each message. Browse the Inset Tokens pop-up for a complete list of contact data tokens, including any custom fields created for your site.

docs.title: Organizational tokens
docs.text: In addition to basic contact data, you can insert standard organization information, such as "Domain (organizational) address," which displays the address of your organization as defined at Administer > Communications > Organization Address and Contact Info.

docs.title: Special tokens available for emails
docs.text:
Some additional tokens are available for use in emails.

Note

In the HTML format editing area, tokens that generate URLs (links) need to be placed in the URL field of the Link creation screen. Otherwise, they will display as text and not a clickable link in the email client of the recipient.

docs.title: Action tokens
docs.text: You can insert action tokens, such as opt-out and unsubscribe tokens. These tokens insert links to take the specified action; to display the links properly in HTML messages, you'll need to add the proper link tags using the Source icon in the editor.

docs.title: Required opt-out tokens for mass emails
docs.text:
You are required to include a token for either opt-out token, {action.optOutUrl} or unsubscribe token, {action.unsubscribeUrl}, as well as the organizational address token, {domain.address} in every CiviMail mailing. You can place these directly in the mailing body, header, or footer. If your organization has developed a standard mailing footer, include these tokens in the footer so that folks don't have to think about them each time they create a new mailing.

In general, including click-able unsubscribe and opt-out links is a bit friendlier for recipients than the reply-to via email method. You can also provide both options.

Some tokens are only available for mass mailings, such as the token to provide a link to a message stored online.

For more details, see opt-out token, unsubscribe token and organizational (domain) address token.

docs.title: Checksum tokens
docs.text:
A particularly useful token is the checksum. The checksum allows you to give people links to contribution forms, profiles, petitions, and event registration forms that are pre-filled with information already in their contact record. This saves your constituents the hassle of filling out forms and increases the chances they will take action (e.g., donate, sign up for an event, sign the petition). It can also be a simple way to keep your data current by asking people to review and update their contact information.

Warning

For security purposes, checksum links only last for seven days, starting from the time the email is sent. To change this duration, go to Administer > System Settings > Misc (Undelete, PDFs, Limits, Logging, etc.). Take caution when adjusting the limit because longer duration means that anyone with the URL will be able to access the account of that user. In some cases, this might mean the user gains full access to their account for long periods.

Note

For tokens to use with Form Builder, see secret links section in creating new forms.

Create a link in the CiviMail message that includes the checksum token {contact.checksum}. When people click on the special link, CiviCRM looks them up in the database and prefills any information on the contribution form or profile with any data that exists in their record.

{contact.checksum} will give the full cs=checksum, so you don't need to add the cs= key to URLs yourself, while {contact.checksum_value} only gives the checksum itself.

docs.title: Checksum for contribution pages
docs.text:
To send people to a contribution page, use this path where IDNUMBER is the ID of your contribution page:

  • Drupal: http://example.org/civicrm/contribute/transact?reset=1&id=IDNUMBER&{contact.checksum}&cid={contact.contact_id}
  • Joomla!: http://example.org/index.php?option=com_civicrm&task=civicrm/contribute/transact&reset=1&id=IDNUMBER&{contact.checksum}&cid={contact.contact_id}
  • WordPress (with Clean URLs): http://example.org/civicrm/contribute/transact?reset=1&id=IDNUMBER&{contact.checksum}&cid={contact.contact_id}
  • WordPress (without Clean URLs): http://example.org/?civiwp=CiviCRM&q=civicrm/contribute/transact&reset=1&id=IDNUMBER&{contact.checksum}&cid={contact.contact_id}

docs.title: Checksum for contribution pages for membership renewals
docs.text:
To send people to a contribution page for membership renewals, use this path where IDNUMBER is the ID of your contribution page. This is typically used in Scheduled Reminders for membership renewals, where the membership.id will be evaluated to the membership to be renewed:

  • Backdrop/Drupal: http://example.org/civicrm/contribute/transact?reset=1&id=IDNUMBER&{contact.checksum}&cid={contact.contact_id}&mid={membership.id}
  • Joomla!: http://example.org/index.php?option=com_civicrm&task=civicrm/contribute/transact&reset=1&id=IDNUMBER&{contact.checksum}&cid={contact.contact_id}&mid={membership.id}
  • WordPress (with Clean URLs): http://example.org/civicrm/contribute/transact?reset=1&id=IDNUMBER&{contact.checksum}&cid={contact.contact_id}&mid={membership.id}
  • WordPress (without Clean URLs): http://example.org/?civiwp=CiviCRM&q=civicrm/contribute/transact&reset=1&id=IDNUMBER&{contact.checksum}&cid={contact.contact_id}&mid={membership.id}

docs.title: Checksum for standard profiles
docs.text:
To send people to a profile, use this path where IDNUMBER is the ID of the Profile you want to send them to:

  • Drupal: http://example.org/civicrm/profile/edit?reset=1&gid=IDNUMBER&{contact.checksum}&id={contact.contact_id}
  • Joomla!: http://example.org/index.php?option=com_civicrm&task=civicrm/profile/edit&reset=1&gid=IDNUMBER&{contact.checksum}&id={contact.contact_id}
  • WordPress (with Clean URLs): http://example.org/civicrm/profile/edit?reset=1&gid=IDNUMBER&{contact.checksum}&id={contact.contact_id}
  • WordPress (without Clean URLs): http://example.org/?civiwp=CiviCRM&q=civicrm/profile/edit&reset=1&gid=IDNUMBER&{contact.checksum}&id={contact.contact_id}

docs.title: Checksum for event registration pages
docs.text:
To send people to an event registration page, use this path where IDNUMBER is the ID of your event:

  • Drupal: http://example.org/civicrm/event/register?reset=1&id=IDNUMBER&{contact.checksum}&cid={contact.contact_id}
  • Joomla!: http://example.org/index.php?option=com_civicrm&task=civicrm/event/register&reset=1&id=IDNUMBER&{contact.checksum}&cid={contact.contact_id}
  • WordPress (with Clean URLs): http://example.org/civicrm/event/register?reset=1&id=IDNUMBER&{contact.checksum}&cid={contact.contact_id}
  • WordPress (without Clean URLS): http://example.org/?civiwp=CiviCRM&q=civicrm/event/register&reset=1&id=IDNUMBER&{contact.checksum}&cid={contact.contact_id}

docs.title: Checksum for petition signature pages
docs.text:
To send people to sign a Petition, use this path where IDNUMBER is the ID of your petition:

  • Drupal: http://example.org/civicrm/petition/sign?reset=1&sid=IDNUMBER&{contact.checksum}&cid={contact.contact_id}
  • Joomla!: http://example.org/index.php?option=com_civicrm&task=civicrm/petition/sign&reset=1&sid=IDNUMBER&{contact.checksum}&cid={contact.contact_id}
  • WordPress (with Clean URLs): http://example.org/civicrm/petition/sign?sid=IDNUMBER&reset=1&{contact.checksum}&cid={contact.contact_id}
  • WordPress (without Clean URLS): http://example.org/?civiwp=CiviCRM&q=civicrm/petition/sign&sid=IDNUMBER&reset=1&{contact.checksum}&cid={contact.contact_id}

docs.title: Checksum for mail 'view in browser' links
docs.text:
In CiviMail you can use a special link to allow contacts to view the email content in their browser, including the content personalised with tokens.

  • Drupal: http://example.org/civicrm/mailing/view?reset=1&id={mailing.key}&cid={contact.contact_id}&{contact.checksum}
  • Joomla!: http://example.org/index.php?option=com_civicrm&task=civicrm/mailing/view&id={mailing.key}&{contact.checksum}&cid={contact.contact_id}
  • WordPress (with Clean URLs): http://example.org/civicrm/mailing/view?id={mailing.key}&{contact.checksum}&cid={contact.contact_id}
  • WordPress (without Clean URLS): http://example.org/?civiwp=CiviCRM&q=civicrm/mailing/view&id={mailing.key}&{contact.checksum}&cid={contact.contact_id}

docs.title: Site tokens
docs.text:
Starting in CiviCRM 5.76, Site Tokens allow site administrators to define pre-set snippets which can then be inserted into various content via CiviCRM's standard token-handling features. Site Tokens marked as "reserved" are also inserted automatically in specific places within CiviCRM features, such as Message Templates.

For example, the {site.message_header} token is automatically inserted into the top of every Message Template. By default this token has an empty value, but site administrators may wish to edit its content to include an organization logo or other branding that should appear at the top of Message Templates. (This removes the need to edit Message Templates directly in order merely to add a logo.)

In addition, you may create any numuber of additional Site Tokens for your own purposes.

Like other tokens, Site Tokens are available in the Insert Tokens utility in various CiviCRM features, grouped in a section labeled "Site". For example, after you've defined a Site Token labeled "Lorem Ipsum", when creating an email, that token is available:

Users with the "edit system workflow message templates" permission can manage Site Tokens by navigating to Administer > Communications > Site Tokens.

See Available Tokens below for details on specific Site Tokens provided and managed by CiviCRM.

docs.title: Custom tokens
docs.text: Developers can create custom tokens which can, for example, display the total amount of contributions from a contact. See the Developer Guide for more info about custom tokens.

docs.title: Date tokens
docs.text:
Dates and times are presented in many ways — using full words (e.g. "September" or "Sunday"), abbreviations ("Sept", "Mon"), numbers, different regional formats (e.g. MM/DD/YYYY vs DD/MM/YYYY), and so on.

During system setup, the administrator may configure date preferences. Tokens such as {event.start_date}, {domain.now}, and {contact.created_date} will be formatted automatically based on these preferences.

Alternatively, you may customize the format of each token individually. This requires the |crmDate filter (CiviCRM v5.43+). Common ways to format a date include:

  • Configured Formats: CiviCRM includes ~7 configurable formats. On new deployments, the initial configuration is tuned to English (US) conventions, but they are often adjusted depending on the organization's language and locale. Here are some examples of how the {domain.now} token could be formatted:

    Format Name Example Token Example Value (US English) "Complete Date and Time" (default) {domain.now|crmDate:"Datetime"} September 18th, 2022 11:58 PM "Complete Date" (default) {domain.now|crmDate:"Full"} September 19th, 2022 "Short Date" {domain.now|crmDate:"shortdate"} 09/18/2022 "Month and Year" {domain.now|crmDate:"Partial"} September, 2022 "Time Only" {domain.now|crmDate:"Time"} 1:34 PM "Year Only" {domain.now|crmDate:"Year"} 2022 "Financial Batch" {domain.now|crmDate:"FinancialBatch"} 09/19/2022

  • Adhoc Formats: The adhoc formatting codes allow full access to a range of details, including the conventional month, day, and year (numbers) as well as day-of-week, day-of-year, week-of-year, timezone, and so on. Here are some examples of how the {domain.now} token could be formatted:

    Example Token Example Value {domain.now|crmDate:"%B %Y"} September 2022 {domain.now|crmDate:"%m/%Y"} 09/2022 {domain.now|crmDate:"%l:%M %P"} 1:34 PM

    For a full list of formatting codes, please see PHP Manual: strftime().

docs.title: Smarty in mail templates
docs.text:
Mail templates use Smarty to include variables, tokens & functions. A more thorough tutorial can be found at http://www.smarty.net/manual. For example, you can use Smarty for if/then logic.

System administrator required

For Smarty to work you must add (or modify) the following line to your civicrm.settings.php file located under sites/default/ for Drupal and administrator/components/com_civicrm for Joomla.

phpdefine('CIVICRM_MAIL_SMARTY', 1);

Tips:

  • You can use CiviCRM tokens within Smarty. If you want to check if a field has a value before using it, use the |boolean modifier:

    {if {contact.email_primary.email|boolean}}
  Email: {contact.email_primary.email|boolean}
{/if}

docs.title: Modifiers for CiviCRM tokens
docs.text:
Modifiers can be used for CiviCRM tokens by adding them to the token after a pipe, e.g. {contribution.total_amount}. Modifiers available for CiviCRM tokens include:

  • upper: Uppercase
  • lower: Lowercase
  • capitalize: Title case (each word capitalized)
  • boolean: Returns 0 or 1
  • crmDate: Formats a date, see Date Tokens
  • default: Returns the value if it exists and isn't falsy in PHP, or the value you provide if not, e.g. {contact.first_name|default:"friend"} returns friend if the contact has no first name.

docs.title: CiviMail click tracking of links with tokens in link URLs
docs.text:
Up to CiviCRM version 5.34 CiviMail’s link click tracking would ignore links with tokens in, so if you had a call to action that used a token in its URL, it was not possible to see how many recipients clicked that link. From CiviCRM version 5.35, using the FlexMailer extension which is shipped with CiviCRM itself, it is possible to track links that include tokens in the query parameters of a URL.
