The chapters in this section cover how to use CiviMember. If you are new to it, review the entire section while considering your organisation's membership scheme and how best to model it within CiviCRM. CiviMember can be configured to meet most requirements.

Adopting CiviCRM will normally require some changes in working practices. As you develop your plans, work closely with the people in your organisation who will manage memberships day to day.

Memberships can last from a day to a lifetime. They can be free or paid, with simple or complex pricing structures. They can be set up to auto-renew where a compatible payment processor is enabled.

A contact's memberships are visible on the contact's summary screen and on the membership dashboard. You can find them through the Membership Search or Advanced Search. CiviMember also provides four membership reports, each of which can be customised to better meet your needs.

Conceptually, members are contacts in your CiviCRM database with one or more memberships. A contact may be an individual, a household, an organisation, or another contact sub-type; the membership is always applied to a contact.

docs.title: Scenario: Driving membership forward
docs.text:
The Atlantic Region Public Transit Association (ARPTA) has four membership categories:

  • Regular Members: Public transit systems. This category has three tiered levels based on the size of the system. Membership is organization-based, and all employees of the member organization receive access to member benefits, such as discounted rates at Association events.
  • Affiliate Members: Businesses providing goods and services to the transit industry. Fees are the same for all Affiliate Members. Membership is organization-based, and up to 10 employees of the member organization receive access to member benefits, such as discounted rates at Association events.
  • Associate Members: Students, government representatives, public interest groups, research institutions, and other interested parties. Fees are the same for all Associate Members. Membership is individual-based.
  • Honorary Members: Retired transit system executives and others who have made a notable contribution to the industry and Association. Membership is individual-based and free for life.

When ARPTA's membership administrator, Sue, initially configured CiviMember, she created a separate membership type for each of the four categories. CiviMember managed this easily. At first, ARPTA continued to process renewals and new sign-ups manually while the system bedded in.

Last year, ARPTA's board agreed that they needed to increase membership income by improving recruitment and renewal rates. They also wanted to keep tight control of the time spent on membership administration and, if possible, reduce it.

To help achieve this, ARPTA used CiviContribute and CiviMember to set up online sign-up and renewal pages for Regular and Affiliate Members. They ran targeted recruitment campaigns linking to the sign-up pages so potential members could join online. Existing members were encouraged to renew online by logging in to the member section of the ARPTA website.

These changes streamlined sign-up and eliminated much of the administrative work. They also gave Sue a clear view of new sign-ups, recent renewals, and expired members who needed to be chased. Through CiviContribute, she can produce a monthly spreadsheet of membership fees received for the accounts department to import into its accounting software. With less paperwork, she can engage more with members and take a greater part in the annual conference, which ARPTA manages using CiviEvent.

ARPTA's board were also pleased with the results of the move to online sign-up and renewal, which, in conjunction with their marketing campaign, led to a 30% jump in new members over a year. Their analysis also showed a 40% improvement in membership retention (in part because Sue was able to devote more time to contacting lapsed and expired members, and in part because members reported that they found it easy and convenient to renew online, and were prompted to do so by the reminder emails that Sue had set up using the Schedule Reminders feature. Their market research also showed that members appreciated the fact that they were being contacted more regularly by Sue, and felt more engaged with ARPTA as a result.

docs.title: Popular extensions
docs.text:
These are widely used extensions in the relevant category of the official CiviCRM Extensions Directory. Usage is a popularity signal, not a compatibility or suitability guarantee.

  • CiviDiscount — reported usage: 1,834
  • Fuzion Tokens — reported usage: 1,489
  • Line Item Editor — reported usage: 565
  • Percentage Price Field — reported usage: 385
  • Membership Extras — reported usage: 295

All extensions for this component

Check development status, current CiviCRM compatibility, CMS requirements, and release notes before installation.

Usage snapshot reviewed: 2026-10-13.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activities provide a unified place to record and view the history of interactions between your organization and your constituents, clients and partners. You can use Activities to track meetings, phone calls and other Activities that you set up. All of CiviCRM's components also use Activities to record things like when contributions are made, when people come to events and when people sign petitions.

All Activities happen at a specific point in time and involve at least one contact; many involve more than one. Activities can be assigned to staff or volunteers, and an email is automatically sent to the assignee.

If it is important to know who at your organisation carried out a task, record it as an Activity. You can record an Activity between a given contact and multiple other contacts by adding as many contacts as you like in the With Contact field on the Add Activity form.

Several types of Activities are included by default, but administrators can create additional Activity Types to define specific things that your organisation does.

Activities have the following attributes by default:

  • date and time: Activities always happen at a certain point in time
  • duration: so you can collect all the time spent on a series of Activities
  • status: is the Activity scheduled, completed, cancelled, etc.
  • added by: the person who added this Activity, or the contact if they carried out the Activity themselves via the website
  • assigned to: the person (usually within your organisation) that will carry out (or has carried out) the Activity
  • with contact(s): the contacts in your database that are the subject of the Activity.

docs.title: Activities and groups
docs.text:
There can be some overlap between the use of Activities and groups. For example, you could record a membership packet being sent to a contact as an Activity or simply add the contact to a group "received membership packet".

Recording it as an Activity would probably be better: you can record when the membership pack was sent, who sent it and any notes about what the person requested. You could also use the Activity to schedule sending membership packs by setting the date to a future day and time and setting the status to "scheduled".

docs.title: Activities and events
docs.text: An event is something that a contact attends, such as a meet-up, a training, a dinner or fundraising event. An Activity can be any type of interaction a contact has with your organisation, from a meeting or a phone call to a donation.

docs.title: Activity status options
docs.text:
The default set of status options is:

  • Scheduled
  • Completed
  • Cancelled
  • Left Message
  • Unreachable
  • Not Required

Administrators can create additional status options.

docs.title: Repeating activities
docs.text:
You can set an Activity to repeat on a certain day and time with a specific end date and include dates to exclude from the repetition.

Once you are in the Activity Screen, reoccurring options can be set under Repeat Activity. The options you can set are:

  • Repetition Start Date and Time
  • Repeats Every: Hour, Day, Week, Month, Year
  • Repeats On: Sun, Mon, Tue, Wed, Thr, Fri, Sat
  • Ends: After a specific number of occurrences or on a specific date
  • Exclude Dates: Multiple dates can be selected

After saving the Activity, a confirmation screen will appear displaying all the dates for which an Activity will be created. A new Activity will be created for each repetition, and these can be individually edited and deleted.

When you edit one repetition of an Activity, you will be given the option to apply the change to that Activity only, that Activity and all future Activities in the series, or every Activity in the series. Changes to the date or time are NOT applied to other repeating Activities.

docs.title: Creating new activity types
docs.text:
You can define Activity Types at Administer > Customize Data and Screens > Activity Types. You can also add custom fields to Activity Types to allow specific data to be collected.

For example, you might create 2 new Activity Types called Training and Interview. You can then set up a custom field set associated with Activities that includes information such as funder and project. This would enable you to produce reports of all the Activities undertaken for a particular funder or as part of a particular project.

You could also create a custom field used for a specific Activity Type. For example, you could classify meetings as a staff meeting, client meeting, other organisation's meeting etc. For more on creating custom fields, refer to the Custom Fields chapter. For details on producing reports, see the Reporting section.

Go to the Activity Type Options page Administer > Customize Data and Screens > Activity Types and click Add Activity Type.

Assign your new Activity Type to the "Contact" component if you want it to be available from the Actions button when viewing a contact record. Assign it to "CiviCase" if these Activities are only for use inside a case.

docs.title: Setting up custom field sets for activities
docs.text: When setting up custom data sets, you will need to specify what the custom data will be used for. One of the options here is Activity and, if you wish, you can further specify which type of Activity. This means that these custom data fields will be available when recording Activities.

docs.title: Creating new activity statuses
docs.text:
If you need to add more options, you can do so from Administer > System Settings > Option Groups.

Before you add too many status options, remember that all status options show up on all Activity Types. Think carefully about what you need to add.

docs.title: Adding contacts
docs.text:
The simplest way to add a single contact is through the navigation menu at the top of a non-public page. To create an Individual, go to Contacts > New Individual:

The Contacts menu lets you create every kind of contact and contact sub-type. Contact creation forms have basic information, such as name and email, at the top. More specific fields are grouped below in accordions by type or subject, such as address fields, communication preferences and any custom fields added for that contact type.

For every contact type, you can use Check for Matching Contacts to help avoid duplicates. After entering the information you have in this section, click Check for Matching Contacts.

To add an Individual, first name and last name OR email address are required. To add an Organization or Household, just Organization/Household name is required. You can fill in as many other fields as you like and make changes later using the edit screen.

docs.title: Useful things to know when adding contacts
docs.text:
Address: You can add multiple addresses to a contact record—for example, home, work and a different billing address.

A checkbox lets you share an existing contact's address or create a new contact. If you select new contact, you need to select its contact type; a pop-up box then appears for adding the record. When a person uses another contact's address, the address can only be edited from the "master contact's" record.

The countries available in the dropdown depend on those made available at Administer > Localization > Languages, Currency, Locations under Available Countries.

You may not need every address field. Available address fields can be edited at Administer > Localization > Address settings. The "Address Name" field can label an address—for example, "Summer Home". It is hidden by default but can be enabled from that screen.

Tags and Groups: You can specify which tags and groups to add the contact to. You may only add to existing groups and tags with existing tags. For more on creating them, see the Groups and Tags chapter of this book.

Once you have filled out the form, choose one of three buttons:

  • Save saves the contact record and takes you to the contact screen.
  • Save and New saves the contact and clears the form so you can add another.
  • Cancel discards the entered information and returns you to your CiviCRM dashboard.

docs.title: Editing contacts
docs.text:
To edit information directly on the summary screen, hover over the upper-right corner of the block you want to change and click Edit Info.

To edit a lot of information for one contact, click the edit button above the tabs to open the entire contact for editing.

On the rare occasions when two admin users both open the edit screen for the same contact and then both save it, the second user is notified of the first user's edit and given a chance to manually 'merge' the edits.

docs.title: Deleting contacts
docs.text:
There is a button to Delete the contact at the top right. A deleted contact does not disappear completely: it moves to the trash, where it can be recovered later using the search in trash feature of advanced search. See "searching" under the "working with your data" chapter for more information).

Deleted contacts move to the "trash" by default and can be restored later. There are several ways to delete contacts:

  • Single contact: Open the contact's record and click the 'delete contact' button at the top of the page. Alternatively, search for the contact and, near the end of its row in the results, click 'More' and select 'Delete Contact'.
  • Multiple contacts: Run an advanced search and check each record you want to delete, or use the header checkbox to select all. In the 'actions' drop-down menu, choose 'Delete Contacts' to send them to the trash (if enabled), or 'Delete Permanently'. On the warning page, click 'Delete' to continue or 'Cancel' to return to the previous screen.

docs.title: Configure contact subtypes and the contact view
Contact subtypes
docs.text:
In addition to the three default contact types (individuals, households and contacts), you can define additional contact types (sometimes referred to as contact subtypes) to suit your needs.

Each contact subtype is based on one of the three core contact types. For example, 'Student' would be based on 'Individual'. 'Farm' could be based on 'Organization' or perhaps 'Household', depending on your use case.

Contact types are useful when you need different sets of custom data for different contacts. For example, you might collect subject areas and qualifications for teachers but not for other individuals. To do this, you would create a contact type called Teacher, based on Individual, and a custom data set that extends only Individuals of the type Teacher. See custom data for more information.

Core contact types are mutually exclusive: a contact cannot be both an organisation and an individual. A contact can, however, have more than one user-defined subtype—for example, Teacher and Parent.

To edit existing contact types or create new ones, go to Administer > Customize Data and Screens > Contact Types. You cannot delete the inbuilt contact types, but you can change their names and associated images.

To add custom fields to specific contact subtypes, see custom fields.

docs.title: Customizing the view of contacts
docs.text:
If sections or fields on the contact editing and summary screens are not useful to your organisation, you can hide some of them. For example, you can remove demographics information by configuring Site Preferences. Using an account with Administer CiviCRM privileges:

  1. Go to Administer > Customize Data and Screens > Display Preferences.
  2. Clear the Demographics box under Editing Contacts.
  3. Click Save.

You can also use this screen to rearrange the order in which information is displayed. For more detail, see Customizing the user interface.

To remove or add fields in the postal address section:

  1. Go to Administer > Localization > Address Settings.
  2. Check or uncheck fields under Address Editing.
  3. Click Save.

You can disable or enable specific tabs from Administer > Customize Data and Screens > Display Preferences. If you do not see some of the tabs described on the contacts page, you may need to enable them. Some tabs also depend on enabled components; for example, the Contributions tab is hidden if the CiviContribute component is disable.

docs.title: Contacts
docs.text:
Contacts are the basic building block of CiviCRM. Relationships, activities, groups and contributions all connect to contacts in some way.

CiviCRM comes with three contact types:

  • Individuals — people
  • Organisations — for example, companies or other non-profit organisations
  • Households — typically families that share a physical location

Each contact record has a set of core fields, including:

  • Names, such as first and last name for individuals and organisation name for organisations
  • Greeting and addressee fields for different communication methods
  • Contact methods, such as email addresses, phone numbers and website addresses
  • Addresses, or physical locations
  • Communication preferences: methods contacts prefer, and methods they do not want used

You can define contact subtypes based on the out-of-the-box contact types. You can add custom fields that extend all contacts, particular contact types or particular subtypes.

docs.title: A quick look at contacts
docs.text:
Contact information is organised into tabs. The first tab is the summary tab, which shows basic information. Other tabs show different aspects of the contact and help organise the data collected over time.

Which tabs you see depends on enabled components and your permissions. For example, you will only see the memberships tab if the CiviMember component is turned on and you have permission to see memberships. You can also define extra tabs to display custom data collected about contacts.

Below we look at the most important parts of the contact screen (including most of the contact with pointers to other parts of the book where appropriate.

docs.title: Contact actions
docs.text: Above the tabs is the Actions button, a shortcut for actions involving this contact. For example, you could add a note or record a new contribution, meeting or other activity.

docs.title: Summary tab
docs.text: The summary tab shows names, addresses, contact details and contact methods. Some fields, such as first name, last name and nickname, are for individuals. Others, such as organisation name, are for organisations.

docs.title: Individual fields
docs.text: An individual's name can have a prefix, first name, middle name, last name, suffix and nickname; you do not have to use every part. Prefixes and suffixes are selected from a drop-down list. If the value you want is missing, you can add options at Administer CiviCRM > Customize Data and Screens > Dropdown Options > Individual Prefixes (Ms., Mr...).

docs.title: Addresses
docs.text:
You can record one or more addresses for a contact. Each address needs a different location type, such as work or home. One address can be marked as primary for postal mailings. You can choose the primary location explicitly or let it default to the first address entered.

You can share addresses between contacts—for example, between an individual and the organisation where they work. When creating or editing the "work" address for an individual, check the "Share Address With" box. If the employer is already in your database, select them from the quick search box that appears. Otherwise, select "New Organisation" from the "create new contact" drop-down to create the employer's organisation record. Shared addresses are synchronized in both directions: if one changes, the other is automatically updated.

If a person pays by credit card, the details used for Billing Address in credit card payments are stored in the Billing location for the contact.

If you have a mapping provider enabled, you can click the map icon next to an address to see the contact's location on a map.

docs.title: Phone numbers
docs.text: You can store multiple phone numbers for each contact. Phone numbers have locations, such as work or home, and types, such as landline, fax or mobile. Phone numbers added as type mobile are available for sending SMS.

docs.title: Email addresses
docs.text: You can store multiple email addresses for each contact. One can be explicitly marked as the address that receives bulk mailings, such as e-newsletters and announcements sent using CiviMail. Bouncing emails are automatically marked as being on hold when sending emails via CiviMail. See the Email section for more information.

docs.title: Communication preferences and privacy options
docs.text:
You can define preferred communication methods and privacy options, such as not contacting someone by email. Privacy options are respected by certain functions: for example, mailing labels are not printed for contacts with the 'do not mail' option, and emails are not sent to contacts with the 'do not email' option.

The privacy options in a CiviCRM contact record are:

  • Do not phone — The end user has elected not to be contacted by telephone.
  • Do not email — The end user has elected not to be contacted by email.
  • Do not mail — The end user has elected not to be contacted by postal delivery (snail mail).
  • Do not SMS — The end user has elected not to be contacted by text messaging service to their mobile device.
  • Do no trade — The user has elected not to share their information with other organizations; you may not share or sell it to other parties.
  • NO BULK EMAILS (User Opt Out) — This is set when a user selects the Opt Out action in a CiviMail Email.

docs.title: Greetings and addressee fields
docs.text:
By default, greeting and addressee fields are calculated from a contact's name fields. For example, the postal greeting for an individual called 'Jenny Soper' is 'Dear Jenny'.

Default greetings can be configured globally at Administer CiviCRM > Communications > Email Greeting Formats or Postal Greeting Formats or Addressee Formats. You can also select a different format for a contact or customise it on a contact-by-contact basis.

docs.title: Demographics and deceased / closed contacts
docs.text:
For Individuals, you can record birth date, gender, whether they are deceased and when they died.

For Organizations or Households that no longer exist, you can record that they are "closed" by clicking to edit the block that contains Nickname and Legal Name.

docs.title: Relationships tab
docs.text:
Relationships connect contact records. Each connection can be named to describe its nature, and a contact can have many relationships with other contacts. The example below lists Current Relationships and Inactive relationships.

You can read more about when to use relationships in the relationships chapter of the organising your data section.

docs.title: Activities tab
docs.text:
The Activities tab lists interactions with a contact, including built-in activities such as event attendance, contributions and phone calls, as well as custom activities you have added. It also lets you record activities. Clicking an icon at the top of the screen (Send an Email, Meeting, Phone call) opens a screen for entering the details.

For more information, see the Activities section in this chapter.

docs.title: Mailings tab
docs.text: This is only visible if at Administer > CiviMail > CiviMail Component Settings you have unselected Enable CiviMail to create activites on delivery. In that case, each bulk email is recorded on the mailings tab instead of the activities tab. This improves the speed at which the activies tab loads if your organisation sends bulk emails to large mailing lists.

docs.title: Contributions tab
docs.text:
The Contributions tab shows financial contributions made by a contact. It also summarises the contact's contribution activity: total amount over time, total number of contributions and average contribution amount.

You can record offline contributions with the Record Contribution button, or record a credit card transaction on behalf of the contact with the Submit Credit Card Contribution button—for example, when a contribution was made by phone. Both buttons lead to forms where you can select the Financial Type in addition to the normal contribution information collected from public contribution pages.

Read more in the Contributions chapter of this book.

docs.title: Memberships tab
docs.text:
The Memberships tab displays a contact's memberships. You can add memberships and submit credit card payments for memberships that require a fee. You can also renew or delete a membership from the "more" link on each existing membership.

Read more in the Membership chapter of this book.

docs.title: Events tab
docs.text:
The Events tab displays events related to the contact, such as events they have registered for, attended or volunteered at.

You can register the contact for an event and use the Submit Credit Card Event Registration button if payment is required. The related payment then appears in the first row of the contact's Contributions tab.

You can also click the Edit link to change event information as it relates to the contact—for example, changing their status from "registered" to "attended."

Read more in the Events chapter of this book.

docs.title: Groups tab
docs.text:
The Groups tab shows the groups a contact belongs to. Groups can be used for mailing lists and permissions (ACLs), among other purposes.

You can add or remove the contact from groups and see a history of groups they have unsubscribed or been removed from.

The Status column displays who added the contact to a group. Whether users can add themselves is a setting you can configure when creating a group. When a group's visibility is set to "Public Listings", users can join through Profile forms. A later section discusses using Profiles for mailing list sign-ups.

For more information, see Groups and Tags.

docs.title: Notes tab
docs.text:
The Notes tab holds ad-hoc information about a contact. Generally, you would use custom fields for information you plan to collect about contacts. Notes are unstructured, so use this tab with care unless you know that you and other users will remember to look there. Both the subject and content of a Note are free-text fields; the subject does not have to be selected from predefined options.

You can set "Author Only" privacy for a note. Only its author or someone with "view all notes" permission (via your CMS) can then view or edit it.

docs.title: Tags tab
docs.text:
Tags are one way to categorise contacts; Custom Data and Groups are other methods. You can configure tags for your organisation, search on them and create Smart Groups based on them.

The tags next to Keywords belong to the Keywords Tagset. A Tagset is a grouping of tags that you can create. Tagsets are non-hierarchical. You can create a tag in a tagset by typing it into the field, or select an existing matching tag from the list that appears.

For more information, see Groups and Tags.

docs.title: Change log tab
docs.text:
This tab gives limited information about changes to a contact record. It shows when the change was made and who made it, but not what changed.

Tip

Administrators can use the Contact Logging Report for detailed information about changes to contact records: who, what and when.

docs.title: Creating custom fields
docs.text:
Custom fields let you collect information beyond what CiviCRM allows by default. For example, you could add checkboxes to organisations to track the clients they serve. You can also restrict custom fields to certain types of an object: if you have a contact type Student, you might add a field listing the subjects they study.

Custom fields are always stored in custom field sets. Adding custom data therefore has two stages:

  1. Create a custom field set—a container for related fields.
  2. Add custom fields to the set. You may find it helpful to read about custom fields first, but you must create the set before creating its fields.

A field is one unit of information entered into the database, such as someone’s primary spoken language or high school graduation date. A custom field set groups related fields, such as fields about a particular activity type, event participation, or contributions.

docs.title: Custom field sets
docs.text:
Each custom field set has a scope as wide or as narrow as you choose. For example, you might associate a set called “nationality” with all contact types, “immigration status” with a specific contact type such as Individuals, or another set with a component such as CiviMember or CiviEvent, or with Relationships or Groups.

The scope of a custom field set is one of the few decisions that is irreversible: you will not be able to change it after creating the set. Consider what you want to associate the set with before you start.

Ask these questions when planning a set:

  • How will its fields be used?
  • Which types of contacts or records are they appropriate for?
  • Do they have broad applicability, or are they relevant to a specific Contact Type, Event, Financial Type, etc.? For example, a person’s entree choice at a dinner event belongs on the Participant record, not the Individual Contact record. It describes their participation in that event; they might make a different choice at another dinner.

Choosing the appropriate scope helps keep application screens relevant and free of unnecessary fields. A field for “color of eyes,” for example, belongs on the Individual contact type rather than the generic Contacts option, because it is irrelevant to Organization and Household contacts. If custom data is specific to a particular event registration page, create it for an Event type Participant for that event.

Consider grouping fields by topic, too. If 12 of 20 fields associated with Individual contacts relate to an online membership directory, you might put those 12 in one set and the more general Individual details in another.

To create a custom field set and custom fields, go to Administer > Customize Data and Screens > Custom Data. On this screen, you can give the set a title, specify the records it will be used for, select display characteristics, and enter help text.

docs.title: Set name
docs.text: For a custom field set displayed inline, this name appears as the field set’s legend. If the set uses the tab display style, the name appears as the navigation tab label.

docs.title: Used For
docs.text:
Use this option to make fields appear only where they are relevant. The following are some of the options; you can add custom fields to more than 20 different entities.

  • Activity: Fields assigned to all activities or to a specific activity type, such as Meeting or Phone Call.
  • Addresses: Creates an address block, allowing the administrator to create additional address-related fields.
  • Contacts: Fields assigned to all contacts.
  • Contributions: Fields assigned to all contributions or to a specific Financial Type, such as Donations or Event Fees.
  • Events: Fields assigned to all events or a specific event type, such as Conference or Fundraiser. These fields apply to an event, not to the participant registration record.
  • Grants: Fields specific to grants.
  • Groups: Fields displayed in Group settings. These fields are not searchable.
  • Household: Fields specific to the Household contact type.
  • Individual: Fields specific to the Individual contact type.
  • Memberships: Fields assigned to all membership records or to a specific membership type.
  • Organization: Fields specific to the Organization contact type.
  • Participants: Fields on the participant registration record. The options are general fields for all registration records, role-type fields for a specific participant role, and event participant fields for a specific event.
  • Pledges: Fields specific to pledges.
  • Relationships: Fields assigned to all relationship records or to a specific relationship type, such as “Spouse of” or “Employee of.”

Adding custom fields to even more entities

It is also possible to add custom fields to entities that are not listed under Used For, or to your own custom entities. Enabling custom fields for unsupported entities might not show those fields in forms for the entity, but they will be available in SearchKit.

Not editable if data exist

You may only make customizations to this field if no data has been recorded with it. Until you record data, you may change Used For using the More > Settings option for the set on Administer > Customize Data and Screens > Custom Fields.

docs.title: Order
docs.text: This controls the order in which custom field sets appear when you have more than one. Lower numbers, such as 1 and 2, appear above higher numbers, such as 8 and 9.

docs.title: Multiple record fieldsets
docs.text:
By default, a custom data set has a one-to-one relationship with the entity it is attached to. For example, one field set for a person’s physical attributes could contain their height and eye colour and be attached to one Individual record.

Some information requires multiple records for one contact. A person might have multiple educational degrees, for example, so an educational history set with fields for subject, institution, and grade should allow multiple records. Multiple record fieldsets provide this option.

You can add multiple record field sets only to contacts, not to other entities. To use the option, select “Does this Custom Field Set allow multiple records?” Bear in mind:

  • Multiple data applies to the whole field set, not to individual fields.
  • Multiple data can only be added to Contacts. It cannot be added to Activities, Contributions, etc.
  • Multiple data cannot currently be exported.
  • Before modelling something as a multiple value custom field set, consider whether it could or should be an activity. An educational degree, for example, could be an activity with custom data added.

docs.title: Display options
docs.text:
The display style tab is visible only for custom data fields attached to contacts. You can display contact field sets inline on the summary screen or in their own tab. The choice depends on factors such as how often you need the data and how large the set is. You can switch display styles later.

You can also set a custom field set to be “collapsed” on initial display. When the page first loads, only the title appears and the fields are hidden. This can reduce the space taken up by infrequently used sets. A similar “collapsed” property is available for custom data in Advanced Search.

The two tab display options are Tab with table and Tab.

Tab with table provides a concise overview of the set’s data. You can add new records and edit existing ones in pop-up windows. Under more, “copy a record” lets you copy a record, change one or two fields, and save it as a new record—useful when consecutive records share many values.

Tab displays data in a format similar to the inline style.

docs.title: Is this Custom Field Set active?
docs.text:
If a custom field set is active, its fields can be viewed and changed. Otherwise, the fields remain in the CiviCVRM system but are hidden from the user interface. This can be useful when migrating from an existing database system.

For example, membership records imported from an MS Access database might each have a unique ID (key) with no direct benefit in CiviCRM. You could create a custom field for that value, import the records, then disable the field by leaving the Activate option unchecked. This keeps the value for historical reference while hiding it from view.

Although users cannot see the field, its value remains stored and can be referenced later—for example, to investigate a discrepancy in archived data or compare it with a printed record.

Once the custom field set is active, you can make individual fields inactive in the form defining those fields.

docs.title: Is this Custom Field Set public?
docs.text:
If a custom field set is marked as public, its fields appear on public-facing pages. Fields intended for an event information page, for example, should belong to a public set; fields containing administrative information about an event should belong to a set that is not public.

This setting applies to every Custom Field in the Custom Field Set. Individual fields cannot be marked as public or not.

docs.title: Pre-form Help and Post-form Help
docs.text: Text entered in Pre-form Help appears above the form field; text entered in Post-form Help appears below it. Use help at this level for instructions about the entire set.

docs.title: Custom fields
docs.text:
After creating a custom field set, click View and Edit Custom Fields, then New Custom Field, to create fields within it.

After configuring a field, click Save to save it and return to the field listing for the current set, or Save and New to save it and begin another field.

Except for the data and input field type selection, you can modify the configuration options after creating a field. You can also preview individual fields or the whole set while defining them. Previewing is particularly useful for checking the layout of radio button and check-box fields with many choices.

docs.title: Field label
docs.text: This is the text displayed next to the field and used as its label when you export data. You can overwrite the Field Label when using a field in a profile, allowing an administrator-facing name here and a more user-friendly name in the profile.

docs.title: Type
docs.text:
When you create a custom field, CiviCRM provides a dropdown list of data types. The menu on the left in the following image selects the format of the data to store; the menu on the right selects how the user interacts with the field.

The field types are:

  • Alphanumeric (text and number fields):
    • Text: a simple area for entering text.
    • Select: a dropdown box limited to one selection.
    • Radio: a list allowing one selection, with all options visible at once.
    • Yes and No: a radio list with two contrasting options.
    • Check-box: a list allowing multiple selections.
    • Multi-select: a list in a single box, allowing multiple selections using control+click.
    • Advanced Multi-select: two side-by-side lists between which items can be moved.
    • Autocomplete select: a widget that completes a selection when the user’s typing uniquely identifies it.
  • Note: A longer, multiple-line text box, available as:
    • plain text; or
    • rich text, with a WYSIWYG editor that allows HTML.
  • Integer: A whole number, displayed as a:
    • text box;
    • select box; or
    • radio list.
  • Number: A number that can include decimals, such as 3.175, displayed as a:
    • text box;
    • select box; or
    • radio list.
  • Money: Similar to a number, but treated according to the local currency configured in CiviCRM’s administrative pages. Displayed as a:
    • text box;
    • select box; or
    • radio list.
  • Date: A date, optionally with a time, entered using a calendar widget. You can set the range of years selectable before and after the current date.
  • State/Province: Geographical locations configured in CiviCRM’s Localization settings (Administer > Configure > Global Settings > Localization), offered as a select box or multi-select box.
  • Country: Geographical locations offered as a select box or multi-select box.
  • File: A browser for selecting and uploading a file.
  • Link: An active internet hyperlink.
  • Contact Reference: An autocomplete widget for an existing CiviCRM contact.

Experimenting with different field types can help you understand their behaviour. Their differences also affect how you use them: for example, check-boxes support OR and AND searches in Advanced Search, whereas multi-select does not.

docs.title: Display in Table?
docs.text:
This check box appears only when creating a field in a multi-record field set displayed as tab with table. It is checked by default. If you unselect it, the field does not appear in the table. This can help keep a large dataset from making the table too wide for the screen.

Fields hidden from the table remain available when you add a record or view, edit, or copy a row.

docs.title: Database Field Length
docs.text: This specifies the number of characters the field can contain. Normally, leave it at the maximum. For extremely large field sets, a shorter length might improve performance and reduce storage space, but it will not make a difference for most users.

docs.title: Order
docs.text: This controls the order of fields within the set. Set it in the field edit form or use the up/down icons in the main field listing table. By default, new fields appear at the bottom of the list.

docs.title: Default Value
docs.text: Where applicable, you can designate a default value. It appears or is selected automatically when users open a form containing the field.

docs.title: Pre-form Help and Post-form Help
docs.text:
A field name should ideally make clear what to enter. Where it does not, or where you want to guide how the field is used, enter help text. Pre-form Help appears above the form field; Post-form Help appears below it.

The text appears wherever the field is used on administration pages and becomes the default help text when the field is assigned to a profile (see the Profiles section in this chapter). The person creating the profile can remove or change that text without changing the original custom field definition.

docs.title: Required
docs.text:
When selected, this requires a value before the form can be submitted. If no value is provided, an error message directs the person to complete the required fields.

To require a field only in a particular profile, leave this box unchecked and check the Required field within the profile instead.

docs.title: Optimize for Search
docs.text:
When selected, this creates a database index on the field, significantly speeding up searches on it. An index can also require more storage and slow the system if the data is frequently updated. It is recommended for fields often used as search or smart group criteria, such as identifiers or values selected from a list. For frequently updated text fields that are seldom used in exact searches, such as notes or comments, an index will most likely slow the system and use disk space inefficiently.

The behaviour of this field changed in CiviCRM 5.75. Before then, it was called “is searchable?” and also determined whether the field appeared in Advanced Search and Reports. From 5.75, all fields are available in Advanced Search and Reports.

docs.title: Active
docs.text: As with the active check-box for a custom field set, this determines whether the field is enabled or disabled when CiviCRM displays it to the user.

docs.title: View Only
docs.text:
This makes a field visible but uneditable. It can be used:

  • To retain imported data for users’ reference without letting them modify it.
  • To store data entered through a method set up by your developer rather than directly through the user interface.

docs.title: Multiple choice options
docs.text:
For fields with selectable options—such as Select, Radio, Check-box, Multi-select, and Advanced Multi-select—you can use an existing option set created for another custom field or create a new one. You can enter values while creating the field or later. The option’s label appears on the form; its value is stored in the contact record.

If several fields share an option set, you will be notified when a change to it will affect those fields.

When creating a set, you can initially enter up to ten options in a table. After saving the field, use Edit Multiple Choice Options to add an unlimited number of further choices. Go to Administer > Customize > Custom Data > View and Edit Custom Fields > Edit Multiple Choice Options. You can return to this screen later to change an option’s label, order, or active status, or to add choices.

You can mark one choice as the default option. Inactive options are hidden when the field is presented.

docs.title: Managing custom field sets
docs.text:
To list all fields in a set, go to Administer > Customize Data and Screens > Custom Data and click View and Edit Custom Fields for that set.

You can edit field settings, edit multiple choice options where applicable, preview, disable, or delete fields. You can also Move a field to another data set. Fields can be moved between sets used for all contacts or contact sub-types; otherwise, they can only be moved between data sets of the same type.

docs.title: Multiple choice options headings
docs.text:
You can add headings to a multiple choice option list, as in this example:

To add headings:

  1. When configuring the field, choose “Select” or “Multi-Select” as the input type.

  2. When configuring the field’s options:

    • Set the Label for each heading to the text displayed to the user.
    • Set its Value to text prefixed by “crm_optgroup_”.

docs.title: Choosing between fields, groups and tags
docs.text:
Data fields, groups, and tags are three ways to associate information with contacts. Before creating a custom data field for every attribute, consider the alternatives. They provide functionality you may otherwise miss; using fields for information better stored as groups or tags can slow the system. Appropriate use of groups and tags can also make records easier for administrative staff to maintain.

These distinctions can help you choose:

  • Store data with a wide range of values, such as a person’s address or biography, in an alphanumeric custom data field.
  • Custom data fields can be grouped and displayed on their own tab on a contact’s record.
  • Groups group contacts: for example, board members, staff, and volunteers might belong to separate groups. If you use Drupal, you can assign permissions based on group membership. A Smart Group automatically adds or removes contacts based on a characteristic.
  • Contacts must be assigned to a Group to receive a particular CiviMail mass mailing. For example, a press release could go to a group of selected contacts, including a Smart Group.
  • Tags and Groups can both have a hierarchy. A group or tag labelled ‘Regions’ could have a subgroup or subtag for each geographic region your organisation covers (see “Case study in hierarchical tags” later in this section).
  • Tags support more powerful searches than data fields or groups. Visitors can search multiple tags using both AND and OR operators. Data fields support only lists of words, effectively an AND operator, except for check-box fields, which support OR operators.
  • The tag interface lets a visitor add and remove tags without reloading the page in edit mode.
  • Custom data fields can be assigned to a specific record type, such as households only. Once defined, tags are assigned to all types.

docs.title: Custom field set storage limitations
docs.text: A large number of custom field sets, or sets containing many fields, may cause problems when searching, exporting data, or running reports. There is no specific limit given here: the appropriate number of sets and fields depends on the data you collect and the server hosting your installation. If in doubt, discuss it with your system administrator or CiviCRM service provider.

docs.title: Group settings and functionality
docs.text:
Give each group a clear name and a description that explains its purpose to other database users. These help users recognise groups in contexts such as CiviMail, particularly when your organisation has many groups. If a group is created for a particular person, consider naming its owner in the description so someone can later check whether the group is still used or can be deleted.

Groups can have these standard types:

  • Mailing List is used when you plan to use the group as a mailing list in CiviMail. It is available for regular and Smart Groups.
  • Access Control (Drupal only) assigns CiviCRM access permissions to a set of contacts. Only regular groups can have this type.

You can create additional group types to reflect your needs. This can be useful if your organisation has hundreds of groups, because group type is a filter on the Manage Groups screen. To create a group type, go to Administer>System Settings>Option Groups and select Group Type.

docs.title: Visibility
docs.text: Visibility determines permissions for joining and removing contacts from groups. Select “User and User Admin Only” if membership is controlled only by authorised CiviCRM users. Select “Public Pages” to let contacts join and remove themselves through Registration and Account Profile forms.

docs.title: Parent/child groups
docs.text:
To create a hierarchy, create one or more parent groups and assign other groups to them. When a user sends a mailing to a parent group or searches for contacts in it, contacts in its child groups are automatically included.

For example, an organisation with a national office and 5 regional offices could put each region's constituents in a separate group. If a National group is the parent of all the regional groups, the national office can mail the National group and include contacts in those regional groups.

docs.title: Group IDs
docs.text: CiviCRM assigns each group a unique numeric ID. A group ID can be used for various operations, such as defining a URL for group sign-ups.

docs.title: Add contacts to groups
docs.text:
You can add contacts to groups:

  • through the Tags and Groups section of the Contact Details edit screen;
  • through a contact's Groups tab;
  • by using the “Add Contacts to Group/Tag contacts” batch action after conducting a search; or
  • by clicking a group's Contacts link in Navigation Menu > Contacts > Manage Groups.

The first two methods also let you remove individual contacts. The last two let you add multiple contacts at once.

Individual contacts can be added to a Group in the contact edit screen or through the Groups tab. To add multiple contacts, conduct a search and select Add Contacts to a Group from the More Actions menu. Alternatively, go to Manage Groups, select Members for the relevant Group, then use Add Members to this Group at the top of the screen.

Contacts can also be added to a group by filling out a Profile.

docs.title: Managing Groups
docs.text:
To view and manage all groups, go to: Navigation Menu > Contacts > Manage Groups.

Use the Find Groups form at the top of the Manage Groups screen to search by name, type, visibility, and whether a group is enabled or disabled. You can also scroll or browse the list below the form, which includes regular and Smart Groups.

From the list, you can:

  • add contacts by clicking the Contacts link in a group's row;
  • edit a group by clicking Settings;
  • disable or delete a group using the links in the “more” pop-up menu; and
  • see how many contacts are currently in each group.

docs.title: Finding contacts in a group
docs.text: Each group's Contacts page has a form for finding contacts in that group. You can search by name, email address, contact type, group status (added, removed, or pending), and tags.

docs.title: Groups and ACL
docs.text:
Access Control Lists (ACL) provide finer-grained permissions than Drupal's Permissions and Roles. The online CiviCRM documentation explains the concept at http://wiki.civicrm.org/confluence/display/CRMDOC/Access+Control.

Set up the required Groups, Custom Data Groups, Profiles, and Roles before using them in ACL.

Note

ACL support for Joomla was introduced in Joomla version 1.6.

docs.title: Removing versus deleting contacts from groups
docs.text:
CiviCRM keeps a history of group membership. If you Remove a contact from a group, you can see when they were removed and by whom. For example, this can help you track former volunteer-group members or explain when an email subscriber opted out of a newsletter.

If a contact was removed in error, Rejoin Group adds them again. Every group record has a status: Added, Removed, or Pending. You can search for group members by status—for example, to list former Advisory Board members.

To search, navigate to Contacts > Manage Groups. Find the group and select Contacts in the right-hand column. Expand the search criteria to find the option to search by status.

You can also Delete a contact from a group. This eliminates any record of the contact being in the group.

docs.title: Working with tags
docs.text:
To view tags, go to: Contacts > Manage Tags (Categories) in the navigation menu.

You can edit or delete a tag using the corresponding link in its row. To create one, click Add Tag on the Manage Tags (Categories) screen or go to Contacts > New Tag in the navigation menu.

Give each tag a clear, unique name and a description that explains its purpose. Tags can form a hierarchy: select a Parent tag from the dropdown list to make a tag its subtag.

Tags can be designated for contacts, activities and/or cases. A tag designated for contacts is available for all contact types and subtypes; it cannot be designated for only one contact type.

Every user can create more tags if needed. Important tags can be locked so that users without the “administer reserved tags” permission cannot modify or delete them. This permission is available in Drupal only.

You can assign tags to contacts, activities, and cases:

  • while creating or editing the record;
  • from the Contact Summary Tags tab; or
  • by using the Tag Contacts batch action after conducting a search.

The first two methods also let you remove tags.

docs.title: Tag sets
docs.text:
Tag sets are a free-form way to tag contacts. They resemble regular tags but differ in several ways:

  • They act as a “bucket” for grouping tags. For example, an Issues People Care About tag set might contain “affordable housing”, “racial justice”, and “water quality”.
  • They let you create tags on the fly without visiting the Manage Tags page.
  • Adding them creates an additional search field in the Basic Criteria section of Advanced Search.

To create a tag set, go to Contacts > Manage Tags (Categories) in the navigation menu and click Add Tag Set. Give the tag set a name and description, and indicate whether it applies to contacts, activities, or cases.

Selecting Reserved makes a tag set more permanent: someone without Administrator permission cannot delete it. Read more about permissions in the Permissions and Access Control chapter of the Initial Set Up section.

You can now use the tag set to tag a contact, activity, or case record.

When you create a new tag set, a new field shows up on the edit pages of the entity's activities or cases as well as in the Tags tab for contacts. For example, if you create a tag set called “Issues Folks Care About” an associate it with Contacts, you will see the tag set next time you go to the Tags tab of a contact's record.

This is an autocomplete field. As you type, CiviCRM displays matching tags from the tag set below the field. Select an existing tag, or type an entire new tag and press Enter. The tag appears in a box within the field. Clicking X untags the contact, case, or activity record you are editing.

Tags created in a tag set also appear in the normal Contacts > Manage Tags (Categories) list, where you can view and edit them. They are available only within their particular tag set.

docs.title: A note about searching on tags and tag sets
docs.text:
Each tag set adds a field to the Basic Criteria section of Advanced Search. You can search only for tags that already exist in that tag set.

The All Tags field finds records with regular tags or tagset tags containing a complete or partial word or phrase. For example, entering ‘Donor’ finds contacts with any tag containing that word.

Read extensively on using Advanced Search in the Searching section.

docs.title: Groups and tags
docs.text:
Groups and tags are two key methods of organising data in CiviCRM. Both can help you segment and search your database, but they serve different purposes.

A common approach is to use tags as descriptive categories for contacts, activities, and cases, and groups for collections of people that need to be treated as a cohesive unit—for example, to receive a mailing. Under this approach, volunteer, ally organisation, vegetarian, and musician would be tags, while Volunteer Committee, Allied Organisations Coalition, Vegetarian Newsletter, and This Awesome Band With A Bad Name would be groups. This is a guideline rather than a rule.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
Groups are collections of contacts that have something in common. They play a role in CiviMail and Profiles and can be used to set up advanced access rights on Drupal. Well-defined groups help segment a CiviCRM contact database.

There are two kinds of groups:

  • Groups, also called regular groups, have contacts that you manually add and remove. For example, you can assign your organisation's board members to a Board of Directors group, then email that group without searching for and selecting each member individually.
  • Smart Groups are configured to include contacts that share characteristics or activities. As contacts are added or edited, CiviCRM checks whether they meet the configured criteria and adds them if they do. For example, a Smart Group for “2010 Contributors from California” could include contacts who contributed in 2010 and have an address in California. New contacts who meet both criteria are automatically added. Another Smart Group could contain donors who have not yet been sent a thank-you letter: as you send letters, their recipients automatically leave the group.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text: Tags categorise contacts, activities, and cases. You can create as many as needed, but avoiding duplicate or unnecessary tags makes them easier to use. A standard process for creating and using tags can help.

docs.title: Groups versus tags
docs.text:
Which method to use depends on how you intend to segment contacts. Having both lets you make refined searches using AND and OR. For example, if journalists, volunteers, and members are groups, while development, art, and history are tags for interests, you can find journalists interested in art or development, volunteers or members interested in history, or other combinations.

Groups also have features that tags do not:

  • Groups are integrated with other CiviCRM functions, notably CiviMail.
  • Contacts can be added to Smart Groups automatically based on their characteristics.
  • Groups can be associated with Drupal Organic Groups.

Tags can be applied to contacts, activities, and cases; groups consist only of contacts.

docs.title: Benefits of tags
docs.text:
• Tags are easy to set up and use.
  • You can search by tag in Basic or Advanced Search.
  • You can combine tags with other properties, such as residence state/province, to create Smart Groups.

docs.title: Limitations of tags
docs.text:
• You cannot create tags for only a specific contact type—for example, tags that are only for Individual contacts.
  • When you export tags, all tags assigned to a record are exported as a list in one cell, such as “Teacher, Volunteer”.
  • Tags allow multiple selections, so they may not suit mutually exclusive characteristics such as “Democrat”, “Republican”, and “Green Party”.
  • You cannot selectively hide or permission tags on built-in or Profile create and edit forms; all tags appear on edit forms.

docs.title: Benefits of groups
docs.text:
• Groups offer a flexible way to segment contacts for a range of purposes.
  • Groups support recurring tasks such as sending an enewsletter or printing mailing labels.
  • Groups let you restrict access to “special” sets of contacts.
  • Groups support administrative and end-user “subscribe” and “unsubscribe” actions, and the system keeps a history of those actions.
  • Visibility settings let you choose which groups appear to end-users on Profile forms; some groups can be “private”.
  • You can create Smart Groups that combine members of Group A + Group B.

docs.title: Limitations of groups
docs.text:
• All existing groups appear under Manage Groups and in search forms. If your organisation has many groups, these lists may become overloaded.
  • Groups used for short-term projects should be “purged” when no longer needed.
  • When you export contact records, all groups a contact belongs to are exported as a single comma-separated list, such as “Administrators,Newsletter Subscribers”.

docs.title: Mapping your data
docs.text:
Your existing data may come from multiple sources: electronic records, paper records, and people's memories. Mapping means taking data labeled in one way and finding its place in CiviCRM's structure. Skipping this step may have unwanted consequences. For example, you may not be able to control or report on data as you expect.

People think about data differently depending on their experience with another CRM, or with no CRM at all. For example, Donation, Opportunity, and Contribution can all refer to money given to your organization. CiviCRM was designed to be flexible and adaptable, so you should have no problem finding a place for every piece of information relevant to your organization.

Resist the temptation to add custom fields right away. Rather than creating a field for manually entering membership expiration dates, learn about CiviCRM's membership module, which automates membership duration, expiration, and renewal reminders. Multiple fields that collect the same data can cause confusion. Make informed choices up front to avoid duplication.

The sections below introduce options CiviCRM provides out of the box. Instead of keeping data in “flat” spreadsheets, you can use relationships to connect it and build a more complete picture of the community that supports your organization.

docs.title: Basic information about your constituents
docs.text:
CiviCRM has default fields for constituent names, addresses, phone numbers, emails, notes, and other contact information. It was designed for non-profits, so mapping basic constituent information should be straightforward.

CiviCRM divides constituents into three categories, called Contact Types:

  • Individuals: Any person your organisation wants to keep a record of.
  • Organizations: Another non-profit, a company, a chapter of your organisation, or a committee. You will generally want to create at least one contact of the Organization type to represent your organization. This is particularly useful when configuring memberships.
  • Households: A family or group of people who share a physical location.

Each contact type has fields suited to the data you may want to track. For example, gender applies to individuals, not organisations or households, so the gender field is available only for Individual contact types and subtypes.

See Contacts to learn more about built-in CiviCRM basic constituents fields and how to use them.

docs.title: Information specific to your organization (custom fields)
docs.text:
Many organizations collect data specific to their mission or structure. CiviCRM provides fields for basic data that non-profits commonly collect, but your organisation may also need to record information such as constituent allergies for individuals or service area for organizations.

When mapping data into CiviCRM, decide whether each piece of information pertains to an individual, organization, or household. For example, “service area” only makes sense for Organizations. To find out how to create custom fields, see Creating Custom Fields.

docs.title: Relationships between constituents
docs.text:
Relationships capture current and historical information about how two records connect.

You or your colleagues may know things about constituents that have never been written down. A flat spreadsheet may not have had space for them, or they may have remained mental notes. A Relationship can capture family members, places of employment, and connections to other constituents in your database.

CiviCRM has predefined relationship Types, including “employer--employee”, “parent--child”, and “employee--employer”. You can create more to describe relationships specific to your organization, such as “vicar--church”. When you create a new Relationship, you can define when it began and, if relevant, when it ends. You can still access a previous relationship after it ends—for example, to see where someone used to work.

The term Household and the relationship Types “household member of--head of the household” confuse many new CiviCRM users. Grouping individuals who share an address in one household can mean they receive only one letter. The “head of the household” designation helps an organization decide whom to address—for example, a parent rather than a child.

To read more about configuring and using relationships, please see the the Relationships section in Organising Your Data.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Knowing how and when constituents engage with your organization can help you understand their involvement. Someone who gives monthly, volunteers frequently, and renews her membership yearly may respond well to opportunities that strengthen her relationship with your organization. CiviCRM lets you record interactions such as phone calls, emails, and meetings between staff and constituents, helping your organization retain a history of those relationships.

CiviCRM calls these exchanges Activities. They are closely linked to other CiviCRM modules. When you record contributions, event attendance, membership subscriptions, and emails, CiviCRM automatically creates a related activity in the Contact record. Decide whether your organization needs activity types beyond those provided, such as training, review, exam, or support.

To read more about configuring and using activities, please see the Activites section in Organising Your Data.

docs.title: Webinars, events, performances, and meetings (CiviEvents)
docs.text:
CiviCRM helps manage and track occasions that bring community members together at a place and time. Webinars, events, performances, and meetings have start and end dates and times, meeting places (including online), and reasons for bringing people together. They can be ticketed, RSVP only, or require no reservation. CiviCRM provides functionality to promote events and record registrations. If you have records of participation in past events, you can transfer them into CiviEvents.

The Event Types field distinguishes the kinds of events your organization hosts. This can help you evaluate participation in a series of similar events or whether someone prefers one kind of event over another.

To read more about configuring and using events , please see the Events chapter later in this book.

docs.title: Memberships
docs.text:
Many organizations offer programs in which community members sign up for benefits for a pre-defined period. Members may choose from dues levels with associated benefits; generally, higher dues bring more benefits. An organization can also give a membership at no price, perhaps as an award. For example, a long-time volunteer might receive a life-time membership. Common benefits include access to member directories, extra content, and discounts. Individuals, families or households, and organizations can all sign up for memberships.

The main difference between membership dues and a donation is that membership changes someone's relationship to an organization for a period of time. Organizations often expect memberships to be renewed from year to year, while a donation is a one-time gift. Organizations need to send an acknowledgement letter, but a donation—or Contribution in CiviCRM—does not promise the donor advertised benefits in return.

Analyze your membership structure before importing membership records into CiviCRM. Take time to eliminate unused membership levels or simplify promised benefits. The information you really need to transfer for each member is start date, duration, membership dues paid, and type of membership.

Generally, more than 10–15 membership types may be hard to manage. Some organizations have many types because they store other constituent information in membership records. Before extending those records, check whether CiviCRM already has membership-related fields for that information.

Information previously recorded as static data may now be calculated dynamically and displayed in reports or other fields. For example, CiviCRM can calculate how many years a constituent has been a member from the “Membership since” date.

To read more about configuring and managing memberships, please see the Memberships chapter later in this book.

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
Contribution in CiviCRM refers to money, goods, or services coming into your organization. Money remains money whether someone buys an event ticket, signs up for a membership, or makes another payment. CiviCRM lets you record incoming money as a Contribution with different Types to retain information about its source. You can also specify the date received, its status—including pending before money is deposited in your bank account—and how it was delivered, such as by check or cash.

If you plan to keep using an external donations system, you may leave transactions there. You may nevertheless want to transfer information about past event or webinar registrations to CiviCRM because it shows a constituent's history of involvement. Consider how far back to import contribution history. Large contributions should be preserved, but a 5-dollar donation from 10 years ago may no longer be relevant.

To read more about configuring and using relationships, please see the Contributions chapter later in this book.

docs.title: Campaigns
docs.text:
Organizations sometimes hold a fundraising gala, send an email appeal, and record contributions in support of one goal—for example, raising $50,000 for a kids camp. Campaigns are usually time limited. They connect a range of activities and provide a high-level view for comparing how people responded to your initiatives.

Campaigns may be useful if your organization's fundraising initiatives fit distinct themes, such as year end pledge drives or project specific fundraisers. An organization may send several appeals for one project or fundraiser, including a 'final notice' and one or more 'countdown' appeals.

docs.title: Grouping and tagging constituents
docs.text:
Development directors, volunteer coordinators, and program managers often carry information in their heads when deciding whom to invite to an event, exclude from an appeal, or consider for a volunteer opportunity.

Groups and tags can store that information and help build email and invitation lists. Groups identify two or more contacts with something in common; relationships capture information about only two contacts. Groups can also serve as mailing lists. A group of newsletter subscribers is one place to start.

Organizations may send different communications to subsets of their community. One Individual can be tagged member and volunteer to receive both member-specific and volunteer-specific communications. Groups can also store issue- or program-specific communication preferences. For example, when creating an email appeal mailing, you can exclude a group of Individuals who have asked not to receive fundraising appeals.

Avoid creating groups for information already stored in other CiviCRM fields. You do not need a group for individuals who have opted out of bulk mailings: that option is selected on their Contact record, and CiviCRM automatically excludes them from bulk mailings. Likewise, you do not need a group called “donors”: an advanced search can find any Contact record with an associated Contribution, including within specified date ranges. Most functions available to groups are also available through the search results screen.

To have new records that meet particular criteria added to a group automatically, create a Smart Group from an advanced search. For example, you might create a Smart Group of members who also donated more than $100 in the past year. If a member makes a new $100 donation after the group is created, their record will be added to the Smart Group.

Tags are more like keywords associated with a record. You can easily add or remove them, but there is no easy way to see their history of changes. Relationships are a better tool for viewing information history.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
CiviCRM lets you assemble sets of fields for different purposes, helping reduce the time staff spend on administrative tasks. These sets are called Profiles.

Profiles determine how data is edited or displayed to staff or other users, not how it is stored.

docs.title: Where next?
docs.text: The sections above describe places where existing data may fit in CiviCRM, but cover only basic functionality. For more about how CiviCRM can work with your data, see later chapters in this book, which explain specific functionality from major extensions.

docs.title: Planning your data in CiviCRM
docs.text: CiviCRM uses several building blocks to store data. Using them effectively takes planning: you need to understand the data you already have, decide what to transfer, and work out how to organise it in CiviCRM.

docs.title: Understand your current data and contacts
docs.text:
Before thinking about CiviCRM’s structure, consider the systems you currently use to store and organise data. Information might be in spreadsheets, another database or CRM (such as Constant Contact, Convio or The Raiser's Edge), paper files, or someone’s memory.

Talk to co-workers about your contacts and their interactions with your organisation. Include people who have been around the longest and people who have just joined. Speaking with as many people as possible will help you understand interactions with different kinds of contacts.

Identify all the people involved with your organisation. What types of people do you interact with, and how do those types differ? Understanding your contacts and their interactions will help you model them in CiviCRM. Anecdotal or systematic feedback from contacts may also be useful.

docs.title: Questions to ask about your current data
docs.text:
• Do you have an existing CRM?
  • Do you have spreadsheets with information about your contacts, donations or other valuable data?
  • Do you have any post-it notes or file cabinets with information about your community?
  • Does anyone at your organization know a lot about community members?
  • How does money come into your organization?
  • What are the day to day tasks your staff and volunteers carry out?
  • How do you currently communicate with your donors, members, volunteers and other community members? How would you like to communicate with them?
  • How do you track activities and communications (emails, meetings, webinars, other events) that you have with your community?
  • Do you have a list of donors interests and preferences?
  • How do you handle new contacts?
  • What classifications or labels are you using for your existing contacts (ie. alumni, students, parents, major donor, volunteer)?
  • Are there any reports you would like to create? What information will they contain?

CiviCRM is designed to be flexible and adaptable, based on feedback from many different non-profits, but it may not map exactly to the way your organisation currently works. Working the CiviCRM way could mean adapting your workflow and adopting best practices in non-profit technology. Be pragmatic about whether your current working practices need to change.

CiviCRM also offers opportunities to interact with contacts in ways you may not have used before. Taking advantage of those possibilities can lead to positive changes and improvements.

docs.title: Think about the move
docs.text:
It may help to think of your existing data as the contents of a house or apartment before a move. Moving is a chance to ask, “Do we really need this? This stuff is too old; let's trash it and get some new stuff once we have moved in.”

Look for data that no longer serve a purpose, such as organisational divisions you have abandoned or office locations in a facility you no longer occupy. But some old data retain their value. One organisation in a financial pinch used an old list of founding donors who had not given money for many years. Those lapsed donors still had strong emotional ties to the organisation they had founded and came to its financial rescue. In that case, keeping the old data was crucial.

A move is also a chance to clean what you decide to keep. Just as you would not pack dusty picture frames and dirty dishes into a clean new home, clean up your data before moving it into CiviCRM. You can read more about this in the Mapping your data section of this chapter.

Allow time to examine your old data, standardise how elements of contact records are stored (for example, whether states are entered as NY or New York), and delete obvious duplicates, accidental entries, outdated information and corrupted records.

The following chapters explain what data CiviCRM can store and how to map your existing records into CiviCRM’s structure.

docs.title: Creating and managing Profiles
docs.text: Create a Profile and choose its basic and Advanced Settings first. Then add fields and choose their settings. Most settings apply only to particular uses, so you can skip settings that do not apply to your Profile.

docs.title: Create a Profile
docs.text:
1. Go to Administer > Customize Data and Screens > Profiles and click Add Profile.
  2. Set Profile Name to a meaningful name.
  3. For Used For, choose from Standalone Form or Directory; Search Views; Drupal User Registration; and View/Edit Drupal User Account. You can check more than one box. Checking Search Views limits your field choices to Contact and Contact type records only.
  4. Set Order if needed. Lower numbers place Profiles before higher numbers when a page includes more than one Profile. The field is filled in automatically when a Profile is created.
  5. Use Pre-form Help and Post-form Help for guidance that appears before or after the Profile.
  6. Leave Is this CiviCRM Profile Active? checked to make the Profile available for insertion into forms and for the Batch Update function. It is checked automatically. To take a Profile out of use later, edit it and uncheck the box.

docs.title: Advanced settings
docs.text: Click the gray advanced settings bar to show these fields. Not every setting applies to every Profile.

docs.title: Limit listings to a specific group
docs.text:
This setting matters when a Profile displays information on your website, such as in a searchable membership directory.
