Feel like helping translating CiviCRM to a new language or improving the current translation? Here's how to do it (provided you have a bit of a technical background):

  1. Go to Transifex and create an account.
  2. Once you are logged-in, look for your language here and either join a team.
  3. Start translating!

To request a new language, please ask on the translation chat.

docs.title: Team work
docs.text:
The CiviCRM translation work flow is still a work-in-progress and until the process becomes more mature, you should probably refer to this page for the most current instructions.

The work flow is heavily based on teamwork. Hopefully, there is already a team of translators for your language that you can join. This team will have built a glossary, will have started a translation set and will be able to review your translations and give constructive criticism. If such a team does not yet exist, the opportunity is all yours to create one.

docs.title: Components and files
docs.text:
There are quite a lot of strings (phrases) to translate in CiviCRM. To make it easier to translate the part that you are interested in (hopefully the one you know best), the strings that need translation have been divided into components, which are CiviCRM plugins (e.g., CiviCRM core, CiviMail, CiviContribute, etc.). A separate component should be available for each version of CiviCRM, starting with version 3.2 (or 3.1, for language teams that have chosen to do so).

Each component itself contains a number of files, which themselves contain the strings to translate. The main component "CiviCRM" (the core) has close to 20 files (for countries, provinces, menu, etc.).

docs.title: Tools and technical details
docs.text: The process you use to do translation depends on whether you prefer to do translation online or offline. Online translation does not require installation of any software. Offline translation is done with files downloaded from the translation website, using software that offers more features than the online system.

docs.title: Online translation
docs.text:
Transifex is the tool to use for online translation. It does not have as many features as an offline tool such as PoEdit, but it's the easiest way to contribute translations and do the occasional quick correction. Every translator should have an account on the Transifex site, because translation teams can use the forums and messaging system to coordinate their work.

The basic steps in online translation are:

  1. Select a component. This will display the list of language teams for this component.
  2. Click on the icon in the Options column next to the language you are interested in. This brings you to the list of files for this component.
  3. Click on the "pencil and paper" icon. This brings you to the online translation screen, which lists all the translatable strings in this file.
  4. For each string, you can then enter a translation.
  5. When you are finished, you can click on the "Send for review" button at the end of the page.

docs.title: Offline translation
docs.text:
If you do not have a reliable Internet connection, you can also download and translate the files locally on your computer. One of the most common editors is PoEdit, which is free software and has a big community of users. The exact steps in translation using an offline tool depend on your tool of choice, but should follow the following steps:

  1. Download the files from transifex.net you want to translate,
  2. Load the files up in your translation tool and do your translations.
  3. Send them back to the site when you are done.

docs.title: Building a translation memory
docs.text:
PoEdit and other translation software will help you build a translation memory for your language. This translation memory can either be restricted to translations done in CiviCRM, or include translations from other projects. If you include other projects, automatic translation might be able to translate more strings, but you will lose consistency and most strings will be marked as fuzzy. This could be a way to bootstrap a new translation, though.

Building a translation memory based on words from the glossary could go a long way in insuring the consistency of your team's work.

docs.title: Using version control (mostly for programmers)
docs.text: Transifex keeps files in a version control system. This is useful to some users who find interacting with the Github site easier than downloading each file separately from Transifex.

docs.title: Consistency & consensus
docs.text:
To insure a good consistency in the translation, every team is encouraged to build and use a glossary and employ peer review. You can use this glossary of common terms. You definitely should translate these terms to your language, and make sure your team reaches a consensus on all terms.

Building and sharing a common translation memory, which is like a specialized glossary that can be used automatically by translation tools, also helps to insure consistency. The PoEdit help system explains how to build this database (and most other translation software should do the same).

docs.title: Team building and sprints
docs.text:
A good way to make progress in translation is to organize translation sprints. This means getting as many people as possible together in the same room to translate as many documents as they can. Here are a few things to keep in mind when organizing a translation sprint:

  • Choose a good location, where people will be able to get online (enough computers for everybody, or desks to set up laptops and with a decent Internet connection).
  • Provide instructions in advance on how to install an offline translation tool such as PoEdit, and have people ready to help others install and use it.
  • Create the glossary in advance. Present the glossary, discuss terms which do not have consensus, make sure everybody has access to a copy of the glossary, and print a sufficient amount of copies beforehand.
  • Determine goals for the sprint: which component will be translated, and what percentage your team is trying to achieve.
  • Make sub-teams with clear objectives: per component or file or a part of it.
  • If your translators are not familiar with CiviCRM, do a demo of the features your team is about to translate.
  • Clearly designate someone who can be interrupted in order to answer questions.
  • Make sure you've got enough coffee, tea, chocolate, etc. in reserve to keep everybody going through the night.
  • At the end of the sprint, present the result of the translation in a demo CiviCRM installation.
  • Discuss whether the team has reached its goal and how to improve further.

docs.title: The CiviCRM community
docs.text: Like many open source projects, CiviCRM is shaped, guided, and driven by a diverse community of users, developers, and implementers who apply their skills and experiences to improve the software for everyone. Community participation is crucial to the continued success of CiviCRM as an open source CRM empowering nonprofits around the world. This chapter is a guide to finding and engaging with the CiviCRM community.

docs.title: Finding the community online
docs.text:
As might be expected of a web-based software project, much of the CiviCRM community's activity occurs online. This means that if you have access to the Internet you also have access to and can participate in the CiviCRM community regardless of where you live or work. English is the predominant language for discussion and contributions.

The CiviCRM website itself is a good starting point for exploring and participating in the community. In addition to general information about getting and using CiviCRM, you'll find blog posts from community members, announcements about upcoming events, and a Get Involved section that lists and links to many of the resources described below.

The CiviCRM Stack Exchange site is specifically designed for asking and answering questions about CiviCRM. This is now the primary site for getting answers to questions on installing, upgrading, configuring, using and customizing CiviCRM. It is a great place to find answers to the millions of questions that have already been asked about CiviCRM, and to ask ones that haven't been asked already.

CiviCRM Chat (powered by Mattermost) offers live group discussion in chat channels as well as direct messaging. It's a great place to go for technical questions, to learn about general happenings within the community as well as to discover new resources that have been shared by community members.

You'll hopefully find that both Stack Exchange and CiviCRM Chat are great sources for help, support, and good ideas. That's all attributable to the good will and generous efforts of people like you! Everyone who visits these sites is encouraged to give back to the community by responding to questions and requests for help and contributing their own ideas and feedback to the conversations. And simply asking your own questions is also a significant contribution to the community. It's likely that someone else is having the same problems or wondering the same thing, and the responses you solicit help build the community's knowledge base.

The CiviCRM blog is another good source of information and discussion. Blog posts are written by both the CiviCRM core team and other community members and cover a wide range of topics, including general news and announcements, upcoming events and accounts of events that have occurred, case studies, use cases and ways to get things done with CiviCRM, and new features and development. Comments are encouraged and can create lively discussions that can in turn direct future CiviCRM development. If you've got something that you'd like to post on the blog, we encourage you to write to info@civicrm.org with your ideas and your request to post.

docs.title: Finding the community offline
docs.text:
Though the online community is both accessible and active, participating in the CiviCRM community offline can be even more rewarding and can help you connect with others in your area who are developing, implementing, and using CiviCRM.

Many cities and regions hold CiviCRM meetups where people gather to learn about CiviCRM, share new ideas, developments, and use cases, and meet other folks involved with the community. CiviCRM also conducts user and developer training in cities around the world. Stay abreast of local events, whether meetups, trainings, or sprints here.

There are also more formal gatherings for CiviCRM users and developers. CiviCRM held the first CiviCon conference in April 2010 in San Francisco. CiviCon brings together prospective and current end-users, administrators and developers of CiviCRM for content-rich discussions, lectures and networking. The number of CiviCons hosted around the world each year is growing.

CiviCamps are one-day, action packed meetups where you can learn about CiviCRM, connect with other users, ask questions, share tips, and more. See if there are any upcoming CiviCamps near you.

CiviCRM core developers and community members also make appearances at other conferences, including DrupalCon, the NonProfit Technology Conference, Joomla! events, and Aspiration Tech events.

docs.title: Open source = community sourced
docs.text:
Here are some additional ways that you can participate in and contribute to the CiviCRM community.

  • Contribute to CiviCRM documentation. This book was written by community members; you can contribute to it by following the instructions here.
  • Contribute content to CiviCRM's website. You can share use cases and case studies that describe how your organization uses CiviCRM and the solutions and processes you've developed around the software. See existing case studies here. You can also share your successes, experiences at Civi-related events, interesting customizations, etc. on the CiviCRM blog. You can add content by registering with CiviCRM or emailing info@civicrm.org with a request to post.
  • Share your training resources and materials with the rest of the community through posts on the CiviCRM blog or on your own sites.
  • Register your organization on CiviCRM's website. This will add your site to a publicly searchable directory and map of CiviCRM installations, supporting CiviCRM's marketing efforts.
  • Contribute code you've written to extend CiviCRM, because it's likely that someone else out there needs the same functionality. Check out the recommended steps for developing and contributing to the CiviCRM how you can help contribute to the core codebase in the Developer Guide. If you've developed a Drupal module, you should contribute it to Drupal.org; see their site for more information on contributing modules. Joomla! extensions can be posted here.
  • Sponsor development of new features. If your organization needs certain features or functionality that doesn't yet exist for CiviCRM and can't develop those features in-house, you can sponsor their development by outside coders and developers. This can be a solo effort on the part of one organization or a coordinated effort sponsored by multiple organizations in need of the same set of functionality. Find out more on CiviCRM's website or write to info@civicrm.org for more information on sponsoring development.
  • Report any bugs that you find in CiviCRM. See the Bug Reporting chapter of this book for more information.

docs.title: The home dashboard & dashlets
docs.text:
When you first log into CiviCRM, you see the dashboard (CiviCRM Home). It displays information about your site and CiviCRM through “dashlets”: reports you can display on your home dashboard. Many dashlets come with CiviCRM by default, and you or your administrator can create others for your organization.

Examples of dashlets that come with CiviCRM include:

  • Donor Report: A bar graph of the amount of total contributions.
  • Activities: A list of recent activities recorded by CiviCRM. These could include emails sent to constituents, donations made or meetings scheduled in CiviCRM.
  • Membership Report: A table summarising information about Members tracked by CiviCRM, broken out by month. It includes the number of Members of each type, total amounts of payments made and the number of contributions made, among other things.

docs.title: Add and refresh dashlets
docs.text:
Click Configure Your Dashboard to see a list of dashlets. Drag dashlets into the right or left column of your dashboard.

Click Done to save. You will see updates to your dashlets when you log in. To check for more recent changes, click Refresh Dashboard Data to reload each dashlet and pull in new information.

For performance reasons, dashlets are cached. To change how often a dashlet refreshes, edit its report. For example, for the Contribution Summary report:

  1. Go to Reports > Contribution Reports and click Contribution Summary.
  2. Under the Access tab, find Cache dashlet for. If that option is unavailable, first select Available for Dashboard?.
  3. Click Actions > Save.

docs.title: Create a dashlet from a report
docs.text:
Any CiviReport can be made available as a dashlet.

  1. Click Reports > My Reports, then click New Report.
  2. Select the report template you want to use.
  3. Configure the report using the Columns, Sorting and Filters tabs. For example, you can use the “Date Received” filter to show data for “This Quarter” or “This Year”.
  4. Click View results.
  5. Choose Tabular, Bar Chart or Pie Chart from the dropdown to the right of the Actions dropdown.
  6. At the bottom of the Access tab, select Available for Dashboard?. Users with permissions to see that information will be able to add the dashlet. See permissions for more information.
  7. Click Actions > Create Report.

Then add the dashlet to your dashboard:

  1. In the menu, click the CiviCRM logo, then CiviCRM Home.
  2. Click Configure Dashboard. Drag the dashlet from “Available Dashlets” to the column where you want it.
  3. Click Done.

See Reporting for more details on working with reports.

Note

You can now use SearchKit with FormBuilder to add dashlets. See FormBuilder for details.

docs.title: Navigation menu
docs.text:
The navigation menu is a small bar at the top of every CiviCRM “back office” page. It groups major areas of functionality alongside search and administration.

The menu includes:

  • Quick Search — Look up a name, email or other custom fields.
  • Menu Search and Logout — Search the entire CiviCRM menu and log out.
  • Search — Search your CRM data.
  • Contacts — Find, add and manage contacts.
  • Contributions — Search contributions and manage contribution pages.
  • Events — Create and manage event registrations.
  • Mailings — Send bulk emails and view mailing history.
  • Reports — Generate and access reports.
  • Administer — Configure system settings and custom data.

The Quick Search field is at the far left of the navigation menu. See the Searching chapter for more details.

docs.title: Quickly finding menu items
docs.text:
Hover over the CiviCRM logo in the top navigation, next to the quick search bar. A panel appears with a search field and a list of available menu items.

  1. Click the search field.
  2. Type part of a menu item name, such as “display preferences” or “groups”. The list filters to matching items.
  3. Click an item to go directly to its page.

docs.title: Modifying the menu
docs.text:
To add, disable or rearrange menu items, go to Administer > Customize > Navigation Menu.

Note

Changes to the navigation menu are visible to everyone with the appropriate permissions to see the menu. Be careful when modifying it.

docs.title: Message token
docs.text:
Create a token for the form in the “Expose” field. This token allows CiviMail authors to link to the form.

You need to set Autofill to Current User in the Individual tab. But you do not need to "accept Id from URL”. If you do not need it, it is more secure not to "accept Id from URL".

In a message template, you can select the Afform Token with the name of your form. Two tokens are created: URL and Hyperlink.

When the recipient clicks the link, they access the form with the contact’s data populated.

docs.title: Undelete
docs.text:
By default, deleted contacts are sent to the trash. An administrator, or anyone holding the "access deleted contacts" permission, can recover them later.

To restore a contact:

  1. Go to Advanced Search, enter the contact’s details, and check the Search in Trash box at the bottom of the Basic Criteria section.
  2. From the results, use the Restore link at the end of the contact’s row. Alternatively, choose Restore contacts from the action drop-down menu.

If you are sure you no longer need a particular contact, you can delete them permanently.

You can disable the trash function in Administer > System Settings > Misc (Undelete, PDFs, Limits, Logging, etc.)

docs.title: Creating custom data entry forms
docs.text: Your organisation can design custom forms to collect information from members, supporters, or staff. Using CiviCRM's form tool FormBuilder, you can build interactive forms for manual data entry, such as creating new contacts or logging specific activities, without needing any technical knowledge.

docs.title: Create a new data entry form
docs.text:
1. Look for the New Submission Form button at the top of the FormBuilder interface.
  2. Click the small downward-pointing arrow to the right of the button text. This reveals a dropdown menu listing the types of items (entities) you can collect data for, such as Activities, Contacts, Cases, etc.
  3. Click the type of item you want your form to create. CiviCRM will automatically open the form design workspace.

docs.title: Set up your form's settings
docs.text: The form workspace is split into two halves. Use the configuration pane on the left side to define how your form behaves, where it lives, and who can see it.

docs.title: Choose who can use the form
docs.text:
Under the Form Settings section, locate the Permission dropdown. Choose the rule that matches your specific purpose - the following three are :

  • The default option is Access CiviCRM backend and API, which means that all users with access to CiviCRM will be able to access the form.
  • Select Generic: Allow any authenticated contact if you want to limit entries to supporters who are logged into your website or accessing the form via a verified email link.
  • Select Generic: Anyone with secret link if you intend to share this form strictly via direct, private email invitations.
  • Select Generic: Allow all users (including anonymous) if the form is public and open to anyone on your website (such as a generic sign-up page).

docs.title: Publish the form to your website
docs.text:
To make your form a standalone page that people can visit:

  1. Scroll down to the Placement options on the left pane.
  2. In the Page Route box, type a clear web path starting with civicrm/ (for example, civicrm/volunteer-signup).
  3. Check the box labeled Accessible on front-end of web site to ensure regular visitors can view the page.
  4. If you want this form to be easily found by your staff, check the option to add the form directly to your CiviCRM navigation menu.

docs.title: Add fields and layout elements
docs.text:
Once your settings are configured, use the second tab in the left-hand configuration pane to add content fields to your form layout. This tab lists the standard fields and custom fields relevant to the entity type you chose, for example 'Inidividual 1'.

  1. Browse the list of available fields in the left pane.
  2. Click and hold the field you want to use, then drag it over to the layout view on the right side of the screen.
  3. Release your mouse button to drop the field into place. You can drag fields up and down to change their order.
  4. Click the small Settings icon directly on any field in the layout pane to customize its specific behavior, like changing the text label or making it a required field.
  5. To structure your form, look under the Elements list in the left pane. Drag and drop structural blocks, text containers, or HTML areas to add instructions and section breaks for your users.

docs.title: Additional permissions
docs.text:
Each entity tab on the left-hand configuration pane also has additional options and settings. For example, if you are building a form to capture information for an Individual, these would be the options:

  • Individual 1: Security: you can choose whether the autofill options work based on the form permissions or the user's permissions
  • Individual 1: Autofill: There are a list of option, for example Current User or the Contact being Viewed.
  • Individual 1: Allowed Actions: The options are create, update or both.
  • Individual 1: Accept ID from URL: If 'Update' is specified for allowed actions, it is possible to pull the ID from the URL to autofill the fields.

docs.title: Save and review your form
docs.text:
When your layout looks correct and all settings are complete:

  1. Click the Save button in the upper-right area of the screen.
  2. Once saved, a View button will appear next to your saving options. Click it to preview exactly how your live form will look to users, and to copy its website link for distribution.

docs.title: Create a donation form with FormBuilder
docs.text:
This example describes how to use FormBuilder to create a public Donation form. It allows you to create flexible online donation forms that do not follow the strict layout of the core Contribution forms.

Note

This example assumes the Stripe Payment Processor is already installed. See the Stripe Extension documentation. Other payment processors are available as FormBuilder Checkout Options.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the form
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Administer > Customize Data and Screens > FormBuilder.
  2. On the Submission Forms tab, click New Submission Form link.
  3. The form will automatically include the Individual and some fields (first name and last name). At the top of the Form, click the + symbol and choose Participant to enable the individual to register for an event.

docs.title: Step 2: Form settings
docs.text:
Use the configuration pane on the left side to configure the following settings for your form:

  • Title: Make a Donation
  • Permission: Change to Allow all users (including anonymous).
  • Page Route: give the form a public URL, such as civicrm/support-us

Note

There is already a packaged form called New Donation with the URL civicrm/donate so you'll need to edit that form if you want your donation page to use that URL. There is more information about this on the Contribution Forms page.

  • Frontend or Backend: Choose the Frontend option so the form can be accessed by members of the public.
  • Post-Submit (Optional): If you wish to redirect people to a specific page after the form has been submitted, add the full web link (e.g., https://example.com) to the Post-Submit text box. Alternatively, add a confirmation message to be displayed when. they submit the form. Make sure you save the message if you add a confirmation message.

docs.title: Step 3: Add the form fields
docs.text:
1. At the top of the Form, click the + symbol and choose Contribution. This creates a new tab called Contribution 1. In the configuration pane on the left side, under Values, set the following values:
    • For the Contact field, remove ‘Select Current User’ and change to Individual 1.
    • Then click the Add Value select list and choose Checkout Option. This will add Checkout Option as a Value. Choose the Stripe Embedded Checkout option from the drop-down.
  2. In the Add column, select Checkout Details and drag it onto the Contribution 1 section on the form Layout.
  3. On the Contribution 1 section on the right panel, click the settings wheel for Contribution Source and choose Remove field.
  4. Click back on the Individual 1 tab on the left panel. In the Add column, select Contact Email(s) and drag it onto the Individual 1 section on the form Layout. Configure the Email block as follows:
    • Toggle the word Multiple so it changes to Single,
    • select is Primary,
    • select a Location type.
  5. While still on the Individual 1 tab, scroll down to Duplicate Matching. Choose the appropriate Duplicate Matching rule, the default is ‘Email (reserved)’.
  6. In the right pane, click the settings wheel symbol on each field in the form Layout and tick the Required option.

Tip

You can also rename each Fieldset or Field, change background colors, and adjust other layout options by clicking the settings wheel symbols. On the Individual 1 tab, you can choose any other individual fields, such as address or phone number, and drag them onto the Individual 1 section on the form Layout.

docs.title: Step 5: Save and access the form
docs.text:
1. Click the Save button at the top right of the form screen.
  2. Once saved, a View Page link will appear next to the Save button. This is the link you will share with members of the public so they can register for the event.

The form can now be tested and adjusted as needed.

docs.title: Example: use FormBuilder to create an event booking form with online payment
docs.text:
This example shows how to use FormBuilder to create a public form that lets people book onto a CiviCRM event with an online payment. It allows you to create flexible event booking forms that do not follow the strict layout of the core Event booking forms.

Note

This example assumes the Stripe Payment Processor is installed on your CiviCRM system. See the Stripe Extension documentation. Other payment processors are available as FormBuilder Checkout Options.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the event
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Administer > Events > New Event.
  2. Create a New Event with a Title ‘Christmas Fundraiser’, Start date and time, Event type, and a default role of attendee. On the Fees tab, add the required Fee options with labels and amounts. Then Save the event.

docs.title: Step 2: Create the form
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Administer > Customize Data and Screens > FormBuilder.
  2. On the Submission Forms tab, click New Submission Form link.
  3. The form will automatically include the Individual and some fields (first name and last name). At the top of the Form, click the + symbol and choose Participant to enable the individual to register for an event.

docs.title: Step 3: Configure form settings
docs.text:
Use the configuration pane on the left side to configure these settings:

  • Title: Register For Our Christmas Fundraiser.
  • Permission: Change to Allow all users (including anonymous).
  • Page Route: Give the form a public URL, such as civicrm/christmasfundraiser.
  • Frontend or Backend: Choose the Frontend option so the form can be accessed by members of the public.
  • Post-Submit (Optional): To redirect people to a specific page after the form has been submitted, add the full web link (e.g., https://example.com) to the Post-Submit text box. Alternatively, add a confirmation message to display when they submit the form. Make sure you save the message if you add a confirmation message.

docs.title: Step 4: Add the form fields
docs.text:
1. At the top of the Form, click the + symbol and choose Participant.
  2. Then, at the top of the form, click the + symbol and choose Contribution. This creates a new tab called Contribution 1, which allows you to add contribution fields.
  3. Click the Participant 1 tab. In the configuration pane on the left side, under Values, set the following values:
    • For the Contact field, remove ‘Select Current User’ and change to Individual 1.
    • For Event, choose the event you created in Step 1.
    • For Status, choose Pending (incomplete transaction).
  4. In the Add column, select Contribution Amount:Christmas Fundraiser and drag it onto the Participant 1 section on the form Layout. This adds the Fee options for the event to the form.
  5. Click the Contribution 1 tab. In the configuration pane on the left side, under Values, set the following values:
    • For the Contact field, remove ‘Select Current User’ and change to Individual 1.
    • Click the Add Value select list and choose Checkout Option. This adds Checkout Option as a Value. Choose the Stripe Embedded Checkout option from the drop-down.
  6. In the Add column, select Checkout Details and drag it onto the Contribution 1 section on the form Layout.
  7. On the Contribution 1 section on the right panel, click the settings wheel by both fields Contribution Amount and Contribution Source and choose Remove field for both.
  8. Click back on the Individual 1 tab on the left panel. In the Add column, select Contact Email(s) and drag it onto the Individual 1 section on the form Layout. Configure the Email block as follows:
    • Toggle the word Multiple so it changes to Single.
    • Select is Primary.
    • Select a Location type.
  9. While still on the Individual 1 tab, scroll down to Duplicate Matching. Choose the appropriate Duplicate Matching rule; the default is ‘Email (reserved)’.
  10. In the right pane, click the settings wheel symbol on each field in the form Layout and tick the Required option.

Tip

You can also rename each Fieldset or Field, change background colors, and adjust other layout options by clicking the settings wheel symbols. On the Individual 1 tab, you can choose any other individual fields, such as address or phone number, and drag them onto the Individual 1 section on the form Layout.

docs.title: Step 5: Save and access the form
docs.text:
1. Click the Save button at the top right of the form screen.
  2. Once saved, a View Page link will appear next to the Save button. This is the link you will share with members of the public so they can register for the event.

The form can now be tested and adjusted as needed.

docs.title: Create a membership signup form with online payment
docs.text:
Use FormBuilder to create a public membership signup form with online payment. This lets you create flexible membership booking forms that do not follow the strict layout of the core Contribution Pages.

Note

This example assumes the Stripe Payment Processor is installed on your CiviCRM system. See the Stripe Extension documentation. Other payment processors are available as FormBuilder Checkout Options.

docs.title: 1. Create the membership type
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Administer > Membership > Membership Types.
  2. Ensure you have a suitable membership Type. For more information, see Membership Types.

docs.title: 2. Create the form
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Administer > Customize Data and Screens > FormBuilder.
  2. On the Submission Forms tab, select New Submission Form.

docs.title: 3. Configure the form settings
docs.text:
Use the configuration pane on the left side to configure these settings:

  • Title: Join As A New Member.
  • Permission: Change to Allow all users (including anonymous).
  • Page Route: Give the form a public URL, such as civicrm/christmasfundraiser.
  • Frontend or Backend: Choose Frontend so members of the public can access the form.
  • Post-Submit (Optional): To redirect people to a specific page after they submit the form, add the full web link (e.g., https://example.com) to the Post-Submit text box. Alternatively, add a confirmation message to display when they submit the form. Make sure you save the message if you add one.

docs.title: 4. Add the form fields
docs.text:
1. At the top of the Form, click the + symbol and choose Membership. This creates a new tab called Membership 1.
  2. On the Membership 1 tab, under Values in the configuration pane on the left side:
    • Click the down symbol and choose Individual 1.
    • Click the Add Value select list and choose Membership Type. This lets you set a default value for the Membership Type. Choose the correct Membership Type for the form.
    • Click the Add Value select list and choose Status. Click on Status and choose Pending.
    • Click the Add Value select list and choose Contribution Amount: Membership Amount. Choose the Membership Amount required for the form.
  3. At the top of the form, click the + symbol and choose Contribution. This creates a new tab called Contribution 1, where you can add contribution fields.
  4. On the Contribution 1 tab, under Values in the configuration pane on the left side:
    • For Contact under the Values subheading, remove ‘Select Current User’ and change to Individual 1.
    • Click the Add Value select list and choose Checkout Option. This adds Checkout Option as a Value. Choose Stripe Embedded Checkout.
  5. In the Add column, select Checkout Details and drag it onto the Contribution 1 section on the form Layout. Click the settings wheel by both Contribution Amount and Contribution Source, and choose Remove field.
  6. Return to the Individual 1 tab on the left panel. In the Add column, select Contact Email(s) and drag it onto the Individual 1 section on the form Layout. Configure the Email block:
    • Toggle Multiple so it changes to Single.
    • Select is Primary.
    • Select a Location type.
  7. On the Individual 1 tab, scroll down to Duplicate Matching. Choose the appropriate Duplicate Matching rule; the default is ‘Email (reserved)’.
  8. In the right pane, click the settings wheel symbol on each field in the form Layout and tick Required.

Tip

You can also rename each Fieldset or Field, change background colors, and adjust other layout options by clicking the settings wheel symbols. On the Individual 1 tab, you can choose any other individual fields, such as address or phone number, and drag them onto the Individual 1 section on the form Layout.

docs.title: 5. Save and access the form
docs.text:
1. Click Save at the top right of the form screen.
  2. Once saved, a View Page link appears next to the Save button. This is the link you will share with members of the public so they can register for the event.

The form can now be tested and adjusted as needed.

docs.title: Creating a custom autocomplete search list
docs.text:
Create a filtered list of existing records with extra details, such as a street address, to help your team identify the right person in a dropdown list.

For example, if you organize an event, you might want to assign certain activities only to contacts with the Volunteer subtype. Showing each volunteer’s name, street, and city in the dropdown can help users choose the right person.

docs.title: Create your search list
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Search in your main CiviCRM menu and click on SearchKit.
  2. Click the New Search button.
  3. In the Search for field, choose Contact (or another specific record type you need to display, such as volunteers).
  4. Use the Where section to filter the list if you only want specific people to appear, such as those matching availability, age, or group membership criteria.

docs.title: Set up the autocomplete display
docs.text:
1. Click the + Add button on the left-hand side and choose Autocomplete.
  2. Put your main searchable field—usually the contact's name—first in the list layout.
  3. Add informative fields below it, such as Street Address and City. These appear alongside the name in the dropdown to help users distinguish people with similar names.
  4. Select an Ascending sort order for the contact name field to display the list alphabetically.
  5. Give the autocomplete display a clear name and save your progress.

docs.title: Add the autocomplete field to a form
docs.text: After creating the autocomplete list in SearchKit, add it to a form using FormBuilder.

docs.title: Add the contact field
docs.text:
1. Open your desired form layout in FormBuilder.
  2. Find the Existing Contact field under Add in the left-hand panel.
  3. Click and drag the Existing Contact field onto the form canvas where you want it to appear.

docs.title: Connect your custom autocomplete list
docs.text:
1. Click the settings wheel for the Existing Contact field on the form canvas to open its properties panel.
  2. If relevant, change the Type to Autocomplete.
  3. Under the Saved Search drop-down, select the custom search list and autocomplete display you created.

docs.title: Configure the field settings
docs.text:
1. Check Required if your team must select a record before submitting the form.
  2. Turn on Auto-open so the dropdown expands when someone clicks inside the field.
  3. Choose the appropriate permission type:
  4. Choose Form-based for most standard administrative forms where anyone filling out the form should be able to see the full list of options.
  5. Choose User-based if your organisation uses Access Control Lists (ACLs) to limit which contacts staff members can view based on their user accounts.
  6. Save your form changes.

docs.title: Pre-filling forms and using secret links
docs.text: To make your forms quicker to fill out and encourage higher response rates, your organisation can create personalized, pre-filled form links. By utilizing URL parameters or specialized security settings, you can pass known default information safely to your users or let them fill out personal records securely without requiring a standard user account login.

docs.title: Set defaults using URL parameters
docs.text:
You can automatically fill out specific text or choice selections on a submission form when a user lands on the page by attaching parameters directly to your form's web link.

  1. Identify the field key names you have used in your FormBuilder setup.
  2. Build your sharing link by taking your form's published page route and adding a question mark, followed by the field key and the desired default text. For example: https://yourorganisation.org/civicrm/volunteer-signup?status=interested
  3. To specify precise dates in a URL default parameter, format the value without spaces or special symbols using one of the following variations:
  4. receive_date=2026-06-30
  5. receive_date=20260630
  6. receive_date=20260630105600 (to specify exact hour, minute, and second values)
  7. Relative dates: receive_date=this.month

(See the list)

docs.title: Configure forms for secret access links
docs.text:
If you want to send form links to contacts via email that dynamically identify who they are—similar to standard CiviCRM checksum behavior—you must adjust your form permissions to support secure anonymous access.

  1. Navigate to Administer > Customize Data and Screens > FormBuilder and open your form.
  2. In the left-side Form Settings pane, click the Permission selection box.
  3. Select Generic: Anyone with secret link. This configuration explicitly signals to CiviCRM that the incoming web traffic will only be authorized if it arrives with a unique security token attached to the link.
  4. Under the Placement section, find the Expose To setting and select Message Tokens. This makes your form visible as an interactive mail-merge selection when designing broadcast communications.

docs.title: Generate and distribute the secret link
docs.text:
Once the form permissions are ready, you can insert individual secret links dynamically into bulk mailings or workflow templates.

  1. Go to your mailings manager or template builder to write a message to your supporters.
  2. Open the Tokens list in your message composer editor.
  3. Locate your newly created form in the token list. Because you exposed the form to "Message Tokens" in FormBuilder, it will appear as a selectable merge choice.
  4. Insert the token into your email text or as the destination address for a "Update Your Info" button.
  5. When CiviCRM sends out the final email delivery, it automatically replaces that token with a uniquely generated, encrypted link for each recipient. When clicked, the link matches the recipient to their database profile and safely pre-populates their existing records without exposing your system to general public tampering.

docs.title: Types of forms
docs.text: The main FormBuilder page has several tabs:

docs.title: Submission Forms
docs.text:
Use FormBuilder to design custom forms that collect information from members, supporters, or staff. You can build interactive forms for manual data entry, such as creating new contacts or logging specific activities, without needing technical knowledge.

For more details, see creating data entry forms.

docs.title: Search Forms
docs.text:
You can connect existing SearchKit configurations directly to FormBuilder to create a directory, volunteer portal, or internal search page tailored to specific criteria. Users can then filter CiviCRM records on a dedicated screen.

For more details, see the searching and reporting pages.

docs.title: Field Blocks
docs.text: Field Blocks are reusable templates for submission forms. By default, CiviCRM has a field block for items that can have more than one, including addresses, emails, and notes, plus a block for each custom field set. You can edit these blocks to suit your site's needs.

docs.title: What is FormBuilder
docs.text:
FormBuilder is a form design workspace for creating custom forms to capture and store information from members, supporters, or staff.

It can also be connected to SearchKit to create a directory, a volunteer portal, or an internal search page tailored to specific criteria.

docs.title: Enabling FormBuilder
docs.text: The extension can be enabled on the extensions page if not already installed. Once enabled, a FormBuilder link will appear in the menu under Administer > Customize Data and Screens.

docs.title: Editing permissions
docs.text:
There are two permissions for controlling who can create and edit new forms:

  • FormBuilder: edit and delete forms
  • FormBuilder: edit and delete own forms

docs.title: User permissions
docs.text:
You can control who can see a form in the settings for each individual form. If a form is used to display a SearchKit display, you can also control which results are displayed, depending on the user.

This is explained in more detail under SearchKit permissions.

docs.title: Popular extensions
docs.text:
These are widely used extensions in the relevant category of the official CiviCRM Extensions Directory. Usage is a popularity signal, not a compatibility or suitability guarantee.

  • Extended Contact Matcher (XCM) — reported usage: 1,089
  • Action Provider — reported usage: 898
  • Mailchimp CiviCRM Integration — reported usage: 818
  • Form Processor — reported usage: 716
  • Data Processor — reported usage: 551

All extensions for this component

Check development status, current CiviCRM compatibility, CMS requirements, and release notes before installation.

Usage snapshot reviewed: 2026-10-13.

docs.title: Translating CiviCRM
docs.text: CiviCRM is written with English-language code and strings for display. Using, Transifex CiviCRM is able to translate the entire interface into dozens of different languages for the use of many different organizations worldwide. Each local language can be installed locally, and then CiviCRM is able to use this base.

docs.title: Localizing CiviCRM
docs.text:
After completing your initial setup of CiviCRM you should be able to further configure your instance with regional settings.

The Localization screen (shown in the following screenshot) lets an administrator select the right locale for the language and country of the organization using CiviCRM. Go to: Administer > Configure > Global Settings > Localization.

docs.title: Translating Your CiviCRM
docs.text:
CiviCRM accommodates different languages, however the developers rely on the community to translate the text displayed where translations are missing or a specific language is not integrated.

Presently, there are several different ways to translate your own custom labels and strings into the languages you wish. We are aiming to migrate this all into one system eventually.

  • FormBuilder
  • Custom Fields and Profiles
  • Option Values and Groups

docs.title: Mapping Languages to Specific Regional Translations
docs.text:
In some cases, you might want to properly map the language you have added to CiviCRM to a more localized version. A common example is that of Canadian French being much different than that of French from France.

To use fr_CA instead of fr_FR (for France French), which is the default you can modify your civicrm.settings.php file with the following code.

  define('CIVICRM_LANGUAGE_MAPPING_FR', 'fr_CA');

See CRM-9558 for more information.

docs.title: Technical
docs.text:
As a basic understanding the way that words are retrieved are as the following:

  1. The system takes the existing string within a translation call (in English)
  2. It checks the current language of the user, and then if it's different than the default (English US) that all strings are referenced against it will attempt to find the appropriate translation.
  3. It first scours the .mo files that are downloaded and installed for different languages
  4. If no matching translation is found, it will then attempting to lookup the strings from the translation repository, and if none are found there it will then continue to look for the strings within the particular (older) translation columns for each custom field and/or option value/group

docs.title: What if I notice strings are not translated
docs.text:
If it's within a custom extension then normally you can contact the author, and propose translations.

CiviCRM is also built by volunteers and we encourage the community to provide translations via the online translation tool Transifex to find out about your language of interest. Download and install it on your CiviCRM installation to find out how well it will suit your needs.

More information can be found here.

docs.title: Translating profiles
docs.text: Profiles work similarly to Custom Fields, with one caveat: if you do not change the default Label, Description, Pre/Post help text, the profile uses the translation already available in core or in the previously translated Custom field.

docs.title: Translating labels
docs.text:
If you change the labels of fields added to a Profile, translate them as follows:

  1. Go to Administrator > Customize Data and Screens > Profiles.
  2. Click the Fields link for the Profile you want to translate.
  3. Click the Edit link for a Field. In this example, First Name has been changed to Your Name.

  4. Click the corresponding translate button. In the popup, translate the label or value.

  5. Click Save.

  6. Repeat the process for the other fields whose default labels you modified.
  7. View the profile in another language to see the fields with your translations.

docs.title: Translating custom fields and groups
docs.text: You can translate existing custom fields and custom groups. After a field has been added, the interface lets you add translations. By default, it normally copies the original labels and values from the default language to the additional languages.

docs.title: Translating a custom field
docs.text:
Note: This process assumes you have already set up a multilingual system.

  1. Go to Administrator > Customize Data and Screens > Custom Fields.
  2. Edit the Custom Group you want to translate.
  3. For each custom field, click the Edit Field link.

  4. Click the corresponding translate button.

  5. In the popup, translate the label or value.

  6. Click Save.

  7. Repeat the process for the other translation options and additional fields.
  8. View the group in another language to see the fields with your translations.

docs.title: Translating a custom group
docs.text: Follow the same process as for Custom fields, but click the Settings link for the Custom Group. You can translate any fields that have the same language button.

docs.title: Translating FormBuilder
docs.text:
As of 6.10, you are able to use the new FormBuilder for labels, and other fields. Normally, during the upgrade the strings should be populated into the new translation system, but I will give instructions on how to go through the entire process.

Note: This process assumes you have already setup a multilingual system.

docs.title: Build your form
docs.text:
1. Go to Administer > Customize Data and Screens > FormBuilder.
  2. Edit your Form.
  3. Make changes to any of the labels, options, and/or descriptions to the Form fields.
  4. Click Save.

The strings from this Form will now have been saved into the new translation repository.

Note: Only labels that are changes to the field label, options and/or descriptions are saved, as the default translations are used when not modified.

docs.title: Translate your form
docs.text:
Each time a new language is added there is now a corresponding translation repository for each different language that is used presently by FormBuilder, Searchkit (soon), and Scheduled Reminders.

  1. Go to Administer > Locations > Translations to yourlanguage (where yourlanguage will be any of the languages presently installed).

  1. Click on the + in order to translate to another language.

docs.title: Technical details
docs.text:
• FormBuilder will search for the appropriate translations in the translation system, and then check internal or extension translation files (.po files) next. This gives us an opportunity to make specific translations for individual fields on each Form on a case-by-case basis and ensure that they are respected if setup by the user.
  • A majority of the strings in FormBuilder can be translated, such as: options, titles, custom text, pre/post text, and labels.
  • If you find a string that should be translated that is not, please open a ticket here.

docs.title: Translate option values and groups
docs.text: When you create new Pricesets or Option Values in a multilingual system, you also need to translate them.

docs.title: Translate option values
docs.text:
Note: This process assumes you have already set up a multilingual system.

  1. Go to Administrator > Customize Data and Screens > Dropdown Options.
  2. Find the specific Option group you want to modify and click Edit Options.
  3. Click the Edit link for an option. Within the Label, click the translation button.

  1. A popup will appear where you can translate the label.

  1. Click Save after translating.
  2. Repeat the process for the other options.
  3. View the group in another language to see the fields with your translations.

docs.title: Translate an option group
docs.text: This process is similar to translating an Option value. Click the Settings link to modify the corresponding Group Title and Description.
